questions.prompt: Which of the following antibody classes is the strongest activator of the complement cascade?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA mainly protects mucous membranes and does not activate the classical complement pathway well.
Incorrect. IgD sits on B cells and does not activate complement.
Incorrect. IgE is involved in allergies and parasites, not complement activation.
Incorrect. IgG can activate complement, but it needs several molecules together, so it is weaker than IgM.
Correct. IgM's five-unit shape lets a single molecule activate complement strongly.

questions.advancedExplanation: The classical complement pathway begins when C1q binds the Fc regions of antibody already bound to antigen. C1q is a hexameric, bouquet-shaped molecule with six globular heads, and it must engage at least two Fc regions simultaneously to be activated. That geometric requirement is the whole answer. Secreted IgM is a pentamer — five monomeric units joined by a J chain and disulfide bonds — so it presents ten Fc-containing heavy chain pairs clustered in one place. A single IgM molecule bound to a surface can therefore satisfy C1q's two-site requirement by itself. In its antigen-bound "staple" conformation, one IgM is enough to initiate the cascade. IgG (D) does fix complement, and IgG1 and IgG3 do it well, but IgG is a monomer with only one Fc region. Two IgG molecules must land close enough on the antigen surface for C1q to bridge them, which requires high antigen density and far more antibody. Molecule for molecule, IgM is on the order of a thousand times more efficient. The remaining classes do not activate the classical pathway at all. IgA (A) is the mucosal antibody, functioning chiefly by neutralization and immune exclusion; it does not fix complement classically (it can weakly engage the alternative pathway), which is deliberate — a complement-driven inflammatory response on every mucosal surface would be ruinous. IgD (B) is a B-cell surface receptor with essentially no known effector function. IgE (C) binds FcεRI on mast cells and basophils to trigger degranulation and defend against helminths. This also explains why IgM — the first antibody produced in a primary response, before class switching and affinity maturation — is so useful despite its low per-site affinity: its ten binding sites give enormous avidity, and its complement-fixing power compensates for the immature response.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgM. The complement system is a group of proteins in the blood that help kill germs. To start the 'classical' complement pathway, a complement protein called C1 must grab onto at least two antibody tails sitting close together on a germ.

IgM is shaped like a star made of five antibodies stuck together (a pentamer). One IgM bound to a germ already has many tails side by side, so it can start complement by itself. IgG can also start complement, but several separate IgG molecules must line up close together, so it is weaker at this. IgA, IgD, and IgE do not activate the classical pathway well.

Big idea: the five antibody classes have different shapes and jobs. IgM is the first antibody made in an infection and is great at activating complement.

questions.prompt: Which class of antibodies can form multimers? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Correct. IgA forms dimers (2 units) in secretions like mucus and breast milk.
Incorrect. IgD is always a single unit.
Incorrect. IgE is always a single unit.
Incorrect. IgG is always a single unit.
Correct. IgM forms pentamers (5 units) in the blood.

questions.advancedExplanation: Only two of the five classes polymerize, and both do so using the J (joining) chain, a small polypeptide made by plasma cells that links monomer units through their tailpiece cysteines. IgM (E) is secreted as a pentamer (occasionally a hexamer without J chain), giving ten antigen-binding sites. The payoff is avidity: individual IgM binding sites have relatively low affinity because IgM is produced early, before somatic hypermutation has refined the response, but ten simultaneous weak grips hold tightly. This also makes IgM an excellent agglutinator — the basis of ABO blood typing, since anti-A and anti-B isohemagglutinins are IgM. IgA (A) is a monomer in serum but is secreted across mucosal surfaces as a dimer (sometimes trimer or tetramer), joined by a J chain. The dimer binds the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor on the basolateral surface of mucosal epithelium, is transcytosed, and is released at the apical surface still wrapped in a cleaved fragment of that receptor called the secretory component — which protects it from the proteases abundant in gut, airway, and breast milk. IgA is the most abundantly produced antibody in the body by mass, precisely because mucosal surfaces are vast. IgD (B), IgE (C), and IgG (D) exist only as monomers. IgG is the most abundant antibody in serum and the only class that crosses the placenta, via FcRn, conferring passive immunity to the newborn — a function that depends on its small monomeric size. IgE is a monomer held on mast cell surfaces by FcεRI. A subtlety: membrane-bound IgM on a naive B cell's surface is a monomer; only the secreted form pentamerizes. The question asks what the classes "can form," so IgM counts.
questions.explanation:
The answers are IgA and IgM. A multimer is a molecule made of several units joined together. Most antibodies are single Y-shaped units (monomers).

IgM forms a pentamer (5 units) when it is released into the blood. IgA forms a dimer (2 units) when it is released into mucus, tears, saliva, and breast milk. A small piece called the J chain holds these units together. IgD, IgE, and IgG are always single units.

Big idea: an antibody's shape affects its job. Having several units lets IgM and IgA grab more germs at once and clump them together.

questions.prompt: Immunoglobulin classes are defined by:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The variable regions decide what the antibody binds, not its class.
Incorrect. The light chain constant region does not decide the class.
Incorrect. There are only two light chain types (kappa and lambda), and they are found in every class.
Incorrect. The heavy chain variable region helps decide what the antibody binds, not its class.
Correct. The heavy chain constant region decides whether an antibody is IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, or IgD.

questions.advancedExplanation: An antibody is built from two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. Each chain has a variable region at the N-terminus, which with its hypervariable complementarity-determining regions forms the antigen-binding site, and a constant region, which forms the Fc portion and determines what the antibody does after it binds. The five classes — IgM, IgD, IgG, IgA, IgE — correspond to the five heavy chain constant region isotypes: μ, δ, γ, α, and ε, encoded by distinct constant-region gene segments downstream of the variable region in the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. Everything that distinguishes the classes functionally flows from the constant region: whether the antibody can bind C1q and fix complement, whether it can be transported across placenta (FcRn) or mucosa (pIgR), whether it binds FcεRI on mast cells, whether it can polymerize with a J chain, and which Fc receptors on phagocytes it engages for opsonization. This is also why class switch recombination works the way it does. An activated B cell can change its heavy chain constant region — swapping μ for γ or α — while keeping the identical rearranged variable region. The result is an antibody with exactly the same antigen specificity but a completely different effector function. That would be impossible if class were defined by any variable-region feature, which is what makes A and D wrong: the hypervariable regions determine specificity, not class, and two IgG antibodies against different antigens are both still IgG. Light chains (B, C) come in only two types, kappa and lambda, and a light chain of either type can pair with any heavy chain isotype. Light chain type is therefore independent of class and cannot define it — though it does have a clinical use: a skewed kappa:lambda ratio signals a monoclonal plasma cell population, and free light chains in urine are Bence Jones proteins in multiple myeloma.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the heavy chain constant region. An antibody is shaped like a Y. It is made of two long 'heavy' chains and two short 'light' chains. The tips of the Y are the variable regions, which change from antibody to antibody so each one can grab a different germ. The rest of the antibody is the constant region.

The constant part of the heavy chain decides the antibody's class: IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, or IgD. It is like the handle of a tool: it decides how the antibody behaves, such as whether it activates complement or sticks to mast cells. The variable regions decide what the antibody grabs, not its class. Light chains come in only two types and do not set the class.

Big idea: an antibody has two jobs. The variable tips recognize a specific target, and the heavy-chain constant region decides what happens next.

questions.prompt: Which of the following applies to the innate immune system? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are made by B cells, part of the adaptive immune system.
Correct. Skin and mucous membranes are innate barriers.
Correct. Fever is an innate, whole-body defense.
Incorrect. Memory cells are part of the adaptive immune system.
Correct. Pattern recognition receptors let innate cells detect common features of germs.

questions.advancedExplanation: The innate immune system is fast (minutes to hours), germline-encoded, non-specific in the sense that it recognizes broad molecular classes rather than individual antigens, and — critically — it generates no immunological memory. The adaptive system is slow on first exposure (days), uses somatically rearranged receptors of exquisite specificity, and remembers. Barriers (B) are the first line and purely innate: intact skin with its keratinized stratum corneum and acidic mantle, mucous membranes and the mucociliary escalator, gastric acid, lysozyme in tears and saliva, antimicrobial peptides such as defensins, and the competitive exclusion provided by normal flora. None of this requires prior exposure. Fever (C) is an innate systemic response. Macrophages encountering a pathogen release the endogenous pyrogens IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α; these act on the organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis to raise prostaglandin E₂ in the hypothalamus, which resets the thermoregulatory set point. Elevated temperature impairs replication of many pathogens, sequesters iron, and accelerates immune cell function. Pattern recognition receptors (E) are the definitional molecular feature of innate immunity. Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors, RIG-I-like receptors, and others are germline-encoded and recognize PAMPs — pathogen-associated molecular patterns such as LPS, peptidoglycan, flagellin, double-stranded RNA, and unmethylated CpG DNA. These are conserved structures essential to microbes and absent from the host, which is why a fixed set of receptors can cover an enormous range of pathogens. Antibodies (A) are the defining product of adaptive humoral immunity, made by plasma cells derived from B cells whose receptors were generated by V(D)J recombination (see #59). Memory cells (D) are the defining feature of adaptive immunity — the reason vaccines work and the reason a second exposure produces a faster, stronger, higher-affinity response. Including either would collapse the distinction the question is testing. (Recent work on "trained immunity" shows innate cells can be epigenetically primed, but that is beyond the intended scope.)
questions.explanation:
The answers are barriers, fever, and pattern recognition receptors. The innate immune system is the defense you are born with. It acts fast and treats all germs in a similar way. It has no memory of past infections.

Barriers such as skin and mucous membranes keep germs out. Fever raises body temperature to slow germ growth. Pattern recognition receptors (like Toll-like receptors) let innate cells spot common features shared by many germs. Antibodies and memory cells belong to the adaptive immune system, which learns to recognize specific germs and remembers them.

Big idea: innate immunity is fast and general; adaptive immunity is slower, specific, and has memory.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a cytokine?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chemokines are cytokines that attract immune cells.
Correct. Endorphins are natural painkillers from the nervous system, not immune messengers.
Incorrect. Interferons are cytokines that help fight viruses.
Incorrect. Interleukins are cytokines that pass signals between white blood cells.
Incorrect. Tumor necrosis factor is a cytokine that drives inflammation.

questions.advancedExplanation: Cytokines are small, secreted signaling proteins or glycoproteins — generally under 30 kDa — released by immune and other cells to communicate over short distances in autocrine, paracrine, or endocrine fashion, binding specific cell-surface receptors to regulate immunity, inflammation, and hematopoiesis. The major families are interleukins, interferons, tumor necrosis factors, chemokines, and colony-stimulating factors. Endorphins are not cytokines. They are endogenous opioid neuropeptides — β-endorphin, enkephalins, dynorphins — cleaved from precursors such as proopiomelanocortin and released by the pituitary and CNS neurons. They bind μ, δ, and κ opioid receptors to produce analgesia and euphoria. They are neuropeptides and hormones, operating in the nervous and endocrine systems rather than as immune signaling molecules. (Neuro-immune crosstalk is real, and opioid receptors appear on some leukocytes, but endorphins are not classified as cytokines.) The four real cytokine families on the list: Chemokines (A) are chemotactic cytokines such as IL-8/CXCL8 and CCL2 that direct leukocyte migration along concentration gradients to sites of infection — CCR5 and CXCR4, the HIV co-receptors in #62, are chemokine receptors. Interferons (C) are antiviral cytokines; type I (α, β) induce an antiviral state in neighboring cells, and type II (IFN-γ) is the principal macrophage-activating cytokine of Th1 immunity. Interleukins (D) are the largest group, originally named for signaling "between leukocytes," now numbering well past 40 — IL-1 and IL-6 drive fever and acute-phase response, IL-2 drives T-cell proliferation, IL-4 drives IgE class switching. Tumor necrosis factors (E) — TNF-α above all — mediate systemic inflammation, fever, and cachexia; TNF inhibitors are mainstays in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. A useful mnemonic for the question's logic: every wrong option ends in a word describing an immune signaling role, while "endorphin" is a contraction of "endogenous morphine" — the name itself places it in pharmacology, not immunology.
questions.explanation:
The answer is endorphins. Cytokines are small proteins that immune cells use to send messages to each other, like text messages that say 'come here' or 'attack'.

Chemokines call immune cells to a site of infection. Interferons warn nearby cells about viruses. Interleukins pass messages between white blood cells. Tumor necrosis factor causes inflammation and helps kill infected or cancer cells. Endorphins are the body's natural painkillers made by the nervous system; they are not cytokines.

Big idea: the immune system relies on chemical signals to coordinate its cells. Knowing the main cytokine families helps explain inflammation and fever.

questions.prompt: Which of these cell types found in Peyer’s patches can be exploited by disease-causing bacteria such as Shigella and Salmonella to penetrate the protective intestinal epithelium?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Ordinary columnar cells absorb nutrients and are tightly sealed together; they are not the main entry point.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells pick up material that M cells deliver, but M cells are the doorway bacteria use.
Incorrect. Macrophages eat germs after they cross; they are not the doorway.
Correct. M cells carry gut contents to immune cells, and some bacteria use them to get across.
Incorrect. T cells sit under the lining and respond to germs; they are not the doorway.

questions.advancedExplanation: Microfold cells, or M cells, are specialized epithelial cells in the follicle-associated epithelium overlying Peyer's patches. They are built differently from their absorptive neighbors in three ways that matter here: they have irregular microfolds instead of a dense brush border, they carry only a thin overlying mucus and glycocalyx layer, and they possess a deep basolateral invagination — a "pocket" — occupied by lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Their physiological job is immune surveillance by transcytosis: M cells sample intact antigens and whole microorganisms from the gut lumen and ferry them across the epithelium to the waiting antigen-presenting cells in the pocket, initiating mucosal IgA responses. This is a deliberate, controlled breach in an otherwise sealed barrier. That deliberate breach is precisely what pathogens hijack. Shigella flexneri and Salmonella Typhimurium cannot efficiently invade the apical surface of ordinary enterocytes, which is tightly sealed and thickly coated. Instead they target M cells, ride the transcytotic pathway across the epithelium, and emerge on the basolateral side — where Shigella then invades enterocytes from behind and spreads cell-to-cell using actin-based motility, and Salmonella is taken up by macrophages in which it survives and disseminates. Yersinia and reovirus use the same door. The lesson is that the gut's sampling port is also its structural weak point. The distractors are all genuinely present in Peyer's patches, which is what makes this a good tie breaker. Columnar epithelial cells (A) are the sealed absorptive cells the bacteria are trying to avoid. Dendritic cells (B) are a real second route — some extend dendrites between tight junctions directly into the lumen — but they are the recipients in the M cell pocket, not the transport cell, and they are not epithelial, so they cannot be what the pathogen crosses the epithelium through. Macrophages (C) are where Salmonella survives after it crosses, not how it crosses. T lymphocytes (E) have no transport function here.
questions.explanation:
The answer is microfold cells (M cells). Peyer's patches are clusters of immune tissue in the wall of the small intestine. Above them are special cells called M cells, whose job is to grab samples of things from inside the gut and pass them to immune cells underneath, so the immune system can check for germs.

Some bacteria, like Salmonella and Shigella, take advantage of this. They get carried through the M cells like passengers, which lets them sneak past the protective lining of the intestine and cause infection.

Big idea: the gut has its own immune tissue (part of MALT) to watch for germs in food. Germs sometimes use the body's own defenses as a way in.

questions.prompt: Which of these cells of the immune system is an important bridge between innate immunity and adaptive immunity?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Basophils release histamine in allergies but do not present antigens to T cells.
Correct. Dendritic cells catch germs and present them to T cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.
Incorrect. Natural killer cells are innate cells that kill infected cells directly.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells are part of the adaptive system; they are activated by dendritic cells.
Incorrect. Plasma cells are adaptive cells that make antibodies.

questions.advancedExplanation: Dendritic cells are the professional antigen-presenting cell par excellence and the only one that can activate a naive T cell. That single capability is what makes them the bridge, because the adaptive response cannot start until a naive T cell is primed. The handoff works in stages. An immature dendritic cell sits in peripheral tissue — the Langerhans cell in epidermis is the classic example — where it is highly phagocytic and continuously samples its environment. When its pattern recognition receptors detect a PAMP (an innate function), it engulfs antigen and matures: phagocytosis is downregulated, MHC class I and II expression soars, costimulatory molecules B7-1/B7-2 (CD80/CD86) appear, CCR7 is upregulated, and the cell migrates up a chemokine gradient to the draining lymph node. There it presents processed peptide on MHC to T cells in the paracortex and delivers all three signals a naive T cell needs: signal 1 (peptide–MHC to TCR), signal 2 (B7 to CD28 costimulation), and signal 3 (polarizing cytokines that determine whether the response becomes Th1, Th2, Th17, or Treg). So a dendritic cell receives information in innate terms — conserved molecular patterns — and transmits it in adaptive terms — a specific peptide on MHC with instructions about what kind of response to mount. Nothing else does both halves. The distractors each sit on one side of the divide. Basophils (A) are innate granulocytes releasing histamine. Natural killer cells (C) are the best wrong answer: they are innate lymphoid cells that kill without prior sensitization, detecting "missing self" when MHC I is downregulated, and they do secrete IFN-γ that shapes adaptive responses — but they do not present antigen to naive T cells. Cytotoxic T cells (D) and plasma cells (E) are purely adaptive effectors, the output of the process rather than its trigger. Macrophages and B cells are also professional APCs, but they activate already-primed T cells rather than naive ones.
questions.explanation:
The answer is dendritic cells. Dendritic cells are part of the innate immune system. They have long arm-like branches and live in places like the skin and the lining of the airways and gut, where they catch germs.

After catching a germ, a dendritic cell travels to a lymph node and shows pieces of the germ (antigens) to T cells. This 'wakes up' the adaptive immune system. So dendritic cells connect the fast, general innate system to the slower, specific adaptive system.

Big idea: the innate and adaptive immune systems work together. Antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells are the messengers between them.

questions.prompt: Which of the following blood cells play a role in the immune system overlapping with that of mast cells, including defending against parasitic infections and triggering allergic reactions?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. B cells make antibodies, including IgE, but they do not release histamine like mast cells.
Correct. Basophils carry IgE and release histamine, just like mast cells.
Incorrect. Eosinophils fight parasites, but they are not the closest match to mast cells.
Incorrect. Monocytes become macrophages that eat germs.
Incorrect. Neutrophils eat bacteria and are the first responders to infection.

questions.advancedExplanation: Basophils are the circulating counterpart of the tissue-resident mast cell, and the resemblance is close enough that they were long thought to be the same lineage (they are not — basophils arise from a granulocyte progenitor and mast cells from a distinct precursor that matures in tissue). The shared features are what the question is after: both carry the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI on their surface, both are packed with basophilic granules containing histamine and heparin, and both degranulate when allergen cross-links surface-bound IgE, releasing histamine along with newly synthesized leukotrienes and prostaglandins. Both therefore drive type I hypersensitivity (see #55) and both participate in defense against helminths. The main distinction is location: basophils circulate in blood and are the rarest leukocyte, under 1% of the white count, while mast cells leave the circulation as precursors and mature in connective tissue, especially at mucosal and perivascular sites. The stem says "blood cells," which fits basophils. Eosinophils (C) are the genuinely difficult distractor and deserve explicit treatment, because they also fight parasites and also participate in allergy. The difference is mechanism. Eosinophils attack large multicellular helminths by degranulating cytotoxic proteins onto them — major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase — in antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and in allergic disease they are the cells of the late-phase response and chronic tissue damage, as in asthmatic airway remodeling. They are effectors of destruction. Basophils and mast cells are IgE-triggered histamine releasers producing the immediate vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and edema. The question specifies overlap with mast cells "including... triggering allergic reactions," and triggering is the basophil's function; eosinophils are recruited by what mast cells and basophils release. The remaining options are distant: B lymphocytes (A) produce the IgE but do not degranulate; monocytes (D) are phagocytic macrophage precursors; neutrophils (E) are the first responders to bacterial infection, with non-basophilic granules and no FcεRI.
questions.explanation:
The answer is basophils. Mast cells live in tissues and are full of granules containing histamine. Basophils are white blood cells in the blood that look and act a lot like mast cells: they also carry histamine and have IgE antibodies on their surface.

When an allergen or parasite cross-links the IgE on their surface, basophils and mast cells release histamine and other chemicals. This causes allergy symptoms and also helps fight parasites. Eosinophils also fight parasites, but basophils are the cells whose job most closely overlaps with mast cells.

Big idea: allergic reactions (type I hypersensitivity) happen when IgE on mast cells and basophils triggers the release of histamine.

questions.prompt: Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency. What is the most important treatment to provide immediately once an anaphylactic reaction is recognized?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antihistamines help itching and hives but act too slowly to treat dangerous airway and blood pressure problems.
Incorrect. Beta-2 agonists open the airways but do not fix the drop in blood pressure.
Incorrect. Steroids take hours to work and are a follow-up treatment.
Correct. Epinephrine quickly raises blood pressure and opens the airways.
Incorrect. Glucagon is only used in special cases, such as patients taking beta-blockers.

questions.advancedExplanation: Anaphylaxis is a massive, systemic type I hypersensitivity reaction: widespread mast cell and basophil degranulation causes profound vasodilation and capillary leak (distributive shock), bronchoconstriction, and laryngeal and mucosal edema. People die of it within minutes from airway obstruction or cardiovascular collapse, so the only thing that matters is what acts fastest on those two mechanisms. Epinephrine is the only drug that reverses every component at once, and it does so within minutes by intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh (0.3 mg adult, 0.15 mg pediatric). Its actions map one-to-one onto the pathology: α₁ agonism causes vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure and — just as importantly — reverses the mucosal and laryngeal edema obstructing the airway; β₁ agonism increases heart rate and contractility, supporting cardiac output; β₂ agonism relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, relieving bronchospasm, and additionally stabilizes mast cells and basophils, shutting down further mediator release at the source. There is no absolute contraindication, and delay in administration is the factor most consistently associated with fatal outcomes. Every distractor is a drug actually used in anaphylaxis — which is what makes the question about priority, not about pharmacology. Antihistamines (A) block H1 receptors but take 30–60 minutes to act, relieve only itching and urticaria, and do nothing for airway edema or hypotension; they are strictly adjunctive, and giving one instead of epinephrine is a well-documented cause of preventable death. Beta-2 agonists (B) such as albuterol help bronchospasm but do not address shock or upper airway swelling. Corticosteroids (C) require 4–6 hours to alter gene transcription and were historically given to blunt the biphasic late-phase reaction; they have no role in the acute minutes. Glucagon (E) is a genuine second-line agent, but only for the narrow case of a patient on beta blockers who is refractory to epinephrine, since glucagon raises cardiac cAMP through a receptor the blockade does not touch.
questions.explanation:
The answer is epinephrine. Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction. The airways can swell and tighten, and blood pressure can drop dangerously low. It can kill within minutes.

Epinephrine (adrenaline), often given with an auto-injector like an EpiPen, works fast on all the main problems: it tightens blood vessels to raise blood pressure, relaxes and opens the airways, and reduces swelling. Antihistamines and steroids are helpful extras but act too slowly to save a life on their own.

Big idea: anaphylaxis is the most dangerous kind of allergic reaction, and epinephrine is the first, most important treatment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are Type I hypersensitivity reactions? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Correct. Anaphylaxis is the most severe type I (IgE) reaction.
Incorrect. Contact dermatitis is a delayed type IV reaction caused by T cells.
Correct. Hay fever is a type I reaction to pollen.
Correct. Drug allergies such as penicillin allergy are usually type I reactions.
Incorrect. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease; the name is just a coincidence.

questions.advancedExplanation: The Gell and Coombs classification sorts hypersensitivity by mechanism. Type I is IgE-mediated and immediate (minutes): allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, which degranulate. Type II is antibody-mediated cytotoxicity, with IgG or IgM against cell-surface or matrix antigens. Type III is immune-complex deposition (see #56). Type IV is delayed and cell-mediated, driven by T cells rather than antibody, taking 24–72 hours. A fast mnemonic: ACID — Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed. Anaphylaxis (A) is the prototype and the namesake of type I, the systemic form of the same reaction (see #54). Hay fever (C), allergic rhinitis, is the localized mucosal form: pollen cross-links IgE on nasal mucosal mast cells, histamine release produces sneezing, rhinorrhea, and itching within minutes of exposure. The immediacy is the giveaway. Drug allergies such as penicillin (D) are the classic cause of drug-induced anaphylaxis and urticaria. The mechanism is instructive: penicillin is a small hapten, too small to be immunogenic alone, but its β-lactam ring opens and binds covalently to serum proteins, and the hapten–carrier conjugate provokes IgE. Note the deliberate wording — penicillin can also cause type II (hemolytic anemia), type III (serum sickness), and type IV (contact dermatitis, DRESS) reactions, but the unqualified "drug allergy" in the IgE sense is type I. Contact dermatitis (B) is Type IV, and it is the best distractor because the word "allergic" attaches to it in ordinary speech. Poison ivy urushiol and nickel act as haptens binding skin proteins, Langerhans cells present them to T cells, and sensitized CD4⁺ T cells produce the rash — 24 to 72 hours later. No antibody is involved, and the delay is the diagnostic feature. The tuberculin/PPD skin test works on the same principle. Type I diabetes (E) is also Type IV despite its confusing name. The "type I" refers to the diabetes classification, which has nothing to do with the Gell and Coombs system — a pun the question is deliberately exploiting. Beta cell destruction is carried out by autoreactive cytotoxic CD8⁺ T lymphocytes, as the stem of #64 states explicitly. Anti-GAD and anti-islet antibodies exist but are diagnostic markers rather than the destructive mechanism.
questions.explanation:
The answers are anaphylaxis, hay fever, and drug allergies like penicillin allergy. Type I hypersensitivity is the 'immediate' allergic reaction. It happens when IgE antibodies on mast cells grab an allergen, causing the cells to release histamine within minutes.

Anaphylaxis, hay fever (allergic rhinitis), and most drug allergies all work this way. Contact dermatitis (like a poison ivy rash) is a type IV reaction, which is caused by T cells and takes a day or two to appear. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease, not an allergy; the 'type 1' in its name has nothing to do with type I hypersensitivity.

Big idea: hypersensitivities are grouped into four types based on what part of the immune system causes them. Type I uses IgE and mast cells and happens fast.

questions.prompt: Solid Snake is a highly skilled special ops soldier who was bitten by a venomous snake during a mission. In spite of his name, he is not immune to the snake venom. He receives treatment with an antivenom originally made in a horse as host. Solid Snake is saved from the envenomation. However, a few days later he develops a fever, skin rash, joint pain, and blood in his urine. Which of the following best explains for his symptoms?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Type I (IgE) reactions happen within minutes, not days later.
Incorrect. Type II reactions happen when antibodies attack the body's own cells, like in a mismatched blood transfusion.
Correct. Antibody-antigen clumps settle in blood vessels and cause inflammation, which is serum sickness.
Incorrect. Type IV reactions are caused by T cells, like poison ivy rashes.
Incorrect. Type V is not part of the standard four-type system; it is sometimes used for antibodies that stimulate receptors, as in Graves' disease.

questions.advancedExplanation: This is serum sickness, the historical prototype of type III hypersensitivity, first described after therapeutic horse antiserum for diphtheria in the early 1900s — and the scenario here is a textbook reproduction of it. The mechanism explains every element of the stem. Horse antivenom is a foreign protein given in large quantity. Over 7–14 days the patient mounts an IgG (and IgM) response against it. Antibody and the still-circulating horse protein form soluble immune complexes. When antigen and antibody are present in roughly equivalent amounts — slight antigen excess, in particular — the complexes are small enough to stay in solution and escape clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system, so they circulate and deposit in vessel walls at sites of filtration and turbulence. There they fix complement, generating C3a and C5a, which recruit neutrophils; the neutrophils cannot phagocytose a complex stuck to a basement membrane, so they degranulate onto it, producing vasculitis. The deposition sites give the symptoms: glomeruli→ hematuria and proteinuria; joint synovium→ arthralgia; skin vessels→ urticarial or purpuric rash; plus fever and low serum complement (C3, C4 consumed). Other type III diseases follow the same pattern — systemic lupus erythematosus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, polyarteritis nodosa, and the localized Arthus reaction. The timing is the single best discriminator, and the question supplies it deliberately with "a few days later." Type I (A) occurs within minutes of exposure and would have presented as anaphylaxis during the infusion, with urticaria, wheeze, and hypotension — not fever and hematuria a week later; antivenom can certainly cause that too, but it did not here. Type II (B) involves antibody directed against antigens fixed on host cells, producing targeted destruction such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture syndrome, or myasthenia gravis — the hallmark is a single cell or tissue type destroyed, not a multisystem complex-deposition picture. Type IV (D) is T-cell mediated and would produce contact dermatitis or granulomas, not glomerular bleeding. Type V (E) is not part of the original Gell and Coombs scheme at all; some texts add it for receptor-stimulating antibodies such as those in Graves disease, and it is here as a pure distractor.
questions.explanation:
The answer is type III hypersensitivity, here called serum sickness. The antivenom was made in a horse, so it contains horse proteins. Solid Snake's immune system sees these proteins as foreign and makes antibodies against them over several days.

The antibodies stick to the leftover horse proteins and form clumps called immune complexes. These clumps get stuck in small blood vessels in the skin, joints, and kidneys, where they trigger inflammation. That causes rash, joint pain, fever, and blood in the urine, about a week after treatment.

Big idea: type III hypersensitivity is caused by antigen-antibody clumps that lodge in tissues. Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction are classic examples.

questions.prompt: Which of these cell types are phagocytes? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Correct. Eosinophils can carry out phagocytosis, though their main job is fighting parasites.
Correct. Kupffer cells are macrophages in the liver.
Correct. Macrophages are large, powerful phagocytes in the tissues.
Correct. Monocytes are phagocytes in the blood that become macrophages.
Correct. Neutrophils are the most common phagocytes in the blood.

questions.advancedExplanation: Every option is a phagocyte, which makes this a question about completeness of knowledge rather than discrimination — and about resisting the instinct that a "select all" question must have at least one wrong answer. Neutrophils (E) are the most abundant leukocyte and the first responders to bacterial infection, arriving within hours. They phagocytose opsonized bacteria and kill them with the respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase generating superoxide, then myeloperoxidase producing hypochlorite) plus granule enzymes, and they also extrude neutrophil extracellular traps. They are short-lived; pus is largely dead neutrophils. Macrophages (C) are the professional phagocytes of tissue — long-lived, capable of repeated phagocytosis, and additionally antigen-presenting via MHC II. They clear pathogens, apoptotic cells, and debris, and orchestrate repair. Monocytes (D) are the circulating precursors of macrophages and dendritic cells. They are phagocytic while still in the blood and become more so after extravasating into tissue and differentiating. Kupffer cells (B) are simply tissue-resident macrophages of the liver sinusoids, so they are phagocytes by definition. They are the body's largest macrophage population, strategically placed to filter portal blood arriving from the gut, and they clear senescent erythrocytes and gut-derived bacteria. The parallel names are worth knowing: microglia in the CNS, alveolar macrophages in the lung, osteoclasts in bone, Langerhans cells in skin, mesangial cells in the kidney. Eosinophils (A) are the one that makes students hesitate, and the hesitation is reasonable. Their principal antiparasitic mechanism is extracellular — degranulating major basic protein onto helminths too large to swallow — and they are far weaker phagocytes than neutrophils. But they are genuinely phagocytic: they express Fc and complement receptors, ingest antigen–antibody complexes, bacteria, and yeast, and are classified among the phagocytic granulocytes in standard immunology texts. The key is reading the question as "are these capable of phagocytosis" rather than "is phagocytosis their main job." The common non-phagocytes, had they appeared, would be lymphocytes (T, B, NK), basophils, mast cells, and plasma cells. Dendritic cells are phagocytic when immature.
questions.explanation:
All five are correct: eosinophils, Kupffer cells, macrophages, monocytes, and neutrophils. A phagocyte is a cell that 'eats' germs and debris by wrapping around them and digesting them (phagocytosis).

Neutrophils are the most common phagocytes and arrive first at infections. Monocytes are phagocytes in the blood that turn into macrophages when they move into tissues. Kupffer cells are macrophages that live in the liver and clean the blood coming from the intestines. Eosinophils can also eat germs, though they mostly fight parasites by releasing toxic chemicals.

Big idea: phagocytes are a key part of the innate immune system. Many white blood cells can phagocytose, and some live in specific organs, like Kupffer cells in the liver.

questions.prompt: Splenectomy (removal of the spleen) can be performed for treatment of certain blood disorders and for traumatic injuries to the spleen. Splenectomy makes a person more susceptible to dangerous and overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) by which of the following pathogenic organisms? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Clostridium difficile causes gut infections, usually after antibiotics, not because of a missing spleen.
Incorrect. Tuberculosis is controlled by T cells and macrophages, not mainly the spleen.
Correct. Neisseria meningitidis is an encapsulated bacterium that the spleen helps clear.
Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of severe infection after spleen removal.
Incorrect. Vibrio cholerae causes cholera through a toxin in the gut, not a blood infection linked to the spleen.

questions.advancedExplanation: The spleen performs one immunologic job that nothing else can replace: it clears encapsulated bacteria from the bloodstream. Polysaccharide capsules are anti-phagocytic — they resist complement deposition and are poorly recognized by phagocyte receptors — so these organisms can only be efficiently removed when opsonized with antibody and complement and then filtered. Two splenic features do this: the marginal zone B cells, which mount rapid T-independent IgM responses against polysaccharide antigens, and the slow percolation of blood through the red pulp cords, where macrophages strip opsonized organisms out. Remove the spleen and encapsulated bacteria that enter the bloodstream multiply unchecked. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is the result: a fulminant sepsis that can progress from mild prodrome to shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and death within 24–48 hours, with mortality historically around 50%. Lifetime risk is highest in the first few years after splenectomy and in children, but never returns to baseline. The classic encapsulated culprits are remembered as SHiN: Streptococcus pneumoniae (D) — by far the most common, causing roughly 50–90% of cases — Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis (C). All three have polysaccharide capsules and all three have vaccines, which is exactly why asplenic patients must receive pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib vaccination, ideally two weeks before an elective splenectomy. Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dog bites and Babesia are additional asplenia-specific risks. The distractors fail the capsule test. Clostridium difficile (A) is a spore-forming anaerobe causing antibiotic-associated colitis through toxins A and B acting locally in the colon lumen; it is not a bloodstream pathogen cleared by the spleen. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (B) is an intracellular organism controlled by cell-mediated immunity — macrophages, Th1 cells, IFN-γ, and granuloma formation — so the relevant immunodeficiency is T-cell deficiency (HIV, TNF inhibitors), not asplenia. Vibrio cholerae (E) is a non-invasive toxigenic organism that stays in the gut lumen and secretes cholera toxin; it never reaches the bloodstream.
questions.explanation:
The answers are Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae. The spleen filters the blood. It is especially important for removing bacteria that have a slippery outer coat called a capsule, which helps them escape being eaten by phagocytes.

Without a spleen, these 'encapsulated' bacteria can multiply quickly in the blood and cause a sudden, dangerous infection. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b are the classic examples, so people without spleens get vaccines against them. The other germs listed cause disease in other ways and are not specially linked to losing the spleen.

Big idea: the spleen is an immune organ that filters blood and helps make antibodies against coated bacteria.

questions.prompt: Losing the function of any of the enzymes responsible for V(D)J recombination will result in:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Autoimmunity is when immune cells attack the body. Here, immune cells are missing.
Incorrect. The enzymes work on immune receptor genes, and losing them mainly causes missing immune cells, not chromosome disorders.
Incorrect. Chronic granulomatous disease is a problem with phagocytes killing bacteria.
Incorrect. In common variable immunodeficiency, B cells exist but make too few antibodies; T cells are usually fine.
Correct. Without V(D)J recombination, both B and T cells fail to develop, causing SCID.

questions.advancedExplanation: V(D)J recombination is the somatic DNA rearrangement that generates antigen receptor diversity. During lymphocyte development, RAG1 and RAG2 recognize recombination signal sequences and introduce double-strand breaks, excising the intervening DNA; the broken hairpin ends are then opened by Artemis and repaired by the non-homologous end-joining machinery (DNA-PKcs, Ku70/80, DNA ligase IV, XRCC4), with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase adding random nucleotides at the junctions. Combinatorial joining plus junctional diversity plus heavy/light chain pairing yields a repertoire estimated in excess of 10¹¹ distinct receptors. The decisive point is that this one process builds both the B-cell receptor and the T-cell receptor. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain loci and TCR α, β, γ, and δ loci are all rearranged by the same enzymes. Break the machinery and neither lineage can produce a functional antigen receptor. Developing lymphocytes that fail to assemble a receptor die at the pre-B/pre-T checkpoint, so the patient has essentially no mature T cells and no mature B cells. That is the definition of severe combined immunodeficiency — "combined" meaning both arms of adaptive immunity. Affected infants present in the first months of life, once maternal IgG wanes, with persistent thrush, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii; untreated it is fatal in infancy, and treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplant or gene therapy. RAG deficiency is one of the autosomal recessive forms (the X-linked common gamma chain mutation is more common overall). The word "any" in the stem is important: it signals that this is a single shared pathway with no redundancy, so no partial phenotype is available. The distractors are all real immunodeficiencies or immune disorders with different mechanisms. Autoimmunity (A) results from failed tolerance — negative selection or regulatory T cells (see #64) — and would require functioning receptor generation. Chromosomal abnormalities (B) is tempting since RAG does cut DNA, and partial/hypomorphic defects can produce translocations, but that is not the defining clinical outcome. Chronic granulomatous disease (C) is a defect of NADPH oxidase in phagocytes, not lymphocytes, causing catalase-positive organism infections. Common variable immunodeficiency (D) is the strongest distractor: it is an antibody deficiency with low IgG, IgA, and IgM, but B cells are present and T cells are largely intact, and it typically presents in adolescence or adulthood — too mild and too B-limited for a complete loss of V(D)J recombination, which must knock out T cells as well.
questions.explanation:
The answer is severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). V(D)J recombination is how developing B and T cells shuffle pieces of their genes to build millions of different receptors. This is what lets them recognize so many different germs.

If the enzymes that do this shuffling are broken, B and T cells cannot build working receptors. Without receptors they die before maturing, so the person has almost no B or T cells. Losing both kinds of adaptive immune cells is 'severe combined' immunodeficiency. Babies with SCID get serious infections and need a bone marrow transplant.

Big idea: B and T cells need working receptors to develop and fight germs. SCID is a genetic immunodeficiency where both are missing.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of artificial active immunity?

choices.explanation: Correct. A vaccine makes your own immune system respond (active) through a medical treatment (artificial).
Incorrect. Recovering from an infection is natural active immunity.

choices.text: An infant acquiring antibodies from mother’s milk
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies from mother's milk are natural passive immunity.
Incorrect. Antivenom gives ready-made antibodies, which is artificial passive immunity.
Incorrect. IVIG gives ready-made antibodies, which is artificial passive immunity.

questions.advancedExplanation: Adaptive immunity is classified along two independent axes, and the question requires getting both right at once. Active vs. passive: active immunity means your own immune system mounts the response, producing its own antibodies and memory cells — slow to develop (days to weeks) but long-lasting. Passive immunity means you receive preformed antibodies made by someone or something else — immediate protection, but temporary, lasting only weeks to months as the transferred antibody is catabolized, and conferring no memory. Natural vs. artificial: natural means it happened through ordinary biological processes without medical intervention; artificial means it was deliberately induced. Crossing the two axes gives four categories, and the five options are built to populate them: A — Influenza vaccination = artificial active. Artificial, because a clinician deliberately administered a preparation; active, because the vaccine contains antigen (inactivated virus or recombinant hemagglutinin) and your B and T cells respond, class switch, affinity mature, and leave memory cells behind. This is the answer. B — Immunity after influenza infection = natural active. Active (your own response) but natural (the virus arrived on its own). C — Antibodies from mother's milk = natural passive. Secretory IgA transferred in colostrum and breast milk — preformed antibody, transferred naturally. (Transplacental IgG is the other natural passive route.) D — Antivenom after snakebite = artificial passive. Preformed antibodies raised in a horse, administered deliberately. This is the same preparation that caused serum sickness in #56, and the two questions reinforce each other: because it is passive, it provides no lasting immunity, which is why Solid Snake would need it again after a second bite. E — IVIG = artificial passive. Pooled human immunoglobulin from thousands of donors, given deliberately; it must be repeated every few weeks because it confers no memory.
questions.explanation:
The answer is vaccination against influenza. Immunity can be described in two ways. 'Active' means your own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells; 'passive' means you receive ready-made antibodies from somewhere else. 'Natural' means it happened in everyday life; 'artificial' means it came from a medical treatment.

A vaccine trains your own immune system (active) using a medical treatment (artificial). Getting sick and recovering is natural active immunity. A baby getting antibodies from breast milk is natural passive immunity. Antivenom and IVIG are artificial passive immunity, because they give ready-made antibodies.

Big idea: active immunity lasts a long time because it creates memory cells, while passive immunity works right away but fades within weeks or months.

questions.prompt: HIV commonly infects which cell types? (Select all that apply.)

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells have CD8, not CD4, so HIV does not commonly infect them.
Correct. Helper T cells have CD4, HIV's main entry point.
Correct. Macrophages have CD4 and can be infected by HIV.
Incorrect. Natural killer cells do not have CD4.
Incorrect. Plasma cells do not have CD4.

questions.advancedExplanation: HIV entry requires two surface molecules on the target cell: the primary receptor CD4, bound by the viral gp120, and a chemokine co-receptor — CCR5 or CXCR4 — engaged after a conformational change, which then allows gp41 to drive membrane fusion. A cell must express both to be efficiently infected, and that requirement determines the answer entirely. Helper T-lymphocytes (B) are CD4⁺ by definition — CD4 is their defining marker, functioning normally as a co-receptor stabilizing TCR binding to MHC class II. They express CXCR4 and, when activated, CCR5. Their progressive depletion is the central event in HIV disease, and the CD4 count is the standard staging marker: AIDS is defined at a CD4 count below 200 cells/µL, the threshold below which opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia appear. Because CD4⁺ T cells coordinate essentially the entire adaptive response — helping B cells class switch, licensing cytotoxic T cells, activating macrophages — losing them collapses both arms of immunity. Macrophages (C) express CD4 at lower levels along with CCR5, and are infected readily by the R5-tropic strains that dominate early infection and sexual transmission. They matter disproportionately for two reasons: unlike T cells they are relatively resistant to the cytopathic effects, so they survive as a long-lived viral reservoir, and they carry virus across the blood–brain barrier as monocytes, seeding CNS infection and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder. Microglia, being CNS macrophages, are infected by the same route. Dendritic cells likewise express CD4 and CCR5 and ferry virus to lymph nodes. The three wrong options all lack CD4. Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (A) are CD8⁺, not CD4⁺ — they are in fact a principal defense against HIV, killing infected cells, and their numbers are preserved or even raised early in infection, which is why the CD4:CD8 ratio inverts. Natural killer cells (D) are CD56⁺/CD16⁺ innate lymphocytes. Plasma cells (E) are terminally differentiated B cells; B-lineage cells are CD19/CD20-positive and CD4-negative. (Hypergammaglobulinemia in HIV reflects dysregulated B-cell activation, not B-cell infection.)
questions.explanation:
The answers are helper T cells and macrophages. HIV gets into cells by grabbing onto a protein called CD4 on the cell's surface, along with a second protein (a co-receptor such as CCR5).

Helper T cells have lots of CD4, which is why they are also called CD4+ T cells. Macrophages also have some CD4 and can be infected and carry the virus around the body. Over time, HIV destroys helper T cells, which weakens the whole immune system and leads to AIDS. Cytotoxic T cells, natural killer cells, and plasma cells do not have CD4, so HIV does not commonly infect them.

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency. Losing helper T cells weakens the immune system because helper T cells direct many other immune cells.

questions.prompt: Stephen Crohn was the first person discovered to be resistant to HIV infection. This resistance was the result of a genetic mutation causing absence of which of the following?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. CD3 is part of the T cell receptor complex, not HIV's entry point.
Incorrect. CD4 is HIV's main receptor, but Crohn still had CD4; his helper T cells needed it.
Incorrect. CD8 is found on cytotoxic T cells and is not used by HIV.
Correct. Crohn lacked CCR5, the co-receptor most HIV strains need to enter cells.
Incorrect. CXCR4 is another co-receptor some HIV strains use, but it was not missing in Crohn.

questions.advancedExplanation: Stephen Crohn remained uninfected despite extensive exposure during the early years of the epidemic, including the death of his partner, and became the first identified HIV-resistant individual — he was studied for years before the mechanism was found in 1996. He was homozygous for CCR5-Δ32, a 32-base-pair deletion in the CCR5 gene that causes a frameshift and premature stop. The truncated protein never reaches the cell surface. The consequence follows from #61: without CCR5 on the membrane, R5-tropic HIV strains — the strains that dominate sexual transmission and establish nearly all new infections — can bind CD4 but cannot complete the conformational change that triggers gp41-mediated fusion. Entry fails. Homozygotes are highly resistant to infection; heterozygotes, who carry roughly half the normal surface CCR5, are not protected from acquisition but progress to AIDS more slowly. The allele is found in about 10% of people of Northern European descent and is essentially absent elsewhere, and because CCR5's normal chemokine-receptor function is largely redundant, homozygous loss causes little harm. This single observation drove two major therapeutic developments: maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist used as an entry inhibitor, and the stem cell transplants that produced the only confirmed HIV cures to date — the Berlin, London, and Düsseldorf patients, each of whom received marrow from a CCR5-Δ32 homozygous donor. The distractors are chosen to test whether you can separate receptor from co-receptor. CD4 (B) is the primary HIV receptor, so its absence would also prevent infection — but CD4 is indispensable for helper T-cell function, and a person lacking it entirely would be profoundly immunodeficient, not healthy. Resistance has to come from a molecule the body can spare, which is exactly why CCR5 is the one that occurs in nature. CXCR4 (E) is the other co-receptor, used by X4-tropic strains that typically emerge later in disease; CXCR4 loss would not block initial transmission and is embryonically lethal in mice. CD3 (A) is the TCR signaling complex and CD8 (C) marks cytotoxic T cells; neither participates in HIV entry.
questions.explanation:
The answer is CCR5. To get into a helper T cell, HIV needs two 'door handles' on the cell: CD4 and a co-receptor, usually CCR5.

Stephen Crohn inherited two broken copies of the CCR5 gene, so his cells had no CCR5 on their surface. The common types of HIV could not get in, so he did not become infected even after many exposures. This discovery led to HIV drugs that block CCR5.

Big idea: viruses need specific receptors to enter cells. If a person lacks the receptor, the virus cannot infect those cells.

questions.prompt: Select TWO of the choices below which are most similar to each other:

choices.explanation: Correct. An autograft comes from the same person, so it is genetically identical.
Incorrect. An allograft comes from a different person, so it is genetically different.
Correct. An isograft comes from an identical twin, so it is genetically identical like an autograft.
Incorrect. A xenograft comes from another species, so it is very different.

questions.advancedExplanation: The four graft types form a ladder of increasing genetic disparity between donor and recipient, and the question asks which two rungs are adjacent: Autograft (A): tissue moved from one site to another within the same individual — a skin graft from thigh to burn, a saphenous vein used for coronary bypass, bone from iliac crest to a spinal fusion. Donor and recipient genome are identical. Isograft (C), also called a syngeneic graft: tissue transferred between genetically identical individuals — monozygotic twins, or inbred laboratory mouse strains. Donor and recipient genome are, again, identical. Allograft (B): between two genetically different members of the same species — the ordinary human-to-human transplant. Xenograft (D): between different species — a porcine heart valve, or the experimental pig kidney transplants now in trials. The reason autograft and isograft are the most similar is not merely that both involve "identical" tissue in the abstract, but that they are immunologically indistinguishable. In both, every MHC (HLA) molecule and every minor histocompatibility antigen on the graft is one the recipient's thymus already deleted self-reactive T cells against. No alloantigen is presented, no T-cell response is mounted, no rejection occurs, and no immunosuppression is required. For practical purposes the recipient's immune system cannot tell the two apart — the first successful human kidney transplant, Murray's 1954 operation between the Herrick twins, worked for exactly this reason, in an era with no immunosuppressive drugs at all. By contrast, allografts provoke a strong T-cell response against mismatched HLA and require lifelong immunosuppression, and xenografts additionally face hyperacute rejection from preformed natural antibodies against α-Gal epitopes, which destroy the graft within minutes. The gap between isograft and allograft is therefore enormous, while the gap between autograft and isograft is essentially zero.
questions.explanation:
The answers are autograft and isograft. A graft is tissue moved from one place to another. An autograft comes from the same person (for example, skin moved from the thigh to a burn). An isograft comes from an identical twin.

Both autografts and isografts are genetically identical to the person receiving them, so the immune system sees them as 'self' and does not reject them. An allograft comes from a different person who is not an identical twin, and a xenograft comes from another species. Both of those look foreign and can be rejected unless drugs suppress the immune system.

Big idea: the immune system rejects transplants when it recognizes them as 'non-self'. Matching the donor and using anti-rejection drugs help prevent this.

questions.prompt: In type I diabetes, auto-reactive T-lymphocytes mistakenly attack and kill pancreatic beta cells that display self-antigens. This immune process can be most accurately described as a failure of:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Affinity maturation is how B cells improve their antibodies; it is not a T cell self-tolerance check.
Incorrect. Antigen processing is how cells cut proteins into pieces to show T cells; it is working normally here.
Incorrect. Regulatory T cells help control self-attacking cells, but the best description is that those cells were never removed.
Incorrect. Positive selection keeps T cells that can recognize MHC; it does not remove self-attacking cells.
Correct. Negative selection removes self-attacking T cells, and its failure lets them attack beta cells.

questions.advancedExplanation: T-cell development in the thymus imposes two sequential quality-control checkpoints on the randomly generated receptor repertoire (see #59), and the question hinges on telling them apart. Positive selection, in the thymic cortex, asks: does this TCR recognize self-MHC at all? Thymocytes that bind self-MHC with low affinity survive; those that cannot bind self-MHC are useless and die by neglect. This ensures MHC restriction — that mature T cells can actually see peptide presented on the body's own MHC molecules. Negative selection, at the cortico-medullary junction and in the medulla, asks the opposite question: does this TCR bind self-peptide too strongly? Thymocytes that bind self-peptide–MHC with high affinity are dangerous and are deleted by apoptosis (or diverted into the regulatory T-cell lineage). This is central tolerance. Its most remarkable feature is the AIRE transcription factor in medullary thymic epithelial cells, which forces ectopic expression of thousands of tissue-restricted antigens — including insulin — inside the thymus, so that T cells specific for peripheral tissues can be screened out before they ever leave. Type I diabetes is a failure of that screening. Autoreactive T cells specific for beta cell antigens — preproinsulin, GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 — escaped deletion, entered the periphery, and destroyed the islets. The genetic evidence is direct: the strongest susceptibility locus is HLA class II (DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8), which determines which self-peptides are presented during selection, and the second strongest is a variable-number tandem repeat upstream of the INS gene that governs how much insulin is expressed in the thymus — less thymic insulin means less efficient deletion of insulin-reactive T cells and higher diabetes risk. Mutations in AIRE itself cause APS-1, a syndrome of multiple simultaneous autoimmune endocrinopathies. Positive selection (D) is the symmetric trap: its failure produces T cells that cannot recognize self-MHC, which simply die — causing immunodeficiency, not autoimmunity. Regulatory T-cell activation (C) is the most defensible alternative, since Tregs enforce peripheral tolerance and their failure does cause autoimmunity (FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX syndrome, which includes neonatal diabetes). But the stem describes autoreactive T cells that recognize "self-antigens" in the first place — a repertoire problem, which is central tolerance — and asks for the most accurate description. Affinity maturation (A) is somatic hypermutation in germinal-center B cells, not a T-cell process at all. Antigen processing (B) is normal here; the problem is not that the antigen was presented wrongly but that a T cell which should never have existed responded to it.
questions.explanation:
The answer is negative selection. T cells grow up in the thymus. While there, they go through tests. In negative selection, T cells that react strongly to the body's own proteins (self-antigens) are destroyed, so they cannot attack the body later.

If negative selection fails, some self-attacking T cells escape into the body. In type 1 diabetes, escaped T cells attack the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas. Positive selection is a different test that keeps T cells able to recognize MHC; affinity maturation improves B cell antibodies; regulatory T cells are a backup system that also helps, but the main failure described is letting self-reactive cells survive.

Big idea: the immune system must learn the difference between 'self' and 'non-self'. Autoimmune diseases happen when that training fails.

questions.prompt: What is chyle? Where and how is it formed? What is its function?
questions.answer: Chyle is a milky fluid of lymph containing lipids suspended as chylomicrons (1 point). It forms in the small intestine: absorbed lipids are packaged and transported into lacteals, where they mix with clear lymph to give the milky appearance, and it enters the lymphatic circulation (1 point). Chyle carries lipids into the systemic circulation and is essential for lipid transport and metabolism (1 point).
questions.advancedExplanation: What it is (1 point). Chyle is lymph with a high content of emulsified dietary fat, which gives it an opaque, milky-white appearance — the name comes from the Greek chylos, juice. The fat travels as chylomicrons, large triglyceride-rich lipoproteins stabilized by a surface shell of phospholipid, cholesterol, and apolipoproteins (B-48, A-I, later C-II and E). It also carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, plus lymphocytes and protein. Where and how it is formed (1 point). In the small intestine, after a fatty meal. The sequence: bile salts emulsify dietary triglyceride, pancreatic lipase and colipase hydrolyze it to monoglycerides and free fatty acids, and these are carried in mixed micelles to the brush border, where they diffuse into the enterocyte. Inside the enterocyte, triglyceride is resynthesized in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and packaged with apolipoproteins in the Golgi into chylomicrons. The chylomicrons are then exocytosed at the basolateral surface — and here is the decisive anatomical point: they are far too large to enter the blood capillaries, so they enter the lacteal, the blind-ended central lymphatic capillary of each villus (label #98 in Part 4). Lacteals are permeable in a way blood capillaries are not, with loose, overlapping endothelial junctions and no continuous basement membrane. Mixing with clear lymph, the chylomicrons turn it milky — chyle. It drains through mesenteric lymphatics to the cisterna chyli (#89), up the thoracic duct (#85), and empties into the venous system at the left jugulo-subclavian junction. Function (1 point). Chyle is the transport route for dietary long-chain fats and fat-soluble vitamins into the systemic circulation. Its indirect path is physiologically significant: because the thoracic duct empties into the subclavian vein rather than the portal vein, dietary fat bypasses the liver's first-pass metabolism and is delivered directly to peripheral tissues, where lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium in muscle and adipose strips the triglyceride before the remnant reaches the liver. The contrast is instructive: carbohydrates and amino acids, being water-soluble and small, go straight into the portal blood and through the liver first. Short-and medium-chain fatty acids also take the portal route, which is why MCT oil is used clinically in fat malabsorption and in chylothorax. The clinical correlate confirms the anatomy: injury to the thoracic duct — during thoracic surgery, or from malignant obstruction — spills chyle into the pleural space, producing a chylothorax with milky fluid high in triglycerides, and causes substantial loss of fat, protein, and lymphocytes.
questions.explanation:
Chyle is a milky-white fluid made of lymph mixed with fat. It forms in the small intestine. Fats from food are packed into tiny fat-and-protein packages called chylomicrons inside intestinal cells. These packages are too big to enter blood capillaries, so they enter small lymph vessels in each villus called lacteals.

When the fat mixes with the clear lymph in the lacteals, it turns milky. This chyle flows through lymph vessels, up through the thoracic duct, and into the blood near the heart. That is how most dietary fat gets into the bloodstream.

Big idea: the lymphatic system connects digestion and immunity. Besides carrying immune cells and returning fluid, it transports absorbed fats.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 75 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The tiny purple fragment with no nucleus, roughly 2–3 µm — far smaller than any cell on the slide, which is the identifying feature. Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments shed from megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate hemostasis by adhering to exposed collagen via von Willebrand factor and GPIb, then aggregating through GPIIb/IIIa.
questions.explanation:
Label 75 is a platelet (thrombocyte). It is the tiny purple dot, much smaller than any cell around it, with no nucleus.

Platelets are fragments of a large bone marrow cell. They help blood clot when a blood vessel is injured.

Big idea: blood contains red blood cells, white blood cells (the immune cells), and platelets, and each looks different under a microscope.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 76 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The small round cell with a dense, round, deeply basophilic nucleus and only a thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm — a nearly nucleus-only appearance. Size is comparable to a red cell. The absence of granules and the unsegmented round nucleus distinguish it from every granulocyte; the scant cytoplasm distinguishes it from the monocyte at #77. The key accepts "B cell" or "T cell," since the two are morphologically indistinguishable on a smear and require flow cytometry (CD19/CD20 vs. CD3) to separate.
questions.explanation:
Label 76 is a lymphocyte. It is a small round cell with a big, dark, round nucleus that fills almost the whole cell and only a thin rim of cytoplasm.

Lymphocytes include B cells and T cells, the cells of the adaptive immune system. B cells and T cells look the same under a regular microscope, so either answer is accepted.

Big idea: you can identify white blood cells by the shape of their nucleus and whether they have granules.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 77 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The largest leukocyte on the slide, with abundant pale blue-gray cytoplasm and a large indented, kidney-or horseshoe-shaped nucleus with lacy chromatin. The combination of great size and plentiful cytoplasm is the giveaway. The key explicitly rules out "macrophage," and correctly: a monocyte becomes a macrophage only after it leaves the bloodstream and differentiates in tissue, so a macrophage cannot be present on a normal peripheral smear. Precision of terminology is the point being tested.
questions.explanation:
Label 77 is a monocyte. It is the biggest white blood cell, with a large, often kidney-shaped nucleus and lots of pale blue-gray cytoplasm.

Monocytes travel in the blood. When they leave the blood and enter tissues, they become macrophages, which eat germs and debris. 'Macrophage' is not accepted here because macrophages live in tissues, not in a blood smear.

Big idea: monocytes and macrophages are the same cell line at different stages, and both are phagocytes.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 78 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: Bilobed nucleus with coarse, uniform granules that stain bright orange-red with eosin — the acidic dye binds the granules' highly basic proteins (major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein). Characteristically has exactly two nuclear lobes connected by a thin bridge, unlike the neutrophil's three to five. Elevated in parasitic infection and allergy (see #53).
questions.explanation:
Label 78 is an eosinophil. It has a nucleus with two lobes and many bright orange-red granules.

Eosinophils fight parasites, such as worms, and are involved in allergic reactions and asthma. Their granules contain toxic proteins they release onto large parasites.

Big idea: granule color helps identify white blood cells: orange-red granules mean eosinophils.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 79 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: Multilobed nucleus — three to five segments joined by thin chromatin threads — with pale lilac, fine, inconspicuous granules that take up neither acidic nor basic dye strongly (hence "neutro-"). The most abundant leukocyte. The key accepts "polymorphonuclear leukocyte" or PMN, a name describing exactly this nuclear segmentation. Hypersegmentation (>5 lobes) suggests B₁₂ or folate deficiency; a left shift toward band forms suggests acute bacterial infection.
questions.explanation:
Label 79 is a neutrophil. It has a nucleus divided into 3-5 lobes and pale cytoplasm.

Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells. They are the first to arrive at an infection and eat bacteria. Dead neutrophils make up most of pus.

Big idea: neutrophils are front-line phagocytes of the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 80 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The cell whose nucleus is obscured by dense, coarse, very dark blue-purple granules — the identifying feature, since in every other granulocyte you can clearly make out nuclear shape. The granules stain intensely with basic dyes because they are packed with heparin and histamine. Rarest leukocyte, under 1% of the differential (see #53).
questions.explanation:
Label 80 is a basophil. It is packed with dark purple-blue granules that hide most of the nucleus.

Basophils are the rarest white blood cells. Their granules hold histamine. Like mast cells, they release histamine in allergic reactions.

Big idea: basophils and mast cells cause the symptoms of type I (allergic) reactions.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 81 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The abundant pink-staining biconcave discs with central pallor — the pale center reflects the thin middle of the biconcave disc, and its presence confirms normal hemoglobin content. Anucleate in mammals, which maximizes hemoglobin volume and flexibility for passage through capillaries.
questions.explanation:
Label 81 is a red blood cell (erythrocyte). Red blood cells are the many pink discs with paler centers that fill the background.

Red blood cells have no nucleus. Their shape gives them lots of surface area, and they are full of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.

Big idea: red blood cells carry oxygen; white blood cells defend the body.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 82 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The single midline mass of lymphoid tissue in the roof of the nasopharynx, the highest green structure in the figure, positioned behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Unlike the palatine tonsils it is covered by ciliated respiratory epithelium and has no true crypts. Its enlargement in children obstructs nasal breathing and the Eustachian tube openings, causing mouth breathing, snoring, and recurrent otitis media.
questions.explanation:
Label 82 is the pharyngeal tonsil, also called the adenoids. It sits high at the back of the nasal cavity, at the top of the throat.

The tonsils form a ring of lymphatic tissue around the throat that watches for germs coming in through the nose and mouth. The adenoids can get swollen in children and block breathing through the nose.

Big idea: tonsils are immune tissue placed where germs enter the body.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 83 in the diagram.
questions.note: The official key lists "palatine tonsil" for #83 and "lingual tonsil" for #84. In the figure, 83 points to the elongated mass on the back of the tongue (lingual tonsil) and 84 to the small round mass below the soft palate (palatine tonsil), so the key has them swapped; the annotated key corrects this.
questions.advancedExplanation: Label 83's leader runs down and to the right and terminates on the lower, elongated green mass lying along the posterior third of the dorsum of the tongue. That position (on the tongue itself, below and anterior to the oropharyngeal mass) defines the lingual tonsil. It is covered by stratified squamous epithelium and forms the inferior part of Waldeyer's ring.
questions.explanation:
Label 83 is the lingual tonsil. Its line points to the long mass on the back of the tongue.

The lingual tonsil is lymphatic tissue at the base of the tongue that helps guard the throat against germs. Note: the official key had 83 and 84 swapped; following the lines in the figure shows 83 is the lingual tonsil.

Big idea: there are several tonsils (pharyngeal, palatine, and lingual), named for where they sit.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 84 in the diagram.
questions.note: The official key lists "palatine tonsil" for #83 and "lingual tonsil" for #84. In the figure, 83 points to the elongated mass on the back of the tongue (lingual tonsil) and 84 to the small round mass below the soft palate (palatine tonsil), so the key has them swapped; the annotated key corrects this.
questions.advancedExplanation: Label 84's leader comes from the upper right and terminates on the small round green mass just below the free posterior edge of the soft palate, in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. That is the palatine tonsil: the one visible when you look into an open mouth, the one removed in a tonsillectomy, and the one with deep branching crypts that trap debris and produce tonsilloliths.
questions.explanation:
