Label 84 is the palatine tonsil. Its line points to the small round mass just below the soft palate, at the side of the throat.

The palatine tonsils are the ones you can see when you open your mouth wide, and the ones removed in a tonsillectomy. Note: the official key had 83 and 84 swapped.

Big idea: the palatine tonsils are part of the ring of immune tissue guarding the throat.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 85 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: Two arrowheads mark the long vertical vessel ascending the midline. The thoracic duct is the body's largest lymphatic vessel, running from the cisterna chyli (#89) at L1–L2 up through the aortic hiatus and the posterior mediastinum to empty into the left jugulo-subclavian junction. It drains the entire body below the diaphragm plus the left upper quadrant — about three-quarters of all lymph. The right lymphatic duct, labeled in the figure's printed text, drains only the right head, neck, arm, and thorax. The asymmetry explains Virchow's node, the left supraclavicular node enlarged by metastatic abdominal cancer.
questions.explanation:
Label 85 is the thoracic duct. It is the long vessel running up the middle of the body.

The thoracic duct is the largest lymph vessel. It collects lymph from most of the body (both legs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head) and empties it into a large vein near the left collarbone.

Big idea: lymph vessels return leaked fluid to the blood. The thoracic duct is the main return pipe.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 86 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The small green worm-shaped projection off the cecum in the right lower quadrant. It is densely packed with lymphoid follicles — gut-associated lymphoid tissue — and is now understood to serve as a reservoir for the commensal microbiota that can recolonize the colon after diarrheal illness, rather than being vestigial. That lymphoid tissue is also why it obstructs and inflames so readily in adolescents, when the follicles are at their largest.
questions.explanation:
Label 86 is the appendix (vermiform appendix). It is the small, finger-like tube hanging from the beginning of the large intestine.

The appendix contains lymphatic tissue, so it is considered part of the immune system. It can become inflamed and infected, which is called appendicitis.

Big idea: lymphatic tissue is found along the digestive tract to protect against germs in food.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 87 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The green tissue within the proximal femur. Bone marrow is a primary (central) lymphoid organ — the site where all blood cells originate from hematopoietic stem cells, and where B lymphocytes both develop and complete their maturation and negative selection. (T cells originate here but mature in the thymus.) Everything else green in this figure is secondary lymphoid tissue, where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen.
questions.explanation:
Label 87 is bone marrow, shown inside the top of the thigh bone.

Red bone marrow makes all blood cells, including every kind of white blood cell. B cells also mature in the bone marrow, which is why it is called a primary lymphatic organ.

Big idea: bone marrow is where immune cells are born.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 88 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The large comma-shaped organ in the left upper quadrant behind the stomach, under ribs 9–11. It is the largest secondary lymphoid organ, with two functionally distinct compartments: white pulp (periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths of T cells and B-cell follicles) mounting immune responses against blood-borne antigen, and red pulp (sinusoids and cords of Billroth) filtering senescent erythrocytes and opsonized encapsulated bacteria — the function whose loss causes OPSI in #58.
questions.explanation:
Label 88 is the spleen, the large organ on the left side of the upper abdomen.

The spleen filters blood. Its red pulp removes old red blood cells, and its white pulp is full of lymphocytes that respond to germs in the blood.

Big idea: lymph nodes filter lymph, while the spleen filters blood.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 89 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The spindle-shaped dilation at the inferior end of the thoracic duct, at roughly L1–L2 behind and to the right of the aorta. It is the confluence where the intestinal trunk — carrying fat-laden chyle from the gut (#65) — joins the right and left lumbar trunks draining the lower limbs and pelvis. Its name records its contents: the "cistern of chyle," milky after a fatty meal.
questions.explanation:
Label 89 is the cisterna chyli. It is the small, swollen sac at the bottom of the thoracic duct in the upper abdomen.

The cisterna chyli collects lymph from the legs and the intestines. Lymph from the intestines contains absorbed fat (chyle), which is how it got its name.

Big idea: the lymphatic system carries fat absorbed from the intestines into the blood.

questions.prompt: Write the correct name of the structure labeled 90 in the diagram.
questions.advancedExplanation: The oval green aggregates studding the wall of the small intestine, concentrated in the ileum. These are aggregated lymphoid follicles — organized B-cell follicles with germinal centers, surrounding T-cell zones, and an overlying follicle-associated epithelium containing the M cells of #51. They are the inductive site for mucosal IgA responses and the single largest collection of lymphoid tissue in the body. Note the relationship to #97: a Peyer's patch is a cluster of the solitary lymphoid follicles seen in that cross-section. Flagged — official key error at 83 and 84. The official key reads "83) Palatine tonsil / 84) Lingual tonsil." The figure shows the reverse. Tracing the leader lines: 83's line enters from the left at the level of the oral cavity and descends to the inferior, elongated green mass lying along the posterior dorsum of the tongue; 84's line enters from the upper right and terminates on the small round green mass immediately below the posterior free edge of the soft palate. In a midsagittal view the three tonsils of Waldeyer's ring stack top to bottom as pharyngeal → palatine → lingual, so the superior small round mass is palatine and the inferior elongated mass on the tongue is lingual. Correct answers: 83 = lingual tonsil, 84 = palatine tonsil. Students who answered correctly will be marked wrong on two labels (2 points) unless this is corrected; students who followed the key's ordering should be credited either way, since the error is the exam's.
questions.explanation:
Label 90 is Peyer's patches. They are the clusters of immune tissue shown along the small intestine.

Peyer's patches are found mostly in the ileum. They sample material from the gut and start immune responses against harmful germs.

Big idea: Peyer's patches are part of MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue), the immune tissue that guards mucous membranes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a component of the immune system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The liver has some immune cells but is mainly a digestive and metabolic organ.
Correct. Lymph nodes filter lymph and hold many immune cells.
Correct. Skin is the body's first barrier against germs.
Correct. The spleen filters blood and contains many lymphocytes.
Correct. Tonsils are lymphatic tissue that guards the throat.
Correct. The thymus is where T cells mature.

questions.explanation:
The answers are lymph nodes, skin, spleen, tonsils, and thymus. The immune system includes barriers that keep germs out and organs where immune cells are made, trained, and gathered.

Skin is a physical barrier. The thymus trains T cells. Lymph nodes filter lymph, the spleen filters blood, and tonsils guard the throat. The liver does contain some immune cells (Kupffer cells), but it is mainly a digestive and metabolic organ, so it is not counted as part of the immune system here.

Big idea: the immune system is spread throughout the body, from barriers like skin to lymphatic organs like the spleen and lymph nodes.

questions.prompt: White blood cells called __________ are important in specific defenses against pathogens.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are proteins made by B cells, not white blood cells.
Incorrect. Granulocytes are part of non-specific (innate) defense.
Correct. B and T lymphocytes provide specific defense.
Incorrect. Monocytes are part of non-specific (innate) defense.
Incorrect. Thrombocytes are platelets that help with clotting.
Incorrect. Vaccines are a medical tool, not a type of white blood cell.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lymphocytes. Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) are the white blood cells of the adaptive immune system. Each one recognizes a specific germ, which is why their defense is called 'specific'.

Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and monocytes are part of the innate, non-specific defense. Antibodies are proteins, not cells. Thrombocytes are platelets that help blood clot. Vaccines are medical products, not white blood cells.

Big idea: specific (adaptive) immunity is carried out by lymphocytes; non-specific (innate) immunity uses other white blood cells and barriers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells produces antibodies?

choices.explanation: Correct. B cells (as plasma cells) make antibodies.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; they do not make antibodies.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells present antigens to T cells.
Incorrect. Helper T cells help B cells, but do not make antibodies themselves.
Incorrect. Myeloid cells are a family of cells like neutrophils and monocytes; they do not make antibodies.
Incorrect. Natural killer cells kill infected cells directly.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B cells. When a B cell meets the germ it recognizes (usually with help from a helper T cell), it multiplies and turns into plasma cells. Plasma cells are B cells that act as antibody factories.

Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells directly. Helper T cells give signals that help B cells, but they do not make antibodies themselves. Dendritic cells show germ pieces to T cells. Natural killer cells kill infected cells without antibodies.

Big idea: antibodies are made by B cells (as plasma cells). This is called humoral immunity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not an innate immune cell?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Basophils are real innate immune cells that release histamine.
Incorrect. Eosinophils are real innate immune cells that fight parasites.
Correct. 'Iodophil' is not a real immune cell.
Incorrect. Neutrophils are real innate immune cells that eat bacteria.
Correct. 'Rheophil' is not a real immune cell.
Correct. 'Thiophil' is not a real immune cell.

questions.explanation:
The answers are iodophil, rheophil, and thiophil, because these are made-up names, not real cells. The real innate immune white blood cells called granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.

Neutrophils eat bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites and help in allergies, and basophils release histamine. All three are part of the innate immune system. Any name not on that list is not a real immune cell.

Big idea: know the real types of white blood cells and their jobs: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of active immunity?

choices.text: Antibodies are introduced from outside of the body
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies coming from outside the body is passive immunity.
Correct. Active immunity creates memory cells that last for years.
Incorrect. Short-term protection describes passive immunity.
Correct. Getting infected and recovering builds natural active immunity.
Correct. Vaccines build artificial active immunity.
Incorrect. Active immunity takes days to weeks to build; passive immunity is immediate.

questions.explanation:
The answers are: it generates long-lasting memory cells, it results from direct infection, and it results from vaccination. Active immunity means your own immune system makes the antibodies and memory cells.

This happens when you get sick and recover (natural active) or when you get a vaccine (artificial active). Because memory cells are made, protection lasts a long time. Passive immunity is the opposite: antibodies come from outside (like from a mother or an injection), work right away, but fade within weeks or months.

Big idea: active immunity is slower to build but long-lasting; passive immunity is immediate but temporary.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of natural passive immunity?

choices.text: Administering an antiserum to a baby born to a mother with Hepatitis B
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Giving antiserum is a medical treatment, so it is artificial passive immunity.

choices.text: Delivering a mother’s antibodies through breast milk
choices.explanation: Correct. Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive immunity.
Incorrect. Getting sick and recovering is natural active immunity.
Incorrect. A vaccine is artificial active immunity.

choices.text: Having at least 85% of a population vaccinated against COVID-19
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccinating most of a population creates herd immunity.

choices.text: Transfering antibodies from maternal blood via the placenta
choices.explanation: Correct. Antibodies crossing the placenta are natural passive immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answers are a mother's antibodies through breast milk and antibodies passing from the mother's blood through the placenta. Natural passive immunity happens when a baby receives ready-made antibodies from its mother in the normal course of life.

IgG antibodies cross the placenta before birth, and IgA antibodies come in breast milk. The baby is protected right away, but the protection fades over months because the baby did not make the antibodies itself. Giving antiserum is artificial passive immunity, getting sick is natural active immunity, a vaccine is artificial active immunity, and vaccinating most of a population creates herd immunity.

Big idea: 'natural' means it happens without medical treatment, and 'passive' means the antibodies were made by someone else.

questions.prompt: Immunoglobulins that protects against parasitic worms are:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA protects mucous membranes like the gut and airways.
Incorrect. IgC is not a real antibody class.
Incorrect. IgD sits on the surface of B cells.
Correct. IgE helps fight parasitic worms (and causes allergies).
Incorrect. IgG is the main antibody in the blood for many germs, but not the special parasite fighter.
Incorrect. IgM is the first antibody made during an infection.

questions.explanation:
The answer is IgE. IgE antibodies attach to mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. When IgE grabs a parasite, these cells release chemicals that attack worms that are too big to be eaten by phagocytes.

IgE is also the antibody that causes allergies, because it can also react to harmless things like pollen. IgA protects mucous membranes, IgG is the most common antibody in blood, IgM is made first in an infection, and IgD sits on B cells. 'IgC' is not a real antibody class.

Big idea: the five antibody classes (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE) each have special jobs. IgE handles parasites and allergies.

questions.prompt: Which of these functions are attributed to T cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Each T cell recognizes one specific antigen, not any antigen.
Correct. Helper T cells drive allergic (adaptive) responses to allergens.
Incorrect. B cells make antibodies, not T cells.
Correct. Regulatory T cells keep the immune response under control.
Correct. Helper T cells release cytokines to signal other cells.
Correct. Cytotoxic T cells can find and kill cancer cells.

questions.explanation:
The answers are: develop adaptive immunity to allergens, regulate the immune response, secrete cytokines, and target cancer cells. T cells are lymphocytes that mature in the thymus.

Helper T cells release cytokines that direct other immune cells, and they are involved in allergic responses. Regulatory T cells calm the immune response so it does not attack the body. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells and cancer cells. T cells do not make antibodies (that is B cells), and each T cell recognizes only one specific antigen, not 'any' antigen.

Big idea: T cells are the managers and soldiers of adaptive immunity, while B cells make antibodies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is involved in the activation of a B cell?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are made after the B cell is activated; they do not activate it.
Correct. The B cell must first bind its specific antigen.
Correct. Cytokines from helper T cells signal the B cell to activate.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; they do not activate B cells.
Correct. Helper T cells give B cells the second signal they need.
Correct. Interleukins are cytokines that help activate B cells.

questions.explanation:
The answers are antigen, cytokine, helper T cell, and interleukin. To become fully active, a B cell usually needs two things. First, its receptor must bind its specific antigen. Second, it needs help from a helper T cell.

The helper T cell touches the B cell and releases cytokines, especially interleukins (a type of cytokine), that tell the B cell to multiply and become antibody-making plasma cells. Antibodies are the result of B cell activation, not a cause. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells and do not activate B cells.

Big idea: the adaptive immune system is a team. Helper T cells are needed to fully turn on B cells.

questions.prompt: Compared to a primary immune response, a secondary response:

choices.text: Appears mainly in the bone marrow
choices.explanation: Correct (per this key). Long-lived plasma cells in the bone marrow make much of the antibody in a secondary response.
Correct. Memory cells let the secondary response start faster.

choices.text: Has a lag phase of 4-7 days
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A 4-7 day lag is typical of the primary response; the secondary lag is shorter.

choices.text: Peaks its antibody levels in 3-5 days
choices.explanation: Correct. Antibody levels in a secondary response peak sooner, in just a few days.

choices.text: Produces a large amount of IgM
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Large amounts of IgM are typical of the primary response; the secondary response is mostly IgG.
Correct. The secondary response makes much more antibody.

questions.explanation:
The official answers are: it appears mainly in the bone marrow, it is faster, its antibody levels peak in 3-5 days, and it makes many more antibodies. The first time you meet a germ, you have a primary response. The next time, memory cells cause a secondary response.

The secondary response starts faster (lag of 1-3 days instead of 4-7), peaks sooner, and makes much more antibody, mostly IgG. Many textbooks note that in a primary response antibodies are made mainly in lymph nodes and spleen, while in a secondary response much of the antibody comes from long-lived plasma cells that settle in the bone marrow. A 4-7 day lag and lots of IgM describe the primary response.

Big idea: memory cells make the second response to a germ faster and stronger. This is how vaccines protect you.

questions.prompt: What is the response of an immune system when tissues are injured by bacteria, toxins, or heat called?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Adaptation is not the name of this immune response.
Incorrect. An allergic reaction is an overreaction to harmless things, not the general response to injury.
Incorrect. Immunization means getting immunity, usually from a vaccine.
Incorrect. Infection is germs invading; the body's response to it is inflammation.
Correct. Inflammation is the response to injured tissue.
Incorrect. Irradiation means exposure to radiation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is inflammation. Inflammation is the body's response to tissue damage from germs, toxins, heat, or injury. It is part of the innate immune system.

Damaged cells and mast cells release chemicals like histamine. Blood vessels widen and become leaky, so more blood and white blood cells reach the area. This causes the four classic signs: redness, heat, swelling, and pain. An allergic reaction is a specific overreaction to harmless things, and infection is the germs getting in, not the body's response.

Big idea: inflammation brings defenders and repair materials to damaged tissue.

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells are primarily targeted by HIV?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells have CD8, not CD4, so HIV does not target them.
Correct. Helper T cells carry CD4, HIV's main receptor.
Incorrect. Natural killer cells are not HIV's main target.
Incorrect. HIV does not primarily target nerve cells.
Incorrect. Some phagocytes (macrophages) can be infected, but helper T cells are the main target.
Incorrect. Regulatory cells are not HIV's main target.

questions.explanation:
The answer is helper T cells. HIV enters cells by attaching to the CD4 protein, which helper T cells have lots of.

Over time, HIV destroys helper T cells. Since helper T cells direct both B cells and cytotoxic T cells, losing them weakens the whole immune system. When helper T cell counts fall very low, the person has AIDS and can get infections a healthy immune system would easily fight off.

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency caused by the loss of helper T cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not an autoimmune disorder?

choices.explanation: Correct. Asthma is an allergic or irritant airway disease, not autoimmune.
Incorrect. Graves' disease is autoimmune; antibodies overstimulate the thyroid.
Correct. Hepatitis is usually caused by viruses, not autoimmunity.
Incorrect. Multiple sclerosis is autoimmune; the immune system attacks nerve myelin.
Correct. Osteoarthritis is joint wear-and-tear, not autoimmune.
Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune; the immune system attacks the joints.

questions.explanation:
The answers are asthma, hepatitis, and osteoarthritis. An autoimmune disease is one in which the immune system attacks the body's own healthy tissue.

Graves' disease (antibodies overstimulate the thyroid), multiple sclerosis (immune cells attack nerve coverings), and rheumatoid arthritis (immune attack on joint linings) are autoimmune. Asthma is usually an allergic or irritant reaction of the airways. Hepatitis is usually caused by a virus (though a rare autoimmune form exists). Osteoarthritis is wear-and-tear of the joints, not an immune attack.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases happen when the immune system cannot tell 'self' from 'non-self'.

questions.prompt: ______ is an enzyme found in fluids like tears, mucus, and saliva

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Amylase in saliva digests starch; it is not found in tears to fight germs.
Incorrect. Proteases digest proteins; they are not the germ-fighting enzyme in tears.
Correct. Lysozyme in tears, saliva, and mucus breaks down bacterial cell walls.
Incorrect. Nucleases digest nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lysozyme. Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears, saliva, mucus, and breast milk. It breaks down the cell walls of many bacteria, causing them to burst.

It is part of the innate immune system's chemical barriers. Amylase in saliva digests starch, proteases digest proteins, and nucleases digest DNA and RNA; none of these is the germ-fighting enzyme found in tears.

Big idea: the body's first line of defense includes physical barriers (skin, mucus) and chemical barriers (lysozyme, stomach acid).

questions.prompt: __________ is the term used when antibodies completely cover a pathogen's binding sites

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Precipitation is when antibodies make dissolved antigens clump and settle out.
Incorrect. Agglutination is when antibodies clump whole cells or germs together.
Incorrect. Complement fixation is when antibodies activate complement proteins.
Incorrect. 'Activation' is not the term for covering a germ's binding sites.
Correct. The right term, neutralization, is not listed.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'None of the above'. When antibodies cover the parts of a germ or toxin that it uses to attach to cells, it is called neutralization. A neutralized virus cannot attach to and enter cells, and a neutralized toxin cannot do harm.

Agglutination is when antibodies clump many germs together. Precipitation is when antibodies make dissolved antigens clump and fall out of solution. 'Fixation' usually refers to complement fixation, when antibodies start the complement system. None of these is the word for covering binding sites.

Big idea: antibodies protect us in several ways: neutralization, agglutination, precipitation, and activating complement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells is not a part of the innate immune system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Basophils are innate cells that release histamine.
Incorrect. Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that kill infected cells without needing training.
Incorrect. Macrophages are innate phagocytes.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells are innate cells, even though they help start adaptive immunity.
Correct. Every listed cell is part of the innate immune system.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'None of the above', because all of the listed cells are part of the innate immune system. The innate system is the fast, general defense we are born with.

Basophils release histamine, natural killer (NK) cells kill virus-infected and cancer cells, macrophages eat germs, and dendritic cells catch germs (and then show them to the adaptive system). Even though dendritic cells link to adaptive immunity, they are innate cells themselves.

Big idea: innate immune cells include neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells. The adaptive system uses B and T lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: What is the correct series of events for phagocyte mobilization in the inflammatory response?

choices.explanation: Correct. More white cells are released, they stick to vessel walls, squeeze out, and follow chemical signals.
Incorrect. Chemotaxis (moving toward the infection) is the last step, not the first.
Incorrect. Leukocytosis (more white cells) comes before margination.
Incorrect. Cells must stick to the vessel wall (margination) before squeezing through it (diapedesis).

questions.explanation:
The answer is leukocytosis, margination, diapedesis, chemotaxis. When tissue is injured or infected, chemicals signal the bone marrow to release more white blood cells into the blood. That increase is leukocytosis.

Next, white blood cells slow down and stick to the walls of nearby blood vessels (margination). Then they squeeze between the cells of the vessel wall into the tissue (diapedesis). Finally, they follow a chemical trail to the site of infection (chemotaxis).

Big idea: inflammation brings white blood cells to the problem in an orderly sequence: more cells, stick, squeeze out, and move toward the trouble.

questions.prompt: Which of the following antibody is the least common in plasma?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgG is the most common antibody in the blood.
Incorrect. IgM is less common than IgG but much more common than IgE.
Incorrect. IgD is rare, but there is still more of it than IgE.
Correct. IgE is the least common antibody in plasma.
Incorrect. IgA is the second most common antibody in the blood and the main one in secretions.

questions.explanation:
The answer is IgE. IgE makes up much less than 1% of the antibodies in blood plasma. Most IgE is not floating freely; it is attached to mast cells and basophils, waiting to react to allergens or parasites.

IgG is the most common antibody in the blood (about 75-80%), then IgA, then IgM. IgD is also rare, but IgE is the rarest of all.

Big idea: each antibody class has a different amount and job. IgE is rare in the blood but powerful in allergies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an antigen-presenting cell?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. T cells look at antigens shown by APCs; they do not present antigens to other T cells.
Correct. B cells present the antigen they bind to helper T cells.
Correct. Dendritic cells are the most powerful antigen-presenting cells.
Correct. Macrophages present pieces of germs they have eaten.

questions.explanation:
The answers are B cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) take in a germ, break it into pieces, and display those pieces on MHC class II molecules on their surface, so helper T cells can recognize them.

Dendritic cells are the best APCs. Macrophages present antigens after eating germs. B cells take in the specific antigen their receptor binds and present it to helper T cells to get help. T cells are the ones that RECEIVE the antigen presentation; they are not APCs.

Big idea: T cells cannot see whole germs; they need APCs to show them pieces of the germ.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are considered antimicrobial proteins?

choices.explanation: Correct. Interferons help cells resist viruses.
Incorrect. A hapten is a small molecule that can trigger immunity only when attached to a larger carrier.
Incorrect. An epitope is the part of an antigen that an antibody binds.
Correct. Complement proteins attack and mark germs.
Incorrect. Haptens and epitopes are not antimicrobial proteins.

questions.explanation:
The answers are interferons and complement. Antimicrobial proteins are proteins of the innate immune system that attack germs or stop them from spreading.

Interferons are released by virus-infected cells to warn neighboring cells to protect themselves. Complement is a group of blood proteins that can poke holes in bacteria, mark them for phagocytes, and boost inflammation. A hapten is a small molecule that only causes an immune response when attached to a bigger protein, and an epitope is the specific part of an antigen that an antibody recognizes; neither is an antimicrobial protein.

Big idea: the innate immune system includes protective proteins, like interferons and complement, as well as cells and barriers.

questions.prompt: Pyrogens, released by leukocytes, target the ________ to initiate a fever response

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Peyer's patches are immune tissue in the intestine, not a temperature control center.
Correct. Pyrogens reset the hypothalamus's thermostat, causing fever.
Incorrect. Helper T cells do not control body temperature.
Incorrect. The thymus trains T cells; it does not set body temperature.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is a part of the brain that acts as the body's thermostat, keeping body temperature near 37 °C (98.6 °F).

When white blood cells fight an infection, they release chemicals called pyrogens. Pyrogens tell the hypothalamus to raise the thermostat setting, so the body warms up and you get a fever. A higher temperature can slow germ growth and speed up immune responses.

Big idea: fever is an innate immune defense controlled by the brain.

questions.prompt: Which receptors are attacked in myasthenia gravis?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Calcium receptors are not the target in myasthenia gravis.
Correct. Antibodies attack the acetylcholine receptors on muscles.
Incorrect. ATP receptors are not the target.
Incorrect. Magnesium receptors are not the target.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is acetylcholine receptors. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease. The immune system makes antibodies that attack the acetylcholine receptors on muscles, at the spot where nerves meet muscles.

Nerves tell muscles to contract by releasing acetylcholine, which must bind to these receptors. With fewer working receptors, the signal is weak, so muscles get tired and weak, especially with use. Common signs are drooping eyelids, double vision, and trouble swallowing.

Big idea: in autoimmune diseases, antibodies or immune cells attack normal parts of the body. In myasthenia gravis, the target is the acetylcholine receptor.

questions.prompt: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) targets which cell?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells have CD8, not CD4.
Incorrect. Memory B cells are not HIV's main target.
Incorrect. Plasma cells are not HIV's main target.
Correct. HIV targets CD4 helper T cells.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is helper T cells. HIV enters cells by binding to a protein called CD4. Helper T cells have lots of CD4 on their surface.

As HIV destroys helper T cells, the immune system loses its 'coordinators', which weakens B cell and cytotoxic T cell responses. Without treatment, this leads to AIDS, when the body cannot fight off infections.

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency caused by the loss of helper T (CD4) cells.

questions.prompt: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Dendrites receive signals; they are not the main target in MS.
Correct. The immune system attacks the myelin sheath in MS.
Incorrect. Axons can be damaged later, but the myelin around them is the main target.
Incorrect. Axon terminals are not the target in MS.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the myelin sheath. Myelin is a fatty covering wrapped around nerve fibers, like the insulation on an electrical wire. It helps nerve signals travel quickly.

In multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disease, immune cells attack the myelin in the brain and spinal cord. Where the myelin is damaged, nerve signals slow down or stop, causing problems like weakness, numbness, and vision trouble.

Big idea: MS is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the protective coating of nerves.

questions.prompt: Provide three differences between innate immunity and adaptive immunity.
questions.answer: Innate immunity is a general, quick response that uses rely on structures present at birth. Adaptive immunity is a specific response to pathogens that takes much longer to activate, with the ability to memorize past infections to protect from future invaders.
questions.explanation:
Innate immunity is the defense you are born with. It works within minutes to hours, attacks all germs in the same general way, and does not remember germs it has met before. Examples include skin, mucus, phagocytes, inflammation, and fever.

Adaptive immunity is learned. It takes days to build the first time, targets one specific germ, and creates memory cells, so the next response to that germ is faster and stronger. It uses B cells (antibodies) and T cells.

Big idea: three key differences are speed (fast vs slow), specificity (general vs specific), and memory (none vs long-lasting).

questions.prompt: What are the classes of MHC proteins? What are two differences between the classes?
questions.answer: Classes I and II. Class I MHC proteins are found on all cells except from RBCs, can be displayed by an antigen-presenting cell or infected cell, and is recognized by cytotoxic T cells. Class II MHC proteins are present only on antigen-presenting cells, recognized by helper T cells, and help to initiated immune response.
questions.explanation:
There are two main classes: MHC class I and MHC class II. MHC proteins are like display stands on a cell's surface that hold up small pieces of protein so T cells can check them.

MHC class I is found on almost all cells with a nucleus (red blood cells do not have it). It shows pieces of proteins made inside the cell, so if a virus is inside, cytotoxic (CD8) T cells can see it and kill the cell. MHC class II is found only on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). It shows pieces of germs the cell has eaten, and helper (CD4) T cells look at it to start an immune response.

Big idea: MHC I says 'here is what is inside me' to cytotoxic T cells; MHC II says 'here is what I found' to helper T cells.

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of antigen-presenting cells.
questions.answer: They phagocytize foreign cells, present fragments of the digested cells on their surface to activate T cells to then deal with said foreign cells.
questions.explanation:
Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) are messengers between the innate and adaptive immune systems. They capture germs, break them into small pieces (antigens), and display those pieces on their surface using MHC proteins.

T cells can only recognize antigens when they are presented this way. When a helper T cell recognizes the antigen on an APC, it becomes activated and starts the adaptive response, helping B cells make antibodies and helping cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. Dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells are the main APCs.

Big idea: APCs 'show' the adaptive immune system what to attack.

questions.prompt: In type I hypersensitivities, explain the difference between initial sensitization and a subsequent/secondary response.
questions.answer: In the initial exposure to an allergen, there are no symptoms present but the person becomes sensitized to the allergen, triggering the release of IgE and attachment to inflammatory cells. In an allergic response, it is a later encounter with an allergen, triggering a release of histamine/inflammatory chemicals.
questions.explanation:
Type I hypersensitivity is an allergy. The first time someone meets an allergen (like pollen), they usually have no symptoms. This is called sensitization: the immune system makes IgE antibodies against the allergen, and the IgE attaches to mast cells and basophils.

The next time the person meets the same allergen, it binds the IgE already sitting on the mast cells. This makes the mast cells release histamine and other chemicals within minutes, causing allergy symptoms like sneezing, itching, swelling, or even anaphylaxis.

Big idea: allergies need a first 'setup' exposure; symptoms appear on later exposures.

questions.prompt: What cells results from B lymphocyte proliferation following contact with a foreign antigen? What are each cell's function?
questions.answer: Effectors B/plasma cells and memory B cells. Plasma cells mass produced antibodies to neutralize the foreign cells and memory B cells have the same surface antibodies, to prepare to a secondary response.
questions.explanation:
When a B cell recognizes its antigen (and gets help from a helper T cell), it divides many times. This makes two kinds of cells: plasma cells (also called effector B cells) and memory B cells.

Plasma cells are antibody factories. They release large amounts of antibodies that neutralize and tag the germ for destruction. Memory B cells live for a long time and carry the same antibody on their surface. If the same germ returns, they respond quickly and strongly (the secondary response).

Big idea: B cells create immediate defenders (plasma cells) and long-term memory (memory B cells).

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between active natural immunity and active artificial immunity. Provide an example of each.
questions.answer: Active natural immunity is the production of antibodies and immune memory from natural exposure to the pathogen, ex: contracting and recovering from a disease. Active artificial immunity is the production of antibodies and immune memory from the artificial exposure through a weakened pathogen or parts of a pathogen, ex: vaccines
questions.explanation:
Both are 'active' immunity, meaning your own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells. The difference is how you are exposed to the germ.

Active natural immunity comes from catching the disease in everyday life and recovering, for example getting chickenpox. Active artificial immunity comes from a medical exposure, a vaccine, which uses a weakened or killed germ or just a part of it, for example the flu shot. Both create memory cells that protect you later.

Big idea: 'natural' vs 'artificial' describes how exposure happened; 'active' vs 'passive' describes who made the antibodies.

questions.prompt: The innate immunity that protects a person digging in the garden from developing a microbial infections includes all the following except ?

choices.explanation: Correct. Lymphocytes are part of adaptive, not innate, immunity.
Incorrect. Skin is an innate physical barrier.
Incorrect. Mucous membranes are innate barriers that trap germs.
Incorrect. Acidic secretions like sweat are innate chemical barriers.
Incorrect. Antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme and complement are innate defenses.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lymphocytes. The question asks which is NOT part of innate immunity. Innate immunity is the general defense we are born with: skin, mucous membranes, acid secretions (like sweat and stomach acid), and antimicrobial proteins like lysozyme and complement.

Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) belong to the adaptive immune system, which learns to target specific germs. They are not part of the first, general defenses that stop germs from a garden scrape.

Big idea: innate immunity is fast and general; adaptive immunity (lymphocytes) is specific and slower.

questions.prompt: What are antigens?

choices.text: proteins found in the blood that cause foreign blood cells to clump
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes antibodies that clump cells (agglutinins), not antigens.

choices.text: proteins embedded in B cell membranes
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes B cell receptors, which bind antigens.

choices.text: proteins that consist of two light and two heavy polypeptide chains
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Two light and two heavy chains describe an antibody.

choices.text: foreign molecules that trigger the generation of antibodies
choices.explanation: Correct. Antigens are foreign molecules that cause antibody production.

choices.text: proteins released during an inflammatory response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inflammatory chemicals are released during inflammation; they are not antigens.

questions.explanation:
The answer is foreign molecules that trigger the generation of antibodies. An antigen is anything the immune system can recognize as foreign, such as proteins on a virus, bacterium, or pollen grain.

When the immune system meets an antigen, B cells make antibodies that fit it like a lock and key. The other choices describe antibodies (proteins with two light and two heavy chains), B cell receptors, or inflammatory chemicals, not antigens.

Big idea: antigens are the targets; antibodies are the weapons made against them.

questions.prompt: A person exposed to a new cold virus would not feel better for one to two weeks because

choices.text: specific B cells and T cells must be selected prior to a protective response.
choices.explanation: Correct. The rare B and T cells that match the new virus must be selected and multiplied, which takes 1-2 weeks.

choices.text: it takes up to two weeks to stimulate immunologic memory cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Memory cells are made during the response; they are not what clears the first infection.

choices.text: phagocytic cells must first be activated.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Phagocytes are activated within hours, so they do not cause a 1-2 week delay.

choices.text: antigen receptors are not the same.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This statement is vague and does not explain the delay.

choices.text: they develop a fever of 100°F or higher.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A fever is a symptom, not the reason recovery takes time.

questions.note: The official key marks C; the delay is because specific B and T cells must be selected and expanded before a protective adaptive response (A).
questions.explanation:
The answer is that specific B cells and T cells must be selected before a protective response. A new cold virus is something your adaptive immune system has never seen. Out of millions of B and T cells, only a few happen to fit this virus.

Those few cells must be found (selected), then multiply into large armies, which takes about a week or two. Until then, the virus keeps spreading and you feel sick. (The official key chose 'phagocytic cells must first be activated', but phagocytes respond within hours, so they do not explain a 1-2 week delay.)

Big idea: the first (primary) adaptive response is slow because the right lymphocytes must be found and multiplied.

questions.prompt: Which of the following cell types are responsible for initiating a secondary immune response?

choices.explanation: Correct. Memory cells start the faster, stronger secondary response.
Incorrect. Macrophages are innate cells without specific memory.
Incorrect. Stem cells make new blood cells; they do not remember germs.
Incorrect. Ordinary (naive) B cells have not met the germ before; memory B cells start the secondary response.
Incorrect. Ordinary T cells have not met the germ before; memory T cells start the secondary response.

questions.explanation:
The answer is memory cells. After you fight off an infection, some B and T cells stay behind as memory cells. They 'remember' that specific germ.

If the same germ returns, memory cells recognize it quickly and multiply fast, starting a secondary immune response that is faster and stronger than the first. Macrophages, stem cells, and ordinary B and T cells do not carry this memory.

Big idea: memory cells are why you usually do not get sick twice from the same germ, and why vaccines work.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of both T cells and B cells?

choices.text: They produce effector cells against specific pathogens.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. A is true, but so is B, so 'Only A and B' is the best answer.

choices.text: They are produced from stem cells of the bone marrow.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. B is true, but so is A, so 'Only A and B' is the best answer.

choices.text: They can attack and destroy invading pathogens.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. B cells do not destroy germs directly; they make antibodies.

choices.text: Only options A and B are true.
choices.explanation: Correct. Both make effector cells, and both come from bone marrow stem cells.

choices.text: Options A, B, and C are true.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Statement C is not true of B cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'Only options A and B are true'. Both B and T cells make effector cells against specific germs: B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies, and T cells become helper or cytotoxic T cells. Both also come from stem cells in the bone marrow.

Option C is not true of both. Cytotoxic T cells directly destroy infected cells, but B cells do not attack germs directly; they make antibodies that mark germs for destruction.

Big idea: B and T cells share an origin and both target specific germs, but they fight in different ways.

questions.prompt: Which cells will respond whether you have a viral infection or a bacterial infection?

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Plasma cells respond to both, but so do helper T cells.
Incorrect by itself. Helper T cells respond to both, but so do plasma cells.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells mainly target virus-infected cells, not typical bacteria.
Correct. Plasma cells and helper T cells respond to both viral and bacterial infections.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells are not main responders to most bacterial infections.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'only options A and B': plasma cells and helper T cells. Plasma cells make antibodies, which can attack both viruses and bacteria floating in body fluids. Helper T cells coordinate almost every adaptive response, so they help against both.

Cytotoxic T cells mainly kill cells that have germs hiding inside them, especially virus-infected cells. Most bacteria live outside cells, so cytotoxic T cells are not the main defenders against a typical bacterial infection.

Big idea: antibodies and helper T cells work against many kinds of germs; cytotoxic T cells specialize in infected cells.

questions.prompt: What happens to people who receive flu vaccinations?

choices.text: They develop active immunity to the flu.
choices.explanation: Correct. Vaccines make your own immune system respond, which is active immunity.

choices.text: They develop passive immunity to the flu.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Passive immunity means receiving ready-made antibodies, which a vaccine does not give.

choices.text: They have immunity to smallpox infection.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A flu vaccine only protects against flu, not smallpox.

choices.text: They have an increased number of natural killer (NK) cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines do not work by increasing natural killer cells.

choices.text: They develop a hypersensitive humoral immune response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines are meant to cause protection, not hypersensitivity.

questions.note: The official key marks B (passive); vaccination produces active immunity (A).
questions.explanation:
The answer is that people develop active immunity to the flu. A flu vaccine contains killed flu virus or pieces of it. Your own immune system responds by making antibodies and memory cells, which is active immunity.

Passive immunity is when you receive antibodies made by someone else, like a baby getting antibodies from its mother. A flu vaccine does not protect against smallpox, does not raise NK cells, and is not meant to cause hypersensitivity. (The official key marked 'passive', which is a mistake.)

Big idea: vaccines create active, artificial immunity: your body does the work, triggered by a medical treatment.

questions.prompt: The major difference between active and passive immunity is that active immunity requires

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are made, not 'identified and activated'; this does not separate active from passive.

choices.text: rapid increase of lymphocytes in the bone marrow.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This does not describe what makes immunity active.

choices.text: transfer of antibodies from a pregnant woman across the placenta.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies crossing the placenta is passive immunity.

choices.text: direct exposure to a living or simulated pathogen.
choices.explanation: Correct. Active immunity requires exposure to the germ or a vaccine version of it.
Incorrect. Erythrocytes are red blood cells; they are not involved.

questions.explanation:
The answer is direct exposure to a living or simulated pathogen. In active immunity, your immune system must actually meet the germ, either by catching it or through a vaccine that imitates it.

That exposure makes your B and T cells respond and form memory cells. Passive immunity skips this step: you receive ready-made antibodies, like those passed from mother to baby across the placenta (which is a type of passive immunity, not active).

Big idea: active immunity requires meeting the antigen; passive immunity does not.

questions.prompt: What aspect of the immune response would a patient who has a parasitic worm infection and another patient responding to an allergen such as ragweed pollen have in common?

choices.text: Both patients would have an increase on cytotoxic T cell number.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells are not the main responders to worms or pollen.

choices.text: Both patients would suffer from anaphylactic shock.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is a rare, severe reaction; most allergies and worm infections do not cause it.

choices.text: Both patients would risk development of an autoimmune disease.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Neither condition is linked to autoimmune disease.

choices.text: Both patients would be suffering from a decreased level of innate immunity.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Innate immunity is not decreased in these patients.

choices.text: Both patients would have increased levels of IgE (immunoglobulin E).
choices.explanation: Correct. Both parasitic infections and allergies raise IgE levels.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that both patients would have increased levels of IgE. IgE is the antibody that responds to parasitic worms and also to allergens like ragweed pollen.

IgE attaches to mast cells and basophils; when it grabs its target, these cells release histamine and other chemicals. Both conditions also often raise eosinophils. Not every allergy leads to anaphylactic shock, and neither condition is mainly about cytotoxic T cells, autoimmunity, or weaker innate immunity.

Big idea: IgE links parasite defense and allergies.

questions.prompt: The stomach is involved in defense against infection by

choices.text: regurgitating any pathogen that might be swallowed.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The stomach does not vomit up every germ.

choices.text: secreting mucus that is carried away by cilia.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cilia moving mucus are found in the airways, not the stomach.

choices.text: possessing acid that destroys potential pathogens that are swallowed.
choices.explanation: Correct. Strong stomach acid kills many swallowed germs.

choices.text: sending potential pathogens to the liver for destruction.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The stomach does not send germs to the liver.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the stomach has acid that destroys swallowed pathogens. The stomach's hydrochloric acid is very strong (pH about 1.5-3.5), which kills most bacteria that come in with food.

This makes stomach acid part of the innate immune system's chemical barriers. The stomach does not regurgitate every germ, does not use cilia (those are in the airways), and does not send germs to the liver.

Big idea: the digestive system protects the body too: stomach acid is a chemical barrier against germs.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a nonspecific defense against pathogens?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. B cells are specific defenders.
Correct. Inflammation is a nonspecific defense.
Incorrect. Helper T cells are part of specific immunity.
Incorrect. Antibodies target specific antigens.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the inflammatory response. Nonspecific (innate) defenses work against any germ in the same way. Inflammation brings blood and white blood cells to an injured or infected area, no matter what caused it.

B cells, helper T cells, and antibodies are part of specific (adaptive) immunity. They recognize particular germs.

Big idea: nonspecific defenses (barriers, inflammation, fever, phagocytes) act first; specific defenses (lymphocytes, antibodies) target particular germs.

questions.prompt: Phagocytes, such as macrophages,

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Phagocytes do not make antibiotics.
Incorrect. Interferon is mostly made by virus-infected cells.
Incorrect. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses, not phagocytes.
Correct. Phagocytes eat and digest germs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that phagocytes ingest and destroy pathogens. 'Phago' means eat and 'cyte' means cell. Phagocytes like macrophages and neutrophils wrap around germs, pull them inside, and digest them with enzymes.

Phagocytes do not make antibiotics, interferon is made mainly by virus-infected cells, and shutting down immune responses is the job of regulatory T cells.

Big idea: phagocytosis is a key innate defense that cleans up germs and debris.

questions.prompt: Where are the cells of the immune system produced in adults?

choices.explanation: Correct. Immune cells are produced in the bone marrow.
Incorrect. The thymus is where T cells mature, not where they are first made.
Incorrect. Mucous membranes are barriers.
Incorrect. Lymph nodes are where immune cells gather and activate.
Incorrect. The thyroid makes hormones.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bone marrow. In adults, all blood cells, including every type of immune cell, are made from stem cells in the red bone marrow.

Some cells mature elsewhere: T cells finish maturing in the thymus. Lymph nodes are where immune cells gather and meet germs. Mucous membranes are barriers, and the thyroid makes hormones, not immune cells.

Big idea: immune cells are born in the bone marrow, then travel to other organs to mature and work.

questions.prompt: Vaccines are effective in preventing disease because they

choices.text: interfere with the release of suppressor T cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines do not work by interfering with suppressor T cells.

choices.text: are antibodies directed against specific pathogens.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines contain antigens, not antibodies.
Correct. Vaccines cause the body to make antibodies and memory cells.

choices.text: contain specific B cells and T cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines do not contain immune cells.
Incorrect. Thrombocytes are platelets for blood clotting.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that vaccines trigger antibody formation. A vaccine contains a weakened or killed germ, or a piece of it. It safely shows the immune system what the germ looks like.

B cells respond by making antibodies, and memory cells are formed. Later, if the real germ shows up, the immune system responds quickly. Vaccines do not contain antibodies or living immune cells, and they do not change thrombocytes (platelets).

Big idea: vaccines train the immune system ahead of time.

questions.prompt: The skin repels pathogens by

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are made by B cells, not skin.
Correct. Skin is a physical barrier that keeps germs out.
Incorrect. Sweat helps a little, but the main defense is the barrier itself.
Incorrect. Hair follicles do not repel germs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the skin functions as a barrier. Skin is made of tightly packed layers of cells, with a tough outer layer of dead, keratin-filled cells that germs cannot easily get through.

Sweat and oils do help (they are slightly acidic and contain antimicrobial chemicals), but the main way skin repels germs is by being a physical wall. Skin does not make antibodies, and hair follicles are actually weak spots where germs can enter.

Big idea: skin is the body's first line of defense.

questions.prompt: When a puncture wound becomes infected,

choices.text: damaged cells release chemicals the promote the immune response.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. This happens, but so do the others.

choices.text: the temperature around the wound increases.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. The area does get warmer, but the other changes happen too.

choices.text: white blood cells move into the injured area.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. White blood cells do arrive, but the other changes happen too.
Correct. All three happen during inflammation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. An infected puncture wound triggers inflammation. Damaged cells release chemicals like histamine that call in the immune system.

Blood vessels widen, bringing more warm blood, so the area heats up and turns red. White blood cells move out of the blood into the injured area to fight the germs.

Big idea: inflammation is the body's organized response to injury and infection.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true about the release of histamine from cells in the nasal passages?

choices.text: It occurs during an allergic reaction.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are true too.

choices.text: It causes nearby capillaries to swell.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are true too.

choices.text: It may cause increased secretion by mucous membranes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are true too.
Correct. All three statements describe histamine's effects.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. In an allergy like hay fever, mast cells in the nose release histamine when they meet pollen.

Histamine makes nearby capillaries widen and leak, so tissues swell (a stuffy nose). It also makes mucous membranes produce more mucus (a runny nose), and it causes itching and sneezing.

Big idea: histamine causes many allergy symptoms, which is why antihistamines help.

questions.prompt: The first line of defense against infection includes _____________________.

choices.explanation: Correct. Mucous membranes are a first-line barrier.
Incorrect. Neutrophils are part of the second line of defense.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells are part of the third (adaptive) line.
Incorrect. Antibodies are part of the third (adaptive) line.
Incorrect. Phagocytes are part of the second line of defense.

questions.explanation:
The answer is mucous membranes. The first line of defense is made of barriers that keep germs from entering the body: skin, mucous membranes, and their secretions (mucus, tears, saliva, stomach acid).

Neutrophils and phagocytes are part of the second line (innate cells and inflammation). Cytotoxic T cells and antibodies are part of the third line (adaptive immunity).

Big idea: the immune system has three lines of defense: barriers, innate responses, and adaptive responses.

questions.prompt: All of the following have mucous membranes except

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The digestive tract is lined with mucous membranes.
Correct. The outer skin is not a mucous membrane.
Incorrect. The nasal passages are lined with mucous membranes.
Incorrect. The vagina is lined with a mucous membrane.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the surface of the skin. Mucous membranes line body passages that open to the outside, like the digestive tract, the airways (including the nasal passages), and the urinary and reproductive tracts.

The outer skin is a different kind of tissue: a dry, tough, layered epidermis covered with dead cells. It does not make mucus.

Big idea: both skin and mucous membranes are first-line barriers, but they are built differently.

questions.prompt: The redness and swelling associated with an inflammatory response is caused by

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies do not cause redness and swelling.

choices.text: the expansion of local blood vessels.
choices.explanation: Correct. Widened, leaky blood vessels cause redness and swelling.

choices.text: the increase in the number of thrombocytes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Thrombocytes (platelets) help with clotting.
Incorrect. NK cells do not cause these signs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the expansion of local blood vessels. During inflammation, chemicals like histamine make nearby blood vessels widen (vasodilation) and become leaky.

More blood flows in, making the area red and warm. Fluid leaks out of the leaky vessels into the tissue, causing swelling. Antibodies, platelets, and natural killer cells do not cause these signs.

Big idea: redness, heat, swelling, and pain are the classic signs of inflammation, caused mostly by changes in blood vessels.

questions.prompt: Which statement(s) are true about B cells?

choices.text: Sometimes remain in the blood for years.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are also true.
Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are also true.

choices.text: Are stimulated by helper T cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other statements are also true.
Correct. All three statements describe B cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. Memory B cells can stay in the body for years. B cells (as plasma cells) secrete antibodies. And most B cells need signals from helper T cells to become fully active.

Together these describe the B cell's role in humoral (antibody-based) immunity.

Big idea: B cells make antibodies, form long-lasting memory, and work with helper T cells.

questions.prompt: An autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks myelinated nerves is called _______________________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis attacks the joints.
Correct. MS is an attack on the myelin covering of nerves.
Incorrect. Crohn's disease causes inflammation in the digestive tract.
Incorrect. Lupus can affect many organs, but it is not mainly an attack on myelin.

questions.explanation:
The answer is multiple sclerosis (MS). In MS, the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord.

Damaged myelin slows or blocks nerve signals. Rheumatoid arthritis attacks joints, Crohn's disease inflames the digestive tract, and lupus can attack many organs.

Big idea: in each autoimmune disease, the immune system attacks a different part of the body.

questions.prompt: After the initial immune response subsides, B cells that patrol body tissues for long periods of time,

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Helper T cells are a different type of cell.
Incorrect. B cells do not turn into phagocytes.
Correct. Long-lived B cells that remember an antigen are memory cells.

choices.text: cannot react to the original antigen.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Memory cells react strongly to the original antigen.

questions.explanation:
The answer is memory cells. After an infection is over, most of the B cells that fought it die, but some remain as memory B cells.

Memory cells live for a long time and patrol the body. If the same antigen returns, they react quickly. Helper T cells are a different cell type, B cells do not become phagocytes, and memory cells are especially good at reacting to the original antigen.

Big idea: memory cells are the basis of long-term immunity.

questions.prompt: The virus HIV causes the disease AIDS by attacking and destroying _________________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. HIV does not destroy antibodies.
Incorrect. HIV's main target is not B cells.
Correct. HIV destroys helper T cells.
Incorrect. Neutrophils are not HIV's main target.
Incorrect. Erythrocytes are red blood cells, which HIV does not infect.

questions.explanation:
The answer is helper T cells. HIV infects cells that have the CD4 protein, especially helper T cells, and destroys them over time.

Without enough helper T cells, the immune system cannot coordinate its defenses, and the person develops AIDS. HIV does not mainly destroy antibodies, B cells, neutrophils, or red blood cells (erythrocytes).

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency caused by losing helper T cells.

questions.prompt: What is the correct function of mucous membranes?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The outside of the body is covered by skin.

choices.text: Line internal body surfaces that are in contact with the environment.
choices.explanation: Correct. Mucous membranes line inner passages that open to the outside.
Incorrect. Antibodies are made by plasma cells, not by the membranes themselves.

choices.text: Secrete sweat, which has antibacterial enzymes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Sweat comes from sweat glands in the skin.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that mucous membranes line internal body surfaces that are in contact with the environment. These include the inside of the mouth, nose, airways, digestive tract, and urinary and reproductive tracts.

They make mucus that traps germs. Skin, not mucous membranes, covers the outside of the body. Mucous membranes do not make antibodies themselves (though B cells nearby release IgA into the mucus), and sweat comes from sweat glands in the skin.

Big idea: mucous membranes are first-line barriers that protect the body's openings.

questions.prompt: Which response correctly describes antibodies?

choices.text: They prevent diseases caused by vaccines.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vaccines prevent disease; they do not cause it.

choices.text: They are produced by bacteria that infect animals like humans.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies are made by our own B cells, not by bacteria.

choices.text: They help destroy microbes that invade the body.
choices.explanation: Correct. Antibodies help destroy invading microbes.

choices.text: They cause viruses to infect bacterial cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies do not help viruses infect anything.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that antibodies help destroy microbes that invade the body. Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by plasma cells (B cells).

They bind to specific antigens on germs. This can block germs from entering cells, clump them together, and mark them so phagocytes and complement can destroy them. Antibodies are made by our own cells, not by bacteria, and they do not cause infections.

Big idea: antibodies are the main weapons of humoral (antibody-based) immunity.

questions.prompt: The virus HIV can be transmitted

choices.text: through sexual intercourse with an infected person.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other routes are also true.

choices.text: by the transfer of body fluids containing HIV or HIV - infected cells.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other routes are also true.

choices.text: by sharing contaminated hypodermic needles and syringes
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the other routes are also true.
Correct. HIV can be spread in all of these ways.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. HIV spreads through certain body fluids: blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk.

It can be passed by sexual contact, by transfer of infected body fluids, and by sharing needles or syringes. It is not spread by casual contact like hugging, sharing cups, or mosquito bites.

Big idea: knowing how a disease spreads tells us how to prevent it.

questions.prompt: The role of helper T cells in immune responses is to,

choices.text: stimulate macrophages to initiate an "alarm signal."
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is not the main job of helper T cells.

choices.text: activate two different types of immune system cells.
choices.explanation: Correct. Helper T cells activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Incorrect. Neutrophils are activated mainly by innate signals.
Incorrect. Only option B is the best answer.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that helper T cells activate two different types of immune cells. Helper T cells release cytokines that activate B cells (to make antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells (to kill infected cells).

They also help activate macrophages, but the classic description is that they coordinate both arms of adaptive immunity: B cells and cytotoxic T cells. They do not mainly start neutrophil activity.

Big idea: helper T cells are the 'coaches' of the adaptive immune system.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 19 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 19 is the tonsils, lymphatic tissue at the back of the throat.

Tonsils trap and respond to germs entering through the mouth and nose.

Big idea: tonsils are immune tissue placed where germs enter the body.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 20 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 20 is the lymph nodes, here the clusters in the armpit (axillary lymph nodes).

Lymph nodes filter lymph, trapping germs so B and T cells can respond. They can swell when you are sick.

Big idea: lymph nodes are checkpoints along the lymphatic vessels.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 21 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 21 is the spleen, the organ on the left side of the upper abdomen.

The spleen filters blood, removes old red blood cells, and contains lymphocytes that respond to germs in the blood.

Big idea: lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen filters blood.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 22 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 22 is the appendix, the small tube attached to the start of the large intestine.

The appendix contains lymphatic tissue that helps the immune system sample gut bacteria. When it gets blocked and inflamed, it causes appendicitis.

Big idea: lymphatic tissue is found along the digestive tract (MALT).

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 23 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 23 is bone marrow, shown inside the thigh bone.

Red bone marrow makes all blood cells, including white blood cells, and is where B cells mature.

Big idea: bone marrow is where immune cells are born.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 24 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 24 is the thymus, the organ where T lymphocytes mature.

Young T cells travel from the bone marrow to the thymus, where they learn to recognize foreign antigens and to ignore the body's own cells.

Big idea: B cells mature in bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.prompt: Identify the item labeled 25 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 25 points to the antigen, the foreign substance arriving at the peripheral lymphoid tissue.

An antigen is a molecule (often from a germ) that B and T cells recognize. Meeting their antigen activates lymphocytes.

Big idea: lymphocytes are activated when they meet the specific antigen they recognize.

questions.prompt: Identify the item labeled 26 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 26 is a B lymphocyte (B cell) traveling to peripheral lymphoid tissue on the humoral immunity pathway.

B cells mature in the bone marrow. When they meet their antigen, they become plasma cells that make antibodies.

Big idea: humoral immunity is the antibody-based branch run by B cells.

questions.prompt: Identify the item labeled 27 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 27 is the antibodies, the small Y-shaped proteins being released by the plasma cell.

Antibodies bind specific antigens, neutralizing germs, clumping them, and marking them for destruction.

Big idea: plasma cells (activated B cells) release antibodies.

questions.prompt: What signal triggers mast cells to release granular contents?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IL-3 helps mast cells grow but does not trigger the release of granules.

choices.text: Cross-linking of cell surface-bound immunoglobin E (IgE) by antigen
choices.explanation: Correct. Allergen cross-linking surface IgE triggers mast cell degranulation.

choices.text: Cross-linking antigen-antibody complexes to immunoglobulin G (IgG) receptors
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgG receptors are not the classic trigger for mast cell degranulation.

choices.text: Release of tissue factors from surface glycoproteins
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Tissue factor is involved in blood clotting.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cross-linking of IgE on the cell surface by antigen. Mast cells carry IgE antibodies on their surface. When an allergen bridges two neighboring IgE molecules (cross-links them), the mast cell is triggered.

It then releases its granules, full of histamine and other chemicals, causing allergic symptoms. This is type I hypersensitivity. IgG, IL-3, and tissue factor are not the trigger for this classic release.

Big idea: allergies are caused when allergens cross-link IgE on mast cells.

questions.prompt: Which structure helps purify blood and contains two forms of pulp?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus is where T cells mature.
Correct. The spleen filters blood and has red and white pulp.
Incorrect. Tonsils guard the throat.
Incorrect. The adenoids are tonsils at the back of the nose.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the spleen. The spleen filters blood and has two kinds of tissue: red pulp and white pulp.

Red pulp removes old or damaged red blood cells. White pulp is full of lymphocytes that respond to germs in the blood. The thymus trains T cells, and the tonsils and adenoids guard the throat.

Big idea: the spleen is the blood's filter.

questions.prompt: A boy frequently comes in because of chronic skin infections that do not heal with time. A check of his antibody levels after immunizations showed normal responses. He also had normal recovery from the measles. A defect in which cell is most likely the cause of his continual skin infections?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. His normal vaccine responses show his B cells work.
Incorrect. His normal antibody levels show his plasma cells work.
Correct. Neutrophils fight bacterial skin infections, and they seem to be the problem.
Incorrect. Macrophages help, but neutrophils are the front-line defense against bacterial skin infections.

questions.explanation:
The answer is neutrophils. The boy's antibodies respond normally to vaccines (so B cells and plasma cells work), and he recovered normally from measles (a virus, which needs working T cells).

His problem is repeated skin infections, which are usually caused by bacteria. Neutrophils are the main cells that eat and kill bacteria in skin infections. A defect in neutrophils would cause exactly these frequent, slow-healing bacterial infections.

Big idea: different immune cells defend against different kinds of germs, so the pattern of infections points to which cell is not working.

questions.prompt: A girl has a runny nose and itchy eyes during the spring of each year. She is sent to an allergist who performs a skin test for different pollens. After the test is administered, the girl exhibits swelling and focal redness. This response is caused by

choices.text: Activation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes to destroy antigens
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; they do not cause allergy test reactions.

choices.text: Activation of CD4 helper cells and the resultant generation of specific antibodies
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Helper T cells helped make the IgE long before the test, but they are not what causes the immediate swelling.

choices.text: Activation of neutrophils due to injected antigens
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Neutrophils are not the cause of the allergy test reaction.

choices.text: Antigen-antibody complexes being formed in blood vessels in the skin
choices.explanation: Correct (per the key). Antigen meets antibody in the skin, causing redness and swelling; the real mechanism is IgE on mast cells.

questions.explanation:
The official answer is D, antigen-antibody complexes forming in blood vessels in the skin. In real life, a pollen skin test causes an immediate allergic (type I) reaction: the pollen cross-links IgE antibodies on mast cells in the skin, and histamine causes a red, swollen bump within about 15 minutes.

None of the choices describes the type I mast cell reaction exactly. The key picks D because the swelling and redness come from antigen meeting antibody in the skin. Strictly, choice D describes a type III reaction (immune complexes in blood vessels), which appears hours later. Cytotoxic T cells and neutrophils are not what causes an allergy test reaction.

Big idea: allergy skin tests work because people with allergies already have IgE against the allergen on their mast cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following cells make up a large proportion of puss?
