choices.explanation: Incorrect. Monocytes arrive later and are fewer.
Incorrect. Basophils are rare and release histamine.
Incorrect. Eosinophils mainly fight parasites.
Correct. Pus is mostly dead neutrophils.

questions.explanation:
The answer is neutrophils. Neutrophils rush to sites of bacterial infection, eat the bacteria, and die in large numbers.

Pus is mostly made of dead neutrophils, dead bacteria, and tissue debris. Monocytes, basophils, and eosinophils are present in much smaller numbers.

Big idea: neutrophils are the main first responders to bacterial infection.

questions.prompt: When inflammatory response occurs, what is the correct order of events?

choices.text: Activation of tissue macrophages, infiltration of neutrophils from the blood, infiltration of monocytes from blood, increased production of neutrophils
choices.explanation: Correct. Resident macrophages act first, then neutrophils, then monocytes, then more neutrophils are made.

choices.text: Infiltration of neutrophils from the blood, increased production of neutrophils, activation of tissue macrophages, infiltration of monocytes from blood
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Tissue macrophages act before neutrophils arrive.

choices.text: Infiltration of monocytes from blood, infiltration of neutrophils from blood, activation of tissue macrophages, increased production of neutrophils
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Neutrophils arrive before monocytes.

choices.text: Increased production of neutrophils, infiltration of monocytes from blood, infiltration of neutrophils from the blood, activation of tissue macrophages
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Increased production in the bone marrow is the last step.

questions.explanation:
The answer is A: activation of tissue macrophages, then neutrophils arrive, then monocytes arrive, then neutrophil production increases. Macrophages already living in the tissue are the first to respond, within minutes.

Within hours, neutrophils from the blood flood into the area. Over the next day or so, monocytes arrive and become new macrophages. Finally, the bone marrow increases production of neutrophils to replace those used up.

Big idea: inflammation is a sequence of 'lines' of defense, from cells already present to new cells made in the bone marrow.

questions.prompt: During an experiment, a rat is injected with a vaccine which consists of attenuated bacteria at two different times. The results following the injection are shown in the graph above. What is most likely causing the immune response represented by the asterisk?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. T cell activation causes the rise, not the fall.
Correct. Activated lymphocytes die off by apoptosis after the germ is cleared.
Incorrect. Antigen recognition starts the response.
Incorrect. Phagocytosis does not explain the fall in antibody levels.

questions.explanation:
The answer is apoptosis of activated lymphocytes. The graph shows antibody levels after two vaccine doses. After each peak, the antibody level drops. The asterisk is on the falling part after the second, bigger peak.

Once the bacteria are cleared, most of the activated B and T cells are no longer needed. They die in a controlled way called apoptosis (programmed cell death), so antibody production falls. A few memory cells remain. Antigen recognition, T cell activation, and phagocytosis happen during the rise, not the fall.

Big idea: after an immune response, most of the immune army is removed by apoptosis, leaving memory cells behind.

questions.prompt: Cellular findings of an animal show cytoplasmic budding, no adjacent inflammation, germinal centers of reactive lymph nodes have shrunk, and intact plasma membranes. What mechanisms most likely caused this?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Phagocytes do clean up the pieces afterward, but they do not cause the cell death.
Incorrect. Lysosomal enzymes are more linked to messy cell death (necrosis).
Correct. Caspases carry out apoptosis.
Incorrect. Low calcium does not cause this pattern.

questions.explanation:
The answer is caspase activation. The findings describe apoptosis, a tidy, planned cell death. Cells shrink and bud off small pieces, their membranes stay intact, and there is no inflammation around them.

Apoptosis is carried out by enzymes called caspases. In lymph nodes, it removes activated lymphocytes after an infection, which is why the germinal centers shrink. Necrosis (messy death) would cause inflammation and burst membranes.

Big idea: the immune system uses apoptosis to remove cells it no longer needs without causing inflammation.

questions.prompt: Wound healing can take place in the absence of neutrophils, but not in the absence of macrophages.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. Neutrophils are important for killing germs early on, but the body can still heal wounds without them.

Macrophages are essential: they clean up dead cells and debris, and they release growth factors that tell new tissue and blood vessels to grow. Without macrophages, wound healing does not proceed properly.

Big idea: immune cells do more than fight germs; macrophages also direct tissue repair.

questions.prompt: This type of cell ingests foreign particles and produces heparin/histamine which causes inflammation (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is basophils. Basophils are white blood cells with dark granules containing histamine and heparin.

When released, histamine widens blood vessels and makes them leaky, causing inflammation and allergy symptoms. Heparin prevents blood clotting. Basophils can also take in some particles, though they are not major phagocytes.

Big idea: basophils (in blood) and mast cells (in tissue) release histamine during inflammation and allergies.

questions.prompt: These types of cells are made in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus gland and help in immune defense (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is T cells. All lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow, but T cells move to the thymus to mature. The 'T' stands for thymus.

In the thymus, T cells learn to recognize foreign antigens and to ignore the body's own cells. B cells mature in the bone marrow instead.

Big idea: B cells mature in Bone marrow; T cells mature in the Thymus.

questions.prompt: This type of immunity is supported by the production of Memory B/T cells which allows the cell to recognize the antigen faster when introduced again (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is the secondary immune response. The first time the body meets an antigen, it mounts a slow primary response and creates memory B and T cells.

The next time it meets the same antigen, those memory cells respond quickly and strongly. This faster, stronger second response is the secondary response.

Big idea: memory cells make the secondary response faster and stronger, which is how vaccines protect us.

questions.prompt: What autoimmune disease does she have?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming fatigue and muscle weakness. Her weakness worsens with activity but improves with rest. She has loss of facial expression and slurred speech after a period but can recover with rest.
questions.explanation:
The answer is myasthenia gravis. Muscle weakness that gets worse with use and better with rest, especially in the face, eyes, and throat (affecting expression and speech), is the classic sign.

In myasthenia gravis, antibodies attack the acetylcholine receptors where nerves meet muscles, so repeated nerve signals get weaker and weaker.

Big idea: myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that blocks nerve-to-muscle signals.

questions.prompt: You run an antibody test and expect to find what present?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming fatigue and muscle weakness. Her weakness worsens with activity but improves with rest. She has loss of facial expression and slurred speech after a period but can recover with rest.
questions.explanation:
The expected finding is antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (a positive AChR antibody test).

In myasthenia gravis, the immune system makes these antibodies, which block and destroy acetylcholine receptors on muscles. Finding them in the blood confirms the diagnosis in most patients.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases can be diagnosed by finding antibodies against the body's own parts.

questions.prompt: You want to administer a common diagnostic test for this autoimmune disease, what do you administer?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming fatigue and muscle weakness. Her weakness worsens with activity but improves with rest. She has loss of facial expression and slurred speech after a period but can recover with rest.
questions.explanation:
The test uses an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at the nerve-muscle junction.

Giving a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor lets acetylcholine last longer. If the patient's strength quickly improves, it supports a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

Big idea: blocking the breakdown of a chemical messenger makes its signal stronger.

questions.prompt: You administer a common diagnostic test for this autoimmune disease, what reaction do you expect from the patient?
questions.context: A patient comes in claiming fatigue and muscle weakness. Her weakness worsens with activity but improves with rest. She has loss of facial expression and slurred speech after a period but can recover with rest.
questions.answer: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor will prevent the degradation of acetylcholine which will increase level and duration of muscle contraction preventing muscle fatigue
questions.explanation:
The muscle weakness should improve for a short time. The acetylcholinesterase inhibitor stops acetylcholine from being broken down, so more acetylcholine stays at the nerve-muscle junction for longer.

Even though the patient has fewer working receptors, the extra acetylcholine can activate the ones that are left, so the muscle contracts more strongly and does not tire as quickly.

Big idea: in myasthenia gravis, boosting acetylcholine can overcome the reduced number of receptors.

questions.prompt: An old woman comes into the ER because she has a week history of a painful rash. The rash started at the lower left side of her chest with a burning sensation. Two days ago, flat, small, and painful macules that developed rapidly progressed to vesicular lesions. The cause of this woman’s illness is a deficiency in which immune system component?
questions.explanation:
The answer is cellular (cell-mediated) immunity. The painful, blistering rash in a band on one side of the chest is shingles, caused by the chickenpox virus (varicella-zoster) waking up after hiding in nerves for years.

T cells normally keep this virus asleep. As people age, cell-mediated immunity (T cell function) weakens, which lets the virus reactivate. A shingles vaccine boosts these T cells.

Big idea: T cells (cell-mediated immunity) control viruses hiding inside our cells.

questions.prompt: Name one symptom of histamine release in urticaria and its cause.
questions.context: A patient comes in with symptoms of urticaria. You know that urticaria results from antigen entering specific skin areas and causing localized anaphylactoid reactions
questions.answer: vasodilation induces an immediate red flare
questions.explanation:
One symptom is a red flare. In urticaria (hives), histamine is released by mast cells in the skin. Histamine widens (dilates) small blood vessels in the area.

More blood flows into the skin, causing redness. This is the 'flare' around a hive.

Big idea: histamine causes the redness, swelling, and itching of allergic skin reactions.

questions.prompt: Name another symptom of histamine release in urticaria and its cause.
questions.context: A patient comes in with symptoms of urticaria. You know that urticaria results from antigen entering specific skin areas and causing localized anaphylactoid reactions
questions.answer: increased local permeability of capillaries leads to local areas of swelling of the skin (hives)
questions.explanation:
Another symptom is swelling (a wheal, or hive). Histamine makes the walls of small blood vessels leaky (more permeable).

Fluid leaks out of the capillaries into the skin, forming raised, swollen bumps. Histamine also stimulates nerves, causing itching.

Big idea: leaky blood vessels cause the swelling in allergic reactions.

questions.prompt: A woman comes in because of a three-week history of throat pain and fever. You find in her physical examination scattered two-to-four-centimeter lymph nodes in the axillae, inguina and neck regions. You also find bilateral tonsillar exudate, but no signs of ulcerations are present. The laboratory examination shows hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL, hematocrit of 30%, leukocyte count of 1499/mm3, platelet count of 60,000/mm3, and a negative heterophile antibody test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is HIV infection (acute HIV). A few weeks after infection, many people get a flu-like or mono-like illness: fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes in many areas.

The negative heterophile test rules out typical mononucleosis. Her low red cells, white cells, and platelets also fit early HIV infection.

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency, and its early stage can look like other viral illnesses.

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the immune system in causing this disorder.
questions.context: An old man is showing common symptoms of multiple sclerosis and is seeking treatment.
questions.answer: The immune system attacks the myelin that covers nerve fibers
questions.explanation:
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin, the fatty coating that insulates nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord.

T cells and antibodies get into the brain and spinal cord and damage myelin, leaving scars (plaques). Without myelin, nerve signals slow down or stop, causing weakness, numbness, vision problems, and trouble with balance.

Big idea: MS is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system.

questions.prompt: You run a test and find that his immune system is attacking this type of cell which is found in the CNS. Which type of cell is being attacked?
questions.context: An old man is showing common symptoms of multiple sclerosis and is seeking treatment.
questions.explanation:
The answer is oligodendrocytes. In the brain and spinal cord (the central nervous system), oligodendrocytes are the cells that make myelin.

In MS, the immune attack on myelin damages and kills oligodendrocytes. (In the rest of the body, Schwann cells make myelin.)

Big idea: knowing which cell makes myelin explains why MS damages nerve signaling in the brain and spinal cord.

questions.prompt: A man comes into the ER with a history of one-week diarrhea that has gotten worse over the past few days. He has low urine output and is admitted for dehydration. Laboratory examination shows his stool has parasitic eggs present. What type of WBC would be elevated?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Monocytes are not the main parasite fighters.
Incorrect. T cells help, but eosinophils are the classic cells raised in parasite infections.
Incorrect. B cells make antibodies, but eosinophils are the cells that rise.
Correct. Eosinophils increase in parasitic infections.

questions.explanation:
The answer is eosinophils. The man's stool has parasite eggs, which means he has a parasitic worm infection.

Eosinophils are the white blood cells that specialize in fighting parasites. They release toxic proteins onto worms that are too big to be eaten. Parasite infections commonly raise the eosinophil count.

Big idea: eosinophils (along with IgE) are the main defense against parasites.

questions.prompt: Which of the following agents of disease are antibodies NOT effective against?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Antibodies work well against many bacteria.
Incorrect. Antibodies can neutralize viruses.
Incorrect. IgE antibodies help fight helminths (worms).
Correct. Prions look like the body's own proteins, so antibodies do not work against them.
Incorrect. Prions are an example where antibodies do not work.

questions.explanation:
The answer is prions. Prions are misfolded proteins that cause brain diseases like mad cow disease. Because they are made from the body's own normal protein, just folded wrong, the immune system does not see them as foreign.

So the body does not make useful antibodies against them. Antibodies do work against bacteria, viruses, and helminths (worms; IgE helps here).

Big idea: antibodies work against foreign antigens; prions look like 'self', so they escape the immune system.

questions.prompt: Select ALL cell types that would be predominant during an innate immune response.

choices.explanation: Correct. Neutrophils are the main first-responder innate cells.
Correct. Eosinophils are innate cells that fight parasites.
Correct. Monocytes are innate cells that become macrophages.
Correct. Mast cells are innate cells that start inflammation.
Incorrect. B cells are part of the adaptive immune system.

questions.explanation:
The answers are neutrophils, eosinophils, monocytes, and mast cells. These are all innate immune cells, which respond quickly to any germ without needing to be trained.

Neutrophils eat bacteria, eosinophils fight parasites, monocytes become macrophages that eat germs, and mast cells release histamine to start inflammation. B cells are part of the adaptive immune system.

Big idea: innate cells respond first; lymphocytes like B and T cells respond later and specifically.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches the immunoglobulin to its function?

choices.text: IgA; involved in the allergic inflammatory response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgE, not IgA, causes allergic reactions.

choices.text: IgD; the primary antibody responsible for preventing infection
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgG, not IgD, is the main infection-fighting antibody in blood.

choices.text: IgE; mediates B cell homeostasis and maturation
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgE triggers allergies and fights parasites; it does not manage B cell maturation.

choices.text: IgG; the first line of defense, especially in mucosal surfaces
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA, not IgG, protects mucosal surfaces.

choices.text: IgM; initiates the classical complement cascade
choices.explanation: Correct. IgM strongly starts the classical complement cascade.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'IgM; initiates the classical complement cascade'. IgM is the first antibody made in a new infection. Its five-part shape makes it very good at starting the complement system.

The others are mixed up: IgE (not IgA) causes allergic reactions; IgA (not IgG) is the first line of defense in mucous membranes; IgG (not IgD) is the main antibody fighting infections in blood; and IgD sits on B cells and helps with their activation, which is not what IgE does.

Big idea: each antibody class has a special job; matching them is a common test question.

questions.prompt: A cutaneous abscess would contain the greatest concentration of:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Bacteria are present, but neutrophils make up most of the pus.
Correct. Pus in an abscess is mostly neutrophils.
Incorrect. CD8+ T cells fight virus-infected cells, not abscesses.
Incorrect. Complement proteins are present but are not cells and are not the main content.
Incorrect. Langerhans cells are skin dendritic cells; they are not the main cells in pus.

questions.explanation:
The answer is neutrophils. An abscess is a pocket of pus in the tissue, usually caused by a bacterial infection.

Pus is mostly made of neutrophils (living and dead), along with bacteria and tissue debris. Neutrophils rush to the area in huge numbers to eat the bacteria. The bacteria themselves (like S. pyogenes or, more often, S. aureus) are there too, but neutrophils outnumber them.

Big idea: neutrophils are the main cells of acute bacterial infection and pus.

questions.prompt: What is herd immunity?

choices.text: The tradition of immunizing entire herds of over ten animals in agriculture
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Herd immunity is not about vaccinating farm animals.

choices.text: Indirect protection from infectious disease, facilitated by vaccinations
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Herd immunity can come from vaccines or past infections, so this is incomplete.

choices.text: A short term immunity acquired by receiving antibodies from another person
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes passive immunity.

choices.text: The immunity of a large portion of a community, reducing the probability of transmission
choices.explanation: Correct. Herd immunity is when enough people are immune to slow the spread.

choices.text: The practice of kicking out all members of a herd that are not immune to a disease
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is not herd immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the immunity of a large portion of a community, which reduces the chance of transmission. When most people in a group are immune, a germ has trouble finding new people to infect.

This protects people who cannot be vaccinated, like newborns or people with weak immune systems. Herd immunity can come from vaccination or from past infection, so choice B is too narrow, and choice C describes passive immunity.

Big idea: vaccinating enough people protects the whole community.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves disease?

choices.text: Hashimoto’s is a type of hyperthyroidism, while Graves disease is a type of hypothyroidism
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hashimoto's causes hypothyroidism; Graves' causes hyperthyroidism.

choices.text: There are generally greater levels of thyroid stimulating hormone in someone with Hashimoto’s
choices.explanation: Correct. Low thyroid hormone in Hashimoto's makes the pituitary release more TSH.

choices.text: Hashimoto’s is associated with weight loss, while Grave’s disease is associated with weight gain
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hashimoto's tends to cause weight gain; Graves' tends to cause weight loss.

choices.text: Hashimoto’s is more common in women, while Grave’s disease is more common in men
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Both are more common in women.

choices.text: Graves disease is an autoimmune disease, whereas Hashimoto’s is not
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Both are autoimmune diseases.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B: people with Hashimoto's usually have higher TSH. Both Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease are autoimmune diseases of the thyroid, but they have opposite effects.

In Hashimoto's, the immune system destroys the thyroid, so it makes too little thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism). The pituitary gland tries to make up for it by releasing more TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). In Graves' disease, antibodies act like TSH and overstimulate the thyroid (hyperthyroidism), so real TSH is low. Both are much more common in women.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases can either destroy a gland or overstimulate it.

questions.prompt: Where are the adenoids located?

choices.explanation: Correct. The adenoids sit behind the nasal cavity.

choices.text: In the upper chest, behind the sternum
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus is behind the sternum.

choices.text: To the left of the stomach
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The spleen is near the stomach.

choices.text: In the distal jejunum and ileum
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Peyer's patches are in the small intestine.
Incorrect. Lymph nodes are found throughout the body, but adenoids are in one place.

questions.explanation:
The answer is behind the nasal cavity. The adenoids (pharyngeal tonsil) are a patch of lymphatic tissue high in the back of the throat, where the nasal cavity meets the pharynx (the nasopharynx).

They help trap germs breathed in through the nose. In children, swollen adenoids can block nasal breathing. Behind the sternum is the thymus, near the stomach is the spleen, and in the ileum are Peyer's patches.

Big idea: tonsils and adenoids form a ring of immune tissue around the entrance to the throat.

questions.prompt: What is the typical lag period between the initial encounter of an antigen and antibody production?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. 1-2 hours is far too fast for a first antibody response.
Incorrect. 18-24 hours is still too fast for a first response.
Correct. Antibodies usually start appearing after about 3-6 days.
Incorrect. Two weeks is closer to the peak, not the start.
Incorrect. Five years is far too long.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 3-6 days. The first time you meet an antigen, the few B cells that recognize it must be activated, multiply, and become plasma cells before antibodies appear in the blood.

This lag phase usually takes several days (often described as 3-6 days, with antibody levels peaking in 1-2 weeks). In a later (secondary) response, memory cells shorten the lag.

Big idea: the primary immune response is slow at first; memory makes later responses faster.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between B and T cells?

choices.text: B cells become immunocompetent in the bone marrow, whereas T cells become immunocompetent in the thymus
choices.explanation: Correct. B cells mature in the bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus.

choices.text: There are more B cells than there are T cells in circulation at any given moment
choices.explanation: Incorrect. There are more T cells than B cells in the blood.

choices.text: B cells are involved in the cell-mediated immune response, while T cells are involved in the humoral immune response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is reversed: B cells are humoral, T cells are cell-mediated.

choices.text: B cells are capable for producing large quantities of cytokines, whereas T cell cytokine production is dependent on their activation conditions
choices.explanation: Incorrect. T cells (especially helper T cells) are the main cytokine producers.

choices.text: Only T cells can form clones; B cells cannot
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Both B and T cells multiply into clones when activated.

questions.explanation:
The answer is A: B cells become immunocompetent (able to recognize antigens) in the bone marrow, while T cells do so in the thymus.

The other statements are wrong. T cells outnumber B cells in the blood. B cells handle humoral (antibody) immunity, and T cells handle cell-mediated immunity. Helper T cells are the main cytokine producers. Both B and T cells form clones when activated.

Big idea: B cells mature in the Bone marrow; T cells mature in the Thymus.

questions.prompt: Select ALL statements that are true in regards to the complement system.

choices.text: Complement proteins are primarily synthesized by the spleen
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Complement proteins are mainly made by the liver.

choices.text: Complement proteins are only secreted into the bloodstream after macrophages and dendritic cells recognize a pathogen
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Complement proteins circulate in the blood all the time.

choices.text: During opsonization, complement proteins bind to bacteria to increase the likelihood of their phagocytosis
choices.explanation: Correct. Opsonization by complement helps phagocytes eat bacteria.

choices.text: Membrane attack complexes form tubes that flood foreign cells with water and salts, lysing them
choices.explanation: Correct. The membrane attack complex punches holes that burst foreign cells.

choices.text: Chemotaxis is the phenomenon that explains the movement of leukocytes towards the site of infection
choices.explanation: Correct. Chemotaxis (which complement helps trigger) moves white blood cells toward infections.

questions.explanation:
The answers are C, D, and E. The complement system is a group of proteins in the blood that help destroy germs.

Complement proteins can coat bacteria (opsonization), making them easier for phagocytes to eat. They can build a membrane attack complex that punches holes in a germ's membrane, letting water and salts rush in so it bursts. And some complement pieces (like C5a) attract white blood cells to the infection, a movement called chemotaxis. Complement proteins are mostly made by the liver, not the spleen, and they are always circulating in the blood, not released only after an infection is found.

Big idea: complement is an innate defense that tags, attracts, and kills.

questions.prompt: Compared to the primary immune response, the secondary immune response:

choices.text: Produces a greater amount of IgM
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The secondary response makes mostly IgG; IgM is typical of the primary response.

choices.text: Has a greater innate immune response, but a lesser adaptive immune response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The secondary response has a stronger adaptive response.

choices.text: Is able to achieve faster antibody production times, thus a shorter lag period
choices.explanation: Correct. Memory cells shorten the lag and speed up antibody production.

choices.text: Uses both thymus-independent and thymus-dependent antibodies
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is not the key difference between the responses.

choices.text: Does not involve the participation of memory cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Memory cells are the reason the secondary response is faster.

questions.explanation:
The answer is C: the secondary response makes antibodies faster, with a shorter lag period. Memory cells from the first exposure recognize the antigen right away and quickly multiply.

The secondary response is also stronger and makes mostly IgG, not IgM. It is an adaptive response that depends on memory cells, so the other statements are wrong.

Big idea: memory makes the second immune response faster and stronger.

questions.prompt: Which of the following occurs during the inflammatory response?

choices.text: Leukocytes initiate sequestration of iron and magnesium by the spleen, limiting bacterial access to necessary minerals
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Iron is mainly held back by the liver and macrophages, not the spleen, and this is not a typical description of inflammation.

choices.text: Macrophages release inflammatory chemicals that decrease capillary permeability, streamlining the immune response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inflammatory chemicals increase capillary permeability.

choices.text: Cells at the injury site release arachidonic acid derivatives (prostaglandins and leukotrienes), which sensitize nociceptors and attract white blood cells
choices.explanation: Correct. Prostaglandins and leukotrienes sensitize pain nerves and attract white blood cells.

choices.text: Damaged cells release pyrogens which target the hypothalamus, increasing body temperature and impairing bacterial and viral replication
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pyrogens come mainly from white blood cells, not damaged cells.

choices.text: Mast cells interact with infectious agents to produce histamines, causing local vasodilation and pausing normal metabolic functions
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mast cells already store histamine; they do not 'produce' it from contact, and metabolism does not pause.

questions.edited: Option C reworded for accuracy (originally: "Damaged cells release arachidonic acid derivatives, increasing white blood cell count and sensitizing nociceptors").
questions.explanation:
The answer is C. During inflammation, cells at the injured area make chemicals from a fat called arachidonic acid. These include prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

Prostaglandins make pain nerves (nociceptors) more sensitive and help cause fever, and leukotrienes help attract white blood cells. The others are wrong: inflammation increases (not decreases) capillary leakiness; pyrogens come mainly from white blood cells, not damaged cells; iron is held back mainly by the liver and macrophages; and histamine is stored in mast cells already, not made on contact.

Big idea: inflammation is driven by chemical signals that widen vessels, cause pain, and call in white blood cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following medications or vaccinations would be most likely to produce serum sickness?

choices.explanation: Not the key's answer. Penicillin can cause a serum-sickness-like reaction, but animal serum is the classic cause.
Correct (best fit). Older rabies treatments used horse serum, the classic cause of serum sickness.
Incorrect. Immunosuppressants for rheumatoid arthritis calm the immune system.
Incorrect. COVID-19 boosters do not typically cause serum sickness.
Incorrect. The varicella vaccine does not typically cause serum sickness.

questions.explanation:
The best answer is the rabies vaccine (this is an uncertain question). Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction that happens about a week after receiving proteins from another animal, such as antibodies made in horses.

The body makes antibodies against the foreign proteins, and the clumps (immune complexes) cause fever, rash, and joint pain. Older rabies treatments used horse serum and commonly caused serum sickness. Penicillin can also cause a similar reaction, which is why this question is uncertain. The other vaccines and drugs listed rarely do.

Big idea: type III reactions are caused by antigen-antibody clumps settling in tissues.
questions.note: Uncertain: serum sickness classically follows animal-derived antisera (e.g. older rabies antiserum); penicillin (A) can also cause a serum-sickness-like reaction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following Toll-like receptors are endosomal in nature? Select ALL that apply.

choices.explanation: Correct. TLR3 is in endosomes and detects viral double-stranded RNA.
Incorrect. TLR4 is on the cell surface and detects bacterial LPS.
Incorrect. TLR5 is on the cell surface and detects bacterial flagellin.
Correct. TLR9 is in endosomes and detects microbial DNA.
Incorrect. TLR10 is on the cell surface.

questions.explanation:
The answers are TLR3 and TLR9. Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are sensors that spot common features of germs. Some sit on the cell surface, and others sit inside endosomes (small bubbles inside the cell where swallowed material goes).

The ones inside endosomes detect germ DNA and RNA: TLR3 (double-stranded viral RNA), TLR7 and TLR8 (single-stranded RNA), and TLR9 (bacterial and viral DNA). TLR4 (bacterial LPS), TLR5 (flagellin), and TLR10 are on the cell surface.

Big idea: TLRs are part of innate immunity; their location matches what they detect.

questions.prompt: Splenomegaly refers to enlargement of the spleen. Considering its function, predict the possible causes of this condition. Select ALL that apply.

choices.text: Sleeping for less than 5 hours a day
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lack of sleep does not cause an enlarged spleen.
Correct. Some anemias make the spleen work harder removing red blood cells.
Correct. Alcohol-related liver disease can back blood up into the spleen.
Correct. Viral infections can make the spleen's immune tissue swell.

choices.text: Eating mint ice cream for breakfast
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Eating ice cream does not cause splenomegaly.

questions.explanation:
The answers are anemia, heavy alcohol use, and severe viral infection. The spleen filters blood and contains lots of immune cells, so anything that makes it work harder or backs up its blood flow can make it swell.

In some anemias, the spleen works overtime removing damaged red blood cells. Heavy drinking can scar the liver (cirrhosis), which backs up blood into the spleen. Viral infections like mononucleosis make the spleen's immune tissue grow. Sleep and ice cream do not cause splenomegaly.

Big idea: the spleen enlarges when it is busy filtering blood, fighting infection, or backed up with blood.

questions.prompt: In what ways is the skin microbiota involved in immunity? Select ALL that apply.

choices.text: Microorganisms lower the skin pH such that pathogenic bacteria cannot survive on it
choices.explanation: Correct. Skin microbes help keep the skin acidic.

choices.text: Some microorganisms produce or stimulate mast cell production of antibiotic compounds, such as cathelicidin
choices.explanation: Correct. Some skin microbes boost production of antimicrobial peptides like cathelicidin.

choices.text: Some microorganisms quickly phagocytose foreign bacteria before they can pervade the skin
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is done by immune cells, not by skin bacteria.

choices.text: Microorganisms that reside in and around the hair follicles compete with foreign bacteria for resources
choices.explanation: Correct. Helpful microbes compete with harmful ones for space and nutrients.

choices.text: Microorganisms are able to protect the skin from ultraviolet radiation and reverse its effects
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Skin microbes cannot protect against or reverse UV damage.

questions.explanation:
The answers are A, B, and D. The skin is covered with helpful microbes (the skin microbiota) that help defend against harmful ones.

Some break down skin oils into fatty acids that keep the skin slightly acidic, which many harmful bacteria do not like. Some trigger the skin's cells to make antimicrobial peptides like cathelicidin. And they take up space and food, so harmful bacteria have trouble growing (competition). Bacteria do not 'phagocytose' other bacteria, and skin microbes do not reverse UV damage.

Big idea: helpful microbes are part of the body's first line of defense.

questions.prompt: Which of the following occurs during anaphylaxis?

choices.text: IgE cross-linking stimulates serotonin secretion by mast cells, inhibiting the release of cytokines
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgE cross-linking causes release of histamine and cytokines; it does not block cytokines.

choices.text: IgE mediates the release of histamine by mast cells and basophils, inducing a Type I hypersensitivity reaction
choices.explanation: Correct. IgE triggers histamine release from mast cells and basophils in type I hypersensitivity.

choices.text: Mast cells catalyze the activity of angiotensin-converting enzymes, where large amounts of angiotensin II constrict the blood vessels
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Anaphylaxis causes blood vessels to widen, not constrict through angiotensin II.

choices.text: Intracellular calcium levels rapidly drop, inhibiting the activity of guanylate cyclase and decreasing diastolic blood pressure
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Calcium rises inside mast cells, triggering release of their granules.

choices.text: IL-10 activates of CD8+ T cells, potentiating the immune response
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IL-10 calms immune responses; this is not part of anaphylaxis.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B. Anaphylaxis is a severe type I hypersensitivity reaction. IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils bind the allergen, causing these cells to release large amounts of histamine and other chemicals all at once.

This widens blood vessels throughout the body (dropping blood pressure) and can tighten the airways. The other choices describe processes that do not happen in anaphylaxis.

Big idea: anaphylaxis is a whole-body IgE and histamine reaction that needs epinephrine right away.

questions.prompt: A mouse has its T cell receptor (TCR) modified such that it is unable to express Class II MHC. Positive selection in these transgenic mice will yield what type of cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. CD4 T cells need MHC class II to pass positive selection.
Correct. Without MHC class II, only CD8 T cells (which use MHC I) can be selected.
Incorrect. CD4 T cells cannot develop without MHC class II.
Incorrect. CD8 T cells can still develop using MHC class I.

choices.text: N/A, positive selection is replaced by negative selection
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Positive selection still happens; it is not replaced.

questions.explanation:
The answer is only CD8 cells. In the thymus, T cells go through positive selection: they survive only if their receptor can recognize MHC molecules.

T cells that recognize MHC class II become CD4 (helper) T cells; those that recognize MHC class I become CD8 (cytotoxic) T cells. If the mouse cannot make MHC class II, no CD4 T cells can pass positive selection, so only CD8 T cells develop. (The question words it oddly, but the idea is that the mouse lacks MHC class II.)

Big idea: helper T cells see MHC II; cytotoxic T cells see MHC I.

questions.prompt: What does HIV stand for? AIDS?
questions.answer: HIV: human immunodeficiency virus. AIDS: acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
questions.explanation:
HIV stands for human immunodeficiency virus. It is the virus that infects and destroys CD4 helper T cells.

AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. It is the late stage of untreated HIV infection, when the immune system is so weak that the person gets serious infections and certain cancers.

Big idea: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the disease it can cause.

questions.prompt: What type of cells are targeted by HIV? What type of cells target HIV? Make sure to give your answers in order.
questions.answer: Targeted by HIV: CD4+ helper T cells (also macrophages and dendritic cells). Cells that target HIV-infected cells: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (and natural killer cells).
questions.explanation:
Cells targeted by HIV: CD4+ helper T cells (and also macrophages and dendritic cells, which have CD4 too). HIV uses the CD4 protein, plus a co-receptor, to get inside.

Cells that target HIV: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, which recognize and kill cells infected with HIV (natural killer cells help as well). Over time, though, HIV destroys so many helper T cells that this defense weakens.

Big idea: HIV attacks the very cells that coordinate the immune response against it.

questions.prompt: Name a difference between SCID and HIV. What is the standard treatment for SCID?
questions.answer: SCID is an inherited (primary) immunodeficiency present from birth with absent/nonfunctional T and B cells, whereas HIV is an acquired viral infection that destroys CD4+ T cells over time. Standard treatment for SCID: hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplant (also enzyme replacement or gene therapy for some forms).
questions.explanation:
One difference: SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) is a genetic disease present from birth, in which both T and B cells do not develop or work. HIV is an infection picked up later in life, which slowly destroys CD4 helper T cells.

The standard treatment for SCID is a hematopoietic stem cell transplant (a bone marrow transplant), which gives the child new stem cells that can make working immune cells. Some forms can also be treated with enzyme replacement or gene therapy.

Big idea: immunodeficiencies can be genetic (primary, like SCID) or acquired (secondary, like HIV/AIDS).

questions.prompt: Identify the disease.
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.explanation:
The disease is multiple sclerosis (MS). Eye pain with gradual vision loss in one eye in a young woman is a classic sign of optic neuritis, inflammation of the optic nerve.

Optic neuritis is often the first symptom of MS, an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin in the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. MS is most common in women aged 20-40. The follow-up questions (about markers in spinal fluid and lesions) also point to MS.

Big idea: MS is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system that often starts with vision problems.
questions.note: Optic neuritis (eye pain with gradual vision loss) in a young woman, plus the follow-up questions (oligoclonal bands, lesions), point to MS.

questions.prompt: Cerebrospinal fluid collected by a lumbar puncture is subjected to a type of gel electrophoresis called SDS-PAGE and Coomassie blue staining. This separates the proteins in the fluid, including immunoglobulins. In this technique, what marker would indicate the disease in the previous question?
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.answer: Oligoclonal bands in the CSF (not present in the serum)
questions.explanation:
The marker is oligoclonal bands. When proteins in spinal fluid are separated by electrophoresis, a healthy person's antibodies form a smooth smear. In MS, B cells inside the brain and spinal cord make a few specific antibodies, which show up as several distinct bands.

If these bands appear in the spinal fluid but not in the blood, it means antibodies are being made inside the central nervous system, which supports a diagnosis of MS.

Big idea: MS involves immune activity inside the brain and spinal cord.

questions.prompt: What two immunoglobulins is this marker associated with? Please give your answers in alphabetical order.
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgG and IgM. Oligoclonal bands in MS are mostly IgG antibodies made by B cells inside the central nervous system.

Some patients also have IgM oligoclonal bands, which may point to a more active disease.

Big idea: B cells and antibodies play a role in multiple sclerosis, alongside T cells.

questions.prompt: This disease is known to form lesions. What type of immune cells would one expect to occur around the edges of lesions? Explain. Are these part of the innate or adaptive immune system?
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.answer: Activated macrophages and microglia line the rims of active lesions, phagocytosing myelin debris (with T lymphocytes infiltrating around vessels). Macrophages/microglia are part of the innate immune system (the T cells are adaptive).
questions.explanation:
Around the edges of active MS lesions (damaged areas), you would expect activated macrophages and microglia (the brain's own macrophage-like cells). They eat the damaged myelin and help drive the inflammation.

Macrophages and microglia are part of the innate immune system. T cells (part of the adaptive immune system) also gather around blood vessels near the lesions and help direct the attack on myelin.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases involve both innate cells (which do much of the damage) and adaptive cells (which target the body's own tissue).

questions.prompt: This disease is an example of an autoimmune disease. Why are autoimmune diseases more common in women than men?
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.answer: Women have two X chromosomes, which carry many immune-related genes (some escape X-inactivation), and estrogens enhance immune responses while testosterone is immunosuppressive, so women mount stronger responses that more easily break self-tolerance.
questions.explanation:
Scientists are still studying this, so several reasons are accepted. One reason is genetic: women have two X chromosomes, and the X chromosome carries many immune-related genes. Some of these genes are active on both X chromosomes, giving women a 'double dose'.

Another reason is hormones: estrogen tends to boost immune responses, while testosterone tends to calm them. Women's stronger immune responses help them fight infections, but also make it easier for the immune system to mistakenly attack the body.

Big idea: genes and hormones both influence how strongly the immune system responds.
questions.note: Uncertain: the causes are still debated; any of these mechanisms should be accepted.

questions.prompt: Name three other Anatomy & Physiology autoimmune diseases.
questions.context: A 32 year old woman reports pain and gradual vision loss in her right eye.
questions.answer: Any three, e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, systemic lupus erythematosus, myasthenia gravis, Graves' disease, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, celiac disease.
questions.explanation:
Any three autoimmune diseases are accepted, such as rheumatoid arthritis (attacks joints), type 1 diabetes (attacks insulin-making cells), systemic lupus erythematosus (attacks many organs), myasthenia gravis (attacks muscle receptors), Graves' disease (overstimulates the thyroid), Hashimoto's thyroiditis (destroys the thyroid), or celiac disease (damages the small intestine).

In each one, the immune system mistakes part of the body for a foreign invader.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases happen when the immune system loses tolerance to 'self'.

questions.prompt: After eating a very large strawberry, Chair's friend, Karp, experiences a slight itching around their mouth and throat. They report similar symptoms when eating other fruits, namely apples, peaches, and cherries, but not when they've been cooked or processed. What condition does Karp have?
questions.context: Bonus: Tea Party Shenanigans (all systems).
questions.explanation:
Karp has oral allergy syndrome (also called pollen-food allergy syndrome). People allergic to certain pollens (like birch) can react to raw fruits that contain similar-looking proteins.

The immune system's IgE mistakes the fruit proteins for pollen, causing itching in the mouth and throat. Cooking or processing changes the shape of these fragile proteins, so cooked fruit does not cause a reaction.

Big idea: allergies are caused by IgE recognizing proteins; similar proteins can trigger cross-reactions.

questions.prompt: Most lymphoid tissues in the GI tract are located in the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The mouth has tonsils but not most of the gut's lymphoid tissue.
Incorrect. The esophagus has relatively little lymphoid tissue.
Incorrect. The stomach's acid keeps bacteria low, and it has little lymphoid tissue.
Debatable. The small intestine has Peyer's patches and is often given as the answer, but the key chose the large intestine.
Correct (per the key). The large intestine has many scattered lymphoid follicles.

questions.note: Uncertain: Peyer's patches make the small intestine (ileum) a common textbook answer; the official key says the large intestine, which has many scattered lymphoid follicles.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is the large intestine. The digestive tract has lots of lymphoid tissue (called GALT) to defend against germs in food.

This question is debatable. Many textbooks point to the small intestine because of Peyer's patches, the big clusters of lymphoid tissue in the ileum. The large intestine, however, has many scattered lymphoid follicles along its length, and it holds the most bacteria. The official key chose the large intestine.

Big idea: lymphoid tissue lines the digestive tract to protect against germs, especially where bacteria are plentiful.

questions.prompt: What phagocytic cell makes up the majority of pus?

choices.explanation: Correct. Pus is mostly dead neutrophils.
Incorrect. Monocytes are present in smaller numbers.
Incorrect. Macrophages arrive later and are fewer.
Incorrect. Basophils release histamine and are rare.
Incorrect. Mast cells live in tissues and release histamine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is neutrophils. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells and the first to arrive at a bacterial infection.

They eat bacteria and then die in large numbers. Pus is mostly made of dead neutrophils, bacteria, and tissue debris.

Big idea: neutrophils are the front-line phagocytes of the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: Oh no– a virus has infected a host cell! What lymphatic cell is responsible for the destruction of this infected cell?

choices.explanation: Correct. NK cells destroy virus-infected cells quickly.
Incorrect for this key. Cytotoxic T cells also kill infected cells, but more slowly; the key chose NK cells.
Incorrect. B cells make antibodies, not kill cells directly.
Incorrect. Plasma cells make antibodies.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells present antigens to T cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is natural killer (NK) cells. NK cells are lymphocytes of the innate immune system. They patrol the body and destroy cells infected with viruses (and some cancer cells) without needing to be trained first.

Cytotoxic T cells also kill virus-infected cells, but they take days to activate the first time. B cells and plasma cells make antibodies, and dendritic cells present antigens.

Big idea: NK cells provide a fast, innate defense against virus-infected cells.

questions.prompt: After macrophages phagocytize bacterial matter, they bring fragments of it to the _______ to alert the immune system to its presence.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. NK cells do not need antigen presentation.
Incorrect. Reticular cells form the framework of lymph nodes.
Incorrect. Reticular fibers are support fibers, not cells.
Correct. Macrophages present antigens to T cells.
Incorrect. B cells recognize whole antigens directly; macrophages present mainly to T cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is T cells. After macrophages eat bacteria, they display pieces of the bacteria (antigens) on their surface using MHC molecules.

Helper T cells recognize these displayed pieces and become activated, alerting the adaptive immune system. This is antigen presentation.

Big idea: antigen-presenting cells show germ pieces to T cells to start specific immunity.

questions.prompt: Immature lymphocytes maturing in the thymus are separated from blood borne antigens via the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The blood-brain barrier protects the brain.
Correct. The blood-thymus barrier protects maturing T cells.
Incorrect. The retroperitoneum is a space in the abdomen.
Incorrect. Costal cartilages connect the ribs to the sternum.
Incorrect. The xiphoid process is the tip of the sternum.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the blood-thymus barrier. In the thymus, young T cells are kept away from antigens floating in the blood.

This barrier lets them develop and learn self-tolerance without being activated too early by foreign antigens. The blood-brain barrier protects the brain, and the other choices are not barriers around the thymus.

Big idea: T cells mature in a protected environment in the thymus.

questions.prompt: ________ are small proteins that regulate inflammation and immunity.

choices.explanation: Correct. Cytokines are small proteins that regulate inflammation and immunity.
Incorrect. Histamine is a small molecule, not a protein.
Incorrect. GPCRs are receptors on cells.
Incorrect. Osteoclasts are bone cells.
Incorrect. White blood cells are cells, not small proteins.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cytokines. Cytokines are small proteins that immune cells use to send messages, telling other cells to grow, move, attack, or calm down.

They regulate inflammation and immunity. Histamine is a small chemical (not a protein) that causes inflammation, GPCRs are receptors, osteoclasts are bone cells, and WBCs are cells, not proteins.

Big idea: cytokines are the immune system's chemical messengers.

questions.prompt: I am inspecting a spinal cord. I would expect to find what type of macrophage here?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Dendritic cells present antigens; they are not the spinal cord's macrophages.
Correct. Microglia are the macrophages of the central nervous system.
Incorrect. Hepatic macrophages (Kupffer cells) are in the liver.
Incorrect. Alveolar macrophages are in the lungs.
Incorrect. Only microglia are found in the spinal cord.

questions.explanation:
The answer is microglia. Microglia are the macrophage-like immune cells of the brain and spinal cord (the central nervous system).

Macrophages have different names in different organs: Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages (dust cells) in the lungs, and microglia in the central nervous system.

Big idea: macrophages live in many tissues, each with a special name.

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of interferons secreted by a cell?

choices.text: To intercept and prevent infection of itself
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Interferons cannot save the cell that is already infected.

choices.text: To interfere with bacterial signaling, reducing infection severity
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Interferons mainly fight viruses, not bacterial signaling.

choices.text: To alert neighboring cells of infection
choices.explanation: Correct. Interferons warn neighboring cells to protect themselves.

choices.text: To reroute blood vessels to sites of infection
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Interferons do not reroute blood vessels.

choices.text: To increase ATP generation in the cytoplasm
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Interferons do not increase ATP production.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to alert neighboring cells of infection. When a cell is infected by a virus, it releases interferons.

Interferons do not save the infected cell, but they warn nearby healthy cells, which then make proteins that block viruses from multiplying. Interferons also activate NK cells and macrophages.

Big idea: interferons are innate antiviral warning signals.

questions.prompt: Complement proteins are primarily synthesized by:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lymph nodes hold immune cells but do not make most complement.
Incorrect. Nerve cells do not make complement.
Incorrect. Heart cells do not make complement.
Correct. The liver makes most complement proteins.
Incorrect. The kidneys do not make most complement.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the liver. Most complement proteins are made by liver cells (hepatocytes) and released into the blood.

They circulate in an inactive form until an infection triggers the complement cascade.

Big idea: the liver supports the immune system by making complement proteins.

questions.prompt: The part of the brain responsible for raising the body’s set point for temperature during the fever is the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The occipital lobe processes vision.
Incorrect. The cerebral cortex handles thinking and sensation.
Correct. The hypothalamus raises the temperature set point during fever.
Incorrect. The parietal cortex processes touch and body sense.
Incorrect. The frontal cortex handles planning and movement.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus is the brain's thermostat.

During an infection, chemicals called pyrogens tell the hypothalamus to raise the body's temperature set point, causing fever. Fever helps slow down germs and speeds up immune responses.

Big idea: fever is controlled by the hypothalamus.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a cardinal sign of fever?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Redness is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Incorrect. Swelling is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Incorrect. Heat is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Incorrect. Pain is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Correct. Bruising is not a cardinal sign of inflammation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bruising. The question says 'fever', but it means the cardinal signs of inflammation: redness, swelling, heat, and pain (and sometimes loss of function).

Bruising is bleeding under the skin from broken blood vessels. It is not one of the cardinal signs of inflammation.

Big idea: inflammation's cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, and pain.

questions.prompt: Increased production of leukocytes is stimulated by what signaling molecule?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytokines is a broad category; colony-stimulating factor is the specific signal.
Incorrect. Bradykinin causes pain and leaky blood vessels.
Incorrect. Leukotrienes attract white cells and tighten airways.
Correct. Colony-stimulating factors increase production of white blood cells.
Incorrect. Selectins help white cells stick to blood vessel walls.

questions.explanation:
The answer is colony-stimulating factor. Colony-stimulating factors (CSFs) are signals that tell the bone marrow to make more white blood cells (leukocytes).

During an infection, they cause leukocytosis, a rise in white blood cells. Bradykinin causes pain and leaky vessels, leukotrienes help attract cells, and selectins help white cells stick to vessel walls.

Big idea: the body increases white blood cell production when fighting infection.

questions.prompt: What method of immunity employs lymphocytes to destroy intracellular threats like bacteria and yeasts?

choices.explanation: Correct. Cell-mediated (T cell) immunity targets intracellular threats.
Incorrect. This describes how immunity was gained, not the method.
Incorrect. This describes how immunity was gained (vaccines), not the method.
Incorrect. This describes receiving antibodies from a mother.
Incorrect. Humoral immunity uses antibodies, which work mostly outside cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cell-mediated immunity. Cell-mediated immunity uses T lymphocytes to deal with germs that hide inside cells, like viruses and some bacteria and yeasts.

Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells, and helper T cells activate macrophages to destroy germs they have swallowed. Humoral immunity uses antibodies, which mostly work outside cells.

Big idea: T cells handle intracellular threats; antibodies handle extracellular ones.

questions.prompt: In humoral immunity, _______ produced by plasma cells bind to _______ on foreign matter.

choices.explanation: Correct. Plasma cells make antibodies that bind antigens.
Incorrect. Antibiotics are medicines, not made by plasma cells.
Incorrect. This is backwards.
Incorrect. Glucagon is a hormone.
Incorrect. Glucagon and pyrimidine are not part of this process.

questions.explanation:
The answer is antibodies; antigens. Plasma cells (activated B cells) make antibodies, which bind to specific antigens on germs or foreign substances.

This binding neutralizes germs, clumps them together, and marks them for destruction. Antibiotics are medicines, and glucagon is a hormone.

Big idea: antibodies bind antigens.

questions.prompt: What type of immunity does the COVID-19 vaccination represent?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. 'Cellular immunity' describes a type of immune response, not how this immunity was gained.
Incorrect. Natural active immunity comes from catching the disease.
Correct. Vaccines give artificial active immunity.
Incorrect. Natural passive immunity comes from a mother's antibodies.
Incorrect. Artificial passive immunity comes from antibody injections.

questions.explanation:
The answer is artificial active immunity. A COVID-19 vaccine trains your own immune system to make antibodies and memory cells, so it is active.

Because it comes from a medical treatment rather than catching the disease, it is artificial.

Big idea: vaccines create artificial active immunity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following molecules cannot act as an antigen?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Venoms contain proteins that can act as antigens.
Incorrect. Food proteins can act as antigens (causing food allergies).
Incorrect. Membrane proteins on foreign cells can act as antigens.
Incorrect. Pollen proteins are common antigens (allergens).
Correct. Glucose is a small, common molecule and does not act as an antigen.

questions.explanation:
The answer is glucose. Antigens are usually large or complex molecules, especially proteins, that the immune system sees as foreign.

Glucose is a small, simple sugar that is found everywhere in the body, so the immune system does not respond to it. Venoms, food proteins, molecules on other cells' membranes, and pollen can all act as antigens.

Big idea: the immune system recognizes large, foreign molecules, not simple nutrients.

questions.prompt: The part of the antigen which is recognized during an immune response is known as the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The antibody is what binds the epitope.
Correct. The epitope is the part of the antigen that is recognized.
Incorrect. A hapten is a small molecule that needs a carrier to trigger immunity.
Incorrect. Immunoglobulin is another name for antibody.
Incorrect. Diapedesis is when white cells leave blood vessels.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the epitope. An epitope is the specific small part of an antigen that an antibody or T cell receptor actually binds to.

One antigen can have many different epitopes. A hapten is a tiny molecule that only causes a response when attached to a carrier protein, and diapedesis is when white blood cells squeeze out of blood vessels.

Big idea: immune receptors recognize specific spots (epitopes) on antigens.

questions.prompt: Antibodies may be found dissolved in:

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Antibodies are in plasma, but also in the others.
Incorrect by itself. Antibodies are in lymph, but also in the others.
Incorrect by itself. IgA is in mucus, but antibodies are also in the others.
Incorrect by itself. IgA is in saliva, but antibodies are also in the others.
Correct. Antibodies are found in all of these fluids.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above'. Antibodies are found in many body fluids.

IgG and IgM are found in blood plasma and lymph, and IgA is found in mucus, saliva, tears, and breast milk, where it protects mucous membranes.

Big idea: antibodies protect the body's fluids and surfaces.

questions.prompt: Lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells communicate via:

choices.explanation: Incorrect for this key. MHC molecules display antigens to T cells, but the key's answer is interleukins.
Incorrect. 'Paracrines' is a general term for local signals, not the specific answer.
Incorrect. Neurotransmitters are used by nerve cells.
Incorrect. Histamines cause inflammation, not lymphocyte-APC communication.
Correct. Interleukins carry messages between white blood cells.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is interleukins. Interleukins are cytokines that carry messages between white blood cells (the name means 'between leukocytes').

When an antigen-presenting cell activates a T cell, they exchange interleukins that tell each other to grow and respond. MHC molecules are also essential, because they display the antigen to T cells, but the key focuses on the chemical messengers.

Big idea: immune cells communicate by direct contact (MHC) and by chemical signals (interleukins).

questions.prompt: An antigen-presenting cell shows a T cell a self-antigen. The most likely result is that the T cell:

choices.text: Destroys the APC and all cells containing the self-antigen
choices.explanation: Incorrect. That would be an autoimmune attack.

choices.text: Destroys all cells containing the self-antigen
choices.explanation: Incorrect. That would be an autoimmune attack.
Incorrect. T cells do not destroy APCs showing self-antigens.

choices.text: Initiates a cascade for NK cells to destroy self-antigen presenting cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This would also be an autoimmune response.
Correct. Tolerant T cells ignore self-antigens.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the T cell disregards the signal. Mature T cells are trained in the thymus to ignore the body's own molecules (self-antigens). This is called self-tolerance.

So when an APC shows a T cell a self-antigen, the T cell does not respond. If it did attack, that would cause autoimmune disease.

Big idea: self-tolerance keeps the immune system from attacking the body.

questions.prompt: The ability for returning pathogens to be recognized in cellular immunity is contributed to:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells but are not the memory cells themselves.
Incorrect. Helper T cells coordinate responses but are not the memory cells.
Incorrect. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses.
Correct. Memory T cells recognize returning pathogens.
Incorrect. B cells are part of humoral, not cellular, immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is memory T cells. After an infection, some T cells become long-lived memory T cells.

If the same germ returns, memory T cells recognize it quickly and start a fast cell-mediated response. Memory B cells do the same for antibodies, but the question asks about cellular immunity.

Big idea: memory cells let the immune system respond faster the second time.

questions.prompt: These T cells are the only T cells that directly kill other cells.

choices.explanation: Correct. Cytotoxic T cells directly kill infected cells.
Incorrect. Helper T cells coordinate but do not directly kill.
Incorrect. Regulatory T cells calm the immune response.
Incorrect. Memory T cells remember germs for later.
Incorrect. Helper T cells do not directly kill cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic (CD8) T cells are the T cells that directly kill other cells, such as virus-infected or cancer cells.

They release perforins (which punch holes) and granzymes (which trigger the cell to self-destruct). Helper T cells coordinate the response, regulatory T cells calm it down, and memory T cells remember germs.

Big idea: cytotoxic T cells are the killers of the adaptive immune system.

questions.prompt: The binding of antibody in humoral immunity to parts of an antigen which are pathogenic is known as:

choices.explanation: Correct. Neutralization blocks the harmful parts of a germ or toxin.
Incorrect. Complement fixation activates complement proteins.
Incorrect. 'Attack' is not the technical term.
Incorrect. Agglutination clumps germs together.
Incorrect. Precipitation makes dissolved antigens clump and settle.

questions.explanation:
The answer is neutralization. In neutralization, antibodies bind to the parts of a germ or toxin that cause harm, such as the parts a virus uses to enter cells.

This blocks the germ or toxin from doing damage. Complement fixation activates complement proteins, agglutination clumps germs together, and precipitation makes dissolved antigens fall out of solution.

Big idea: antibodies protect us in several ways, including neutralization.

questions.prompt: Macrophage activation and the killing of cancer cells is a function of which chemical?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Perforins punch holes in target cells but do not activate macrophages.
Incorrect. Granzymes trigger target cells to self-destruct.
Incorrect. Secretin is a digestive hormone.
Incorrect. Interferons mainly fight viruses (interferon-gamma does activate macrophages, but the key is TNF).
Correct. Tumor necrosis factor activates macrophages and helps kill cancer cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is tumor necrosis factor (TNF). TNF is a cytokine released mainly by macrophages and T cells.

It activates macrophages, causes inflammation, and can kill some cancer cells. Perforins and granzymes are used by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells to kill cells directly, secretin is a digestive hormone, and interferons mainly fight viruses.

Big idea: cytokines like TNF coordinate inflammation and help destroy tumor cells.

questions.prompt: Symptoms depend on phase of infection, has an acute stage, chronic stage, and symptomatic stage
questions.context: Match the following descriptions to the disorders which they correspond closest to: A. Multiple sclerosis B. HIV/AIDS C. Rheumatoid arthritis D. Urticaria E. Common variable immunodeficiency

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = multiple sclerosis.
Correct. B = HIV/AIDS.
Incorrect. C = rheumatoid arthritis.
Incorrect. D = urticaria.
Incorrect. E = common variable immunodeficiency.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B, HIV/AIDS. HIV infection goes through stages: an acute stage soon after infection (flu-like illness), a long chronic stage with few symptoms, and a symptomatic stage (AIDS) when the immune system is badly damaged.

Big idea: HIV/AIDS is an acquired immunodeficiency that progresses in stages.

questions.prompt: Rare and presents with multiple phenotypes, generally presents with pneumonia, ear and GI infections
questions.context: Match the following descriptions to the disorders which they correspond closest to: A. Multiple sclerosis B. HIV/AIDS C. Rheumatoid arthritis D. Urticaria E. Common variable immunodeficiency

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = multiple sclerosis.
Incorrect. B = HIV/AIDS.
Incorrect. C = rheumatoid arthritis.
Incorrect. D = urticaria.
Correct. E = common variable immunodeficiency.

questions.explanation:
The answer is E, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID is a rare condition in which B cells do not make enough antibodies. It can look different in different people and commonly causes repeated pneumonia, ear infections, and gut infections.

Big idea: without enough antibodies, people get repeated infections.

questions.prompt: Results from degradation of the central nervous system
questions.context: Match the following descriptions to the disorders which they correspond closest to: A. Multiple sclerosis B. HIV/AIDS C. Rheumatoid arthritis D. Urticaria E. Common variable immunodeficiency

choices.explanation: Correct. A = multiple sclerosis.
Incorrect. B = HIV/AIDS.
Incorrect. C = rheumatoid arthritis.
Incorrect. D = urticaria.
Incorrect. E = common variable immunodeficiency.

questions.explanation:
The answer is A, multiple sclerosis. In MS, the immune system attacks the myelin in the brain and spinal cord, damaging the central nervous system.

Big idea: MS is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system.

questions.prompt: Starts from fingers and progresses towards the trunk with symptoms that might also affect the salivary glands and blood vessels, generally presents in flares
questions.context: Match the following descriptions to the disorders which they correspond closest to: A. Multiple sclerosis B. HIV/AIDS C. Rheumatoid arthritis D. Urticaria E. Common variable immunodeficiency

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = multiple sclerosis.
Incorrect. B = HIV/AIDS.
Correct. C = rheumatoid arthritis.
Incorrect. D = urticaria.
Incorrect. E = common variable immunodeficiency.

questions.explanation:
The answer is C, rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA often starts in the small joints of the fingers and spreads to larger joints, comes in flares, and can affect other parts of the body, such as the salivary glands (dry mouth) and blood vessels.

Big idea: RA is an autoimmune disease that mainly attacks the joints.

questions.prompt: Involves swollen patches of skin that last over one to two months, generally triggered by exercise or stress
questions.context: Match the following descriptions to the disorders which they correspond closest to: A. Multiple sclerosis B. HIV/AIDS C. Rheumatoid arthritis D. Urticaria E. Common variable immunodeficiency

choices.explanation: Incorrect. A = multiple sclerosis.
Incorrect. B = HIV/AIDS.
Incorrect. C = rheumatoid arthritis.
Correct. D = urticaria.
Incorrect. E = common variable immunodeficiency.

questions.explanation:
The answer is D, urticaria (hives). Urticaria causes swollen, itchy patches of skin. When it lasts more than six weeks it is called chronic urticaria, and it can be triggered by things like exercise, stress, heat, or pressure.

Big idea: hives are caused by histamine release in the skin.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a part of Type II hypersensitivity response?

choices.explanation: Also not part of type II (IgE belongs to type I), but the key does not mark it.
Incorrect. IgM is part of type II reactions.
Also not part of type II (basophils belong to type I), but the key does not mark it.
Correct (per the key). T cells cause type IV, not type II, reactions.

questions.note: Uncertain: IgE (A) and basophils (C) are also not part of type II hypersensitivity (they belong to type I); the official key marks only T cells.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is T cells. Type II hypersensitivity happens when antibodies (IgG or IgM) attach to the body's own cells, for example red blood cells in a mismatched blood transfusion. The marked cells are then destroyed by complement or phagocytes.

T cells are not part of this; they cause type IV (delayed) reactions. However, IgE and basophils are not part of type II either: they belong to type I (allergic) reactions. So this question really has three correct answers, and only IgM truly belongs to type II.

Big idea: type I = IgE and mast cells/basophils; type II = IgG/IgM against cells; type III = immune complexes; type IV = T cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not an IgE mediated disease/disorder?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Allergic asthma is IgE-mediated.
Incorrect. Anaphylaxis is IgE-mediated.
Correct. Contact dermatitis is a T cell (type IV) reaction.
Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated.

questions.explanation:
The answer is allergic contact dermatitis. Contact dermatitis, like a poison ivy rash, is a type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity caused by T cells, not IgE. It appears a day or two after contact.

Asthma (allergic type), anaphylaxis, and allergic rhinitis (hay fever) are all caused by IgE antibodies on mast cells (type I hypersensitivity).

Big idea: IgE causes fast allergic reactions; T cells cause delayed ones.

questions.prompt: What cell releases granules containing histamine and other reactive agents?

choices.explanation: Correct (per the key). Mast cells release histamine-filled granules.
Incorrect. Langerhans cells are skin dendritic cells that present antigens.
Incorrect. Macrophages eat germs; they do not release histamine granules.
Also correct in real life. Basophils release histamine granules too, but the key marks only mast cells.

questions.note: Uncertain: basophils (D) also release histamine-containing granules; the official key marks mast cells.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is mast cells. Mast cells live in tissues like the skin, airways, and gut. They are packed with granules containing histamine and other chemicals.

When triggered (for example by an allergen binding IgE on their surface), they release these granules, causing inflammation and allergy symptoms. Basophils, found in the blood, do the very same thing, so they are also a correct answer, which makes this question uncertain. Langerhans cells and macrophages do not release histamine granules.

Big idea: mast cells and basophils are the histamine-releasing cells of allergic reactions.

questions.prompt: All of the following are examples of macrophages except?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Kupffer cells are the liver's macrophages.
Incorrect. Sinus histiocytes are macrophages in lymph nodes.
Incorrect. Microglia are the macrophages of the central nervous system.
Correct. Osteoblasts build bone; they are not macrophages.

questions.explanation:
The answer is osteoblasts. Osteoblasts are bone-building cells; they are not immune cells.

Macrophages live in many organs and have special names: Kupffer cells in the liver, sinus histiocytes in lymph nodes, and microglia in the brain and spinal cord. (The bone's macrophage-related cell is the osteoclast, which breaks bone down, not the osteoblast.)

Big idea: macrophages are found throughout the body under different names.

questions.prompt: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) primarily infects what kind of white blood cell?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. CD8 is found on cytotoxic T cells.
Incorrect. CD56 is found on natural killer cells.
Correct. HIV infects CD4 helper T cells.
Incorrect. CD11c is found on dendritic cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is CD4. HIV attaches to the CD4 protein on helper T cells (and some macrophages) to get inside.
