CD8 is on cytotoxic T cells, CD56 is on natural killer cells, and CD11c is on dendritic cells. These are 'name tags' (CD markers) used to identify immune cells.

Big idea: HIV destroys CD4 helper T cells, causing immunodeficiency.

questions.prompt: All of the following are common symptoms of anaphylaxis EXCEPT:

choices.explanation: Correct. Fever is not a typical symptom of anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Low blood pressure is a key sign of anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Swelling (angioedema) is common in anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Blurred vision can happen as blood pressure falls.

questions.explanation:
The answer is fever. Anaphylaxis is a fast, severe allergic reaction. Histamine and other chemicals cause blood vessels to widen and leak, leading to low blood pressure (hypotension), swelling of the face and throat (angioedema), and sometimes blurred vision from low blood pressure.

Fever is a sign of infection or inflammation over time; it is not a typical part of anaphylaxis.

Big idea: anaphylaxis affects the whole body within minutes and needs epinephrine.

questions.prompt: The production of antibodies is the body's __________ line of defense.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The first line is barriers like skin and mucus.
Incorrect. The second line is innate responses like inflammation and phagocytes.
Correct. Antibodies are part of the third (adaptive) line.
Incorrect. There are three lines of defense.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the third line of defense. The first line is barriers like skin and mucous membranes. The second line is innate defenses inside the body, such as phagocytes, inflammation, and fever.

The third line is the adaptive immune system: B cells making antibodies and T cells attacking specific germs.

Big idea: the immune system has three lines of defense.

questions.prompt: Which of the following antibodies are involved in causing basophils to release histamine?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA protects mucous membranes.
Incorrect. IgG is the main antibody in the blood but does not trigger histamine release this way.
Correct. IgE on basophils triggers histamine release.
Incorrect. IgM is the first antibody made in an infection.

questions.explanation:
The answer is IgE. Basophils (and mast cells) have IgE antibodies attached to their surface. When an allergen binds and links these IgE molecules together, the cell releases histamine.

This is how allergic (type I) reactions happen. IgA, IgG, and IgM do not do this.

Big idea: IgE is the allergy antibody.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes an autoimmune disease?

choices.text: Infection and death of T-helper cells by a virus, resulting in a loss of adaptive immunity
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes HIV, an infection.

choices.text: Antibody binding to acetylcholine receptors of the motor end plate resulting in muscle weakness
choices.explanation: Correct. This describes myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease.

choices.text: Uncontrolled cell division resulting in cell surface abnormalities recognized by NK cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the immune system responding to cancer.

choices.text: Release of bacterial endotoxins that block acetylcholine release resulting in muscle paralysis
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes botulism, caused by a bacterial toxin.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B: antibodies binding to acetylcholine receptors at the muscle, causing weakness. This describes myasthenia gravis, where the immune system attacks the body's own receptors.

Choice A describes HIV (an infection), C describes the immune response to cancer cells, and D describes botulism (a bacterial toxin). None of those is the immune system attacking healthy self tissue.

Big idea: autoimmune disease means the immune system attacks the body's own healthy parts.

questions.prompt: Inflammation ________

choices.text: Brings more leukocytes to the infection site
choices.explanation: Correct. Inflammation brings white blood cells to the infection.

choices.text: Slows the healing process with swelling that can impair bodily function
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inflammation helps healing overall.

choices.text: Is caused by viral activity to enhance the spread of disease
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inflammation is the body's defense, not a virus's tool.

choices.text: Is caused by bacterial activity to enhance spread of disease
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inflammation is the body's defense, not a bacteria's tool.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that inflammation brings more leukocytes (white blood cells) to the infection site. Blood vessels widen and become leaky, and chemical signals call white blood cells into the area.

Although swelling can be uncomfortable, inflammation helps healing overall. It is the body's own response, not something viruses or bacteria cause in order to spread.

Big idea: inflammation brings defenders and repair materials to damaged tissue.

questions.prompt: Identify the above white blood cell.
questions.explanation:
The cell is a neutrophil. It has a nucleus divided into several lobes (here 3-4 connected lobes) and pale, lightly speckled cytoplasm.

Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells. They are the first to arrive at an infection and eat bacteria.

Big idea: a many-lobed nucleus with pale cytoplasm means neutrophil.

questions.prompt: Identify the above white blood cell.
questions.explanation:
The cell is an eosinophil. It has a two-lobed nucleus and its cytoplasm is packed with bright orange-red granules.

Eosinophils fight parasites and are involved in allergic reactions.

Big idea: orange-red granules mean eosinophil.

questions.prompt: What is A referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label A is the tonsils, the lymphatic tissue in the throat.

Tonsils trap and respond to germs entering through the mouth.

Big idea: tonsils guard the entrance of the digestive and respiratory tracts.

questions.prompt: What is B referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label B is the adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil), high at the back of the nasal cavity.

The adenoids trap germs breathed in through the nose.

Big idea: the adenoids are tonsils behind the nose.

questions.prompt: What is C referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label C is the thymus, in the upper chest behind the sternum.

The thymus is where T cells mature. It is largest in children and shrinks in adults.

Big idea: T cells are trained in the thymus.

questions.prompt: What is D referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label D is the lymph nodes, the small bean-shaped clusters along the lymph vessels.

Lymph nodes filter lymph and are where B and T cells meet germs.

Big idea: lymph nodes are the checkpoints of the lymphatic system.

questions.prompt: What is E referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label E is the lymph vessels, the network of tubes carrying lymph.

Lymph vessels collect fluid that leaks from the blood and return it to the bloodstream, passing through lymph nodes along the way.

Big idea: lymph vessels return fluid and carry immune cells.

questions.prompt: What is F referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label F is the bone marrow, shown inside the arm bone.

Bone marrow makes all blood cells, including white blood cells, and is where B cells mature.

Big idea: immune cells are born in the bone marrow.

questions.prompt: What is H referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label H is the spleen, on the left side of the upper abdomen.

The spleen filters blood, removes old red blood cells, and helps fight blood-borne germs.

Big idea: the spleen is the blood's filter.

questions.prompt: What is G referring to?
questions.context: Use the diagram for questions 50-57.
questions.explanation:
Label G is Peyer's patches, the lymphoid tissue in the wall of the small intestine.

Peyer's patches watch for germs in the intestine and start immune responses.

Big idea: Peyer's patches are part of the gut's immune tissue (MALT).

questions.prompt: What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.context: A 25 year old woman comes in with the following presentation of symptoms: anxiety, hand tremor, heat sensitivity, weight loss, puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid.
questions.explanation:
The likely diagnosis is Graves' disease. Anxiety, hand tremor, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, bulging or puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid (goiter) are classic signs of an overactive thyroid.

Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. The eye changes are a special clue that points to Graves' disease.

Big idea: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease that overstimulates the thyroid.

questions.prompt: What is the common cause of this disease?
questions.context: A 25 year old woman comes in with the following presentation of symptoms: anxiety, hand tremor, heat sensitivity, weight loss, puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid.
questions.answer: An autoimmune reaction: the immune system makes antibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins) that switch on the TSH receptor, so the thyroid makes too much thyroid hormone (and TSH from the pituitary becomes low).
questions.officialAnswer: Too much thyroid hormone and low TSH (all or nothing) (thyroid issues)
questions.note: The official key ("Too much thyroid hormone and low TSH") describes the lab results, not the cause; the cause is autoimmune antibodies that stimulate the thyroid.
questions.explanation:
Graves' disease is caused by an autoimmune reaction. The immune system makes antibodies, called thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, that act like TSH and switch on the thyroid's TSH receptors.

The thyroid then makes too much thyroid hormone. The pituitary senses the high hormone level and makes less TSH, so blood tests show high thyroid hormone and low TSH. (The official key described these lab results rather than the cause.)

Big idea: in Graves' disease, antibodies stimulate a gland instead of destroying it.

questions.prompt: What foods should this patient avoid consuming?
questions.context: A 25 year old woman comes in with the following presentation of symptoms: anxiety, hand tremor, heat sensitivity, weight loss, puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid.
questions.answer: Foods high in iodine (such as kelp, seaweed, and iodine supplements), because iodine is used to make thyroid hormone, and caffeine, which worsens a fast heartbeat, tremor, and anxiety.
questions.note: The official key lists "caffeine, any allergens, gluten/wheat products"; avoiding excess iodine is the main dietary advice for Graves' disease.
questions.explanation:
The main foods to limit are those high in iodine (like kelp, seaweed, and iodine supplements), because the thyroid uses iodine to make thyroid hormone. Caffeine is also best avoided, because it worsens a racing heart, tremor, and anxiety.

Diet does not cure Graves' disease; treatment uses medicines, radioactive iodine, or surgery. (The official key also listed allergens and gluten, which matter only for people who have those specific problems.)

Big idea: treatment and prevention include medicines and avoiding things that make symptoms worse.

questions.prompt: What blood test can be run to confirm a diagnosis?
questions.context: A 25 year old woman comes in with the following presentation of symptoms: anxiety, hand tremor, heat sensitivity, weight loss, puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid.
questions.answer: Thyroid blood tests showing low TSH and high T4/T3, plus TSH-receptor antibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, TSI/TRAb), which confirm Graves' disease.
questions.note: The official key says thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies, which are mainly a marker of Hashimoto's thyroiditis; TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves' disease.
questions.explanation:
Blood tests show low TSH and high thyroid hormone (T4 and T3), confirming an overactive thyroid. A test for TSH-receptor antibodies (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, TSI or TRAb) confirms the cause is Graves' disease.

Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies, which the official key listed, are mainly a marker for Hashimoto's thyroiditis, though some Graves' patients have them too.

Big idea: antibody tests help identify which autoimmune disease is present.

questions.prompt: What is another name for this disease aside from the common name?
questions.context: A 25 year old woman comes in with the following presentation of symptoms: anxiety, hand tremor, heat sensitivity, weight loss, puffy eyes, and an enlarged thyroid.
questions.explanation:
Another name for Graves' disease is Basedow's disease. Robert Graves described it in Ireland and Karl von Basedow described it in Germany at about the same time.

In Europe it is often called Basedow's disease, and in English-speaking countries Graves' disease.

Big idea: some diseases have more than one name, often from the people who first described them.

questions.prompt: Which of the following antibodies can fix complement?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA does not activate the classical complement pathway well.
Incorrect. IgD does not activate complement.
Incorrect. IgE works with mast cells, not complement.
Correct. IgG can activate complement.
Correct. IgM is the strongest complement activator.

questions.explanation:
The answers are IgG and IgM. 'Fixing complement' means activating the complement system, a group of blood proteins that destroy germs.

IgM is the strongest at this because its five-unit shape lets one molecule start the process. IgG can also activate complement. IgA, IgD, and IgE do not activate the classical complement pathway well.

Big idea: IgM and IgG activate complement.

questions.prompt: Red pulp - contains red blood cells, __________, and ____________ (ENTER ALPHABETICALLY)
questions.explanation:
The answers are lymphocytes and macrophages. The spleen's red pulp is full of blood.

It contains red blood cells, plus macrophages that eat old and damaged red blood cells, and lymphocytes. (The white pulp is where most lymphocytes cluster.)

Big idea: the red pulp filters old red blood cells out of the blood.

questions.prompt: Eosinophils are most effective against __________infections
questions.explanation:
The answer is parasitic. Eosinophils fight parasites, especially worms that are too big to be eaten.

They attach to the parasite (often with help from IgE) and release toxic proteins from their granules.

Big idea: eosinophils and IgE are the main defense against parasites.

questions.prompt: A CD4 Cell is a(an)______cell
questions.explanation:
The answer is a T cell (a helper T cell). CD4 is a protein on the surface of helper T cells.

CD4 helps the T cell recognize antigens shown on MHC class II molecules. HIV uses CD4 to infect these cells.

Big idea: CD4 marks helper T cells; CD8 marks cytotoxic T cells.

questions.prompt: _______ is the breakdown of a cell caused by damage to its plasma (outer) membrane
questions.explanation:
The answer is lysis. Lysis means a cell bursting open because its outer membrane is damaged.

The complement system's membrane attack complex and cytotoxic T cells' perforin both cause lysis by punching holes in a cell's membrane.

Big idea: lysis is one way the immune system destroys germs and infected cells.

questions.prompt: ____ is a rare disease where a baby is born with very few or no T Lymphocytes. (initials)
questions.explanation:
The answer is SCID, severe combined immunodeficiency. Babies with SCID are born with very few or no working T cells (and usually B cells that do not work properly).

Without these cells, they get severe infections and need a bone marrow (stem cell) transplant.

Big idea: SCID is a genetic immunodeficiency affecting both arms of adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: ___________ highlight molecules to be phagocytosed and engage with receptors on phagocytic cells
questions.explanation:
The answer is opsonins. Opsonins are molecules, such as antibodies and complement proteins, that coat germs and make them easier for phagocytes to eat.

Phagocytes have receptors that grab onto opsonins, like a handle. This coating process is called opsonization.

Big idea: opsonins tag germs for phagocytosis.

questions.prompt: These anti-microbial substances promote cytolysis, phagocytosis and inflammation._______
questions.note: The official key says "transferrins"; transferrin carries iron and does not cause cytolysis, phagocytosis, and inflammation. These three effects describe complement.
questions.explanation:
The answer is complement (the complement proteins). The complement system is a group of blood proteins that, once activated, punch holes in germs (cytolysis), coat germs for phagocytosis (opsonization), and attract white blood cells and boost inflammation.

The official key said 'transferrins', but transferrin is a protein that carries iron in the blood; it does not do these three things.

Big idea: complement is one of the main antimicrobial proteins of the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: What structure allows lymph from the upper right limb to enter the bloodstream? _________ ________
questions.note: The official key says "thoracic duct", but lymph from the upper right limb drains through the right lymphatic duct; the thoracic duct drains the rest of the body.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the right lymphatic duct. Lymph from the right arm, the right side of the head and neck, and the right side of the chest drains into the right lymphatic duct, which empties into a large vein near the right collarbone.

The official key said 'thoracic duct', but the thoracic duct drains the rest of the body (both legs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and chest).

Big idea: lymph returns to the blood through two main ducts.

questions.prompt: ___ are protein-shredding enzymes released by cytotoxic T-cells that induce apoptosis.
questions.explanation:
The answer is granzymes. Cytotoxic T cells (and NK cells) release perforin, which makes holes in a target cell, and granzymes, which enter through these holes.

Granzymes are protein-cutting enzymes that trigger the infected or cancerous cell to destroy itself (apoptosis).

Big idea: cytotoxic T cells kill using perforin and granzymes.

questions.prompt: Red and white pulp in the __________ help to purify ______________.
questions.explanation:
The answers are spleen and blood. The spleen has red pulp, which removes old and damaged red blood cells, and white pulp, which contains lymphocytes that respond to germs.

Together, they filter and clean the blood.

Big idea: lymph nodes filter lymph, and the spleen filters blood.

questions.prompt: How does the thymus change as an individual ages?
questions.answer: The thymus is conical, red, and much larger in children. As an individual ages, however, it starts to shrink and loses lymphatic tissue, becoming gray and then yellow in color as more fat is stored
questions.explanation:
The thymus is largest and most active in childhood, when lots of new T cells are being trained. After puberty, it slowly shrinks (involution).

Its active tissue is gradually replaced by fat, so it turns from pinkish-red to gray and then yellow. Fewer new T cells are made in older age, which is one reason the immune system weakens with age.

Big idea: the thymus is most important early in life.

questions.prompt: Collectins, ficolins and pentraxins: which two pathways do they activate complement through?
questions.answer: activate complement through classical or lectin pathway
questions.explanation:
They activate complement through the classical pathway and the lectin pathway. Collectins and ficolins recognize sugar patterns on germs and start the lectin pathway.

Pentraxins (like C-reactive protein) bind to germs and can start the classical pathway. These are all pattern-recognizing proteins of the innate immune system.

Big idea: complement can be started by antibodies (classical), sugar-recognizing proteins (lectin), or directly on germ surfaces (alternative).

questions.prompt: Where are histatins produced? Which type of Monocytes are they active against?
questions.answer: histatins are produced in the oral cavity - active against pathogenic fungi eg candida
questions.explanation:
Histatins are made in the mouth by the salivary glands and are found in saliva. They are small antimicrobial proteins.

They are especially active against fungi, such as Candida, the yeast that causes oral thrush. (The question says 'monocytes', but it means germs; histatins act against fungi.)

Big idea: saliva contains antimicrobial proteins that are part of the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: The tonsils increase in size in adults.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The tonsils are largest in childhood, when the immune system is meeting many new germs.

As people grow into adults, the tonsils usually shrink.

Big idea: lymphatic tissues like the tonsils and thymus are most active in childhood.

questions.prompt: The spleen has white pulp associated with the arteries.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. The spleen's white pulp is lymphoid tissue (mainly lymphocytes) that surrounds small arteries running through the spleen.

This lets immune cells check the blood as it flows in. The red pulp, around the blood-filled sinuses, removes old red blood cells.

Big idea: white pulp is for immunity; red pulp filters red blood cells.

questions.prompt: Red pulp contains mostly lymphocytes.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Red pulp is mostly full of blood (red blood cells) and macrophages that remove old red blood cells.

The white pulp is the part made mostly of lymphocytes.

Big idea: red pulp = red blood cells and macrophages; white pulp = lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: The thymus increases in mass through childhood and then atrophies during adulthood.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. The thymus grows during childhood, when it trains large numbers of new T cells.

After puberty, it gradually shrinks (atrophies) and is replaced by fat, so fewer new T cells are made in adulthood.

Big idea: the thymus is most important early in life.

questions.prompt: The largest percentage of antibodies in the blood are IgE.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. IgG is the most abundant antibody in the blood, making up about 75-80% of antibodies.

IgE is the least common in the blood (much less than 1%); most of it is attached to mast cells.

Big idea: IgG is most common; IgE is rarest in the blood.

questions.prompt: Epithelial cells within the thymus secrete hormones that are important to lymphocyte development.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. Epithelial cells in the thymus release hormones, such as thymosin and thymopoietin.

These hormones help young T cells mature and become able to recognize antigens.

Big idea: the thymus provides the environment and signals for T cell development.

questions.prompt: Phagocytosis occurs in the innate immune system.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. Phagocytosis, when cells like neutrophils and macrophages eat germs, is a key part of the innate immune system.

It works right away against any germ, without needing to learn about it first.

Big idea: phagocytes are first responders of innate immunity.

questions.prompt: Only the adaptive immune response requires the ability to distinguish between self and non-self.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Both the innate and adaptive immune systems must tell self from non-self.

Innate cells recognize patterns found on germs but not on our own cells, and they are kept in check by 'self' signals on our cells. Adaptive cells learn self-tolerance in the thymus and bone marrow.

Big idea: all immune defenses must avoid attacking the body's own cells.

questions.prompt: Vaccination mimics acquired immunity.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. A vaccine safely shows the immune system an antigen, so it makes antibodies and memory cells as if it had fought the real disease.

This acquired (adaptive) immunity protects you later, without having to get sick first.

Big idea: vaccines create active, acquired immunity.

questions.prompt: In the embryo, both T cells and B cells are produced in the:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus is where T cells mature, not where they are produced.
Correct. Both T and B cells are produced in the red bone marrow.
Incorrect. The spleen is where lymphocytes gather and work.
Incorrect. The fetal liver makes blood cells early on, but the key's answer is red bone marrow.
Incorrect. The brain does not make lymphocytes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the red bone marrow. B cells and T cells both start from stem cells in the red bone marrow.

B cells finish maturing there, while T cells move to the thymus to mature. (Very early in an embryo, blood cells are also made in the liver, but the key focuses on red bone marrow, where lymphocytes are produced.)

Big idea: lymphocytes come from bone marrow stem cells.

questions.prompt: The two general kinds of antigens, from the perspective of the immune system, are:

choices.explanation: Correct. Antigens are either self or foreign.
Incorrect. 'T antigens and B antigens' is not how antigens are classified.
Incorrect. A and B antigens are blood type antigens, just one example.
Incorrect. 'Gamma and beta antigens' is not a real classification.

questions.explanation:
The answer is self-antigens and foreign antigens. The immune system sorts every antigen into 'self' (molecules belonging to your own body) or 'foreign' (from germs, other people's cells, pollen, and so on).

Healthy immune cells ignore self-antigens and attack foreign ones. Autoimmune diseases happen when this sorting fails.

Big idea: telling self from non-self is the immune system's most basic job.

questions.prompt: With innate immunity,

choices.text: each time the body is exposed to a substance, the response is the same.
choices.explanation: Correct. Innate responses are the same each time; they have no memory.
Incorrect. Specificity and memory belong to adaptive immunity.

choices.text: we can become immune to a disease.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Becoming immune to a disease comes from adaptive memory.
Incorrect. Antibodies are made by the adaptive immune system.
Incorrect. Only A describes innate immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that each time the body is exposed to a substance, the response is the same. Innate immunity does not learn or remember.

Specificity, memory, becoming immune to a disease, and making antibodies are all features of adaptive immunity.

Big idea: innate = same response every time; adaptive = learns and improves.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of innate immunity?

choices.text: Tears and saliva wash away microorganisms.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. This is innate, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. This is innate, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. This is innate, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. This is innate, but so are the others.
Correct. All four are examples of innate immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above'. Tears and saliva washing away germs are innate barriers. Basophils releasing histamine and leukotrienes is part of inflammation, an innate response.

Neutrophils eating germs (phagocytosis) and the complement cascade are also innate defenses.

Big idea: innate immunity includes barriers, chemicals, cells, and proteins that act fast and generally.

questions.prompt: The type of lymphocyte that is responsible for the secondary antibody response is the

choices.explanation: Correct. Memory B cells cause the secondary antibody response.
Incorrect. Ordinary (naive) B cells start the primary response; memory B cells start the secondary.
Incorrect. T cells do not make antibodies.
Incorrect. Helper T cells help, but memory B cells make the secondary antibody response.
Incorrect. NK cells are innate and have no antibody memory.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the memory B cell. After the first exposure to an antigen, some B cells become long-lived memory B cells.

On the next exposure, they quickly multiply and become plasma cells, producing a fast, strong secondary antibody response.

Big idea: memory B cells power the secondary antibody response.

questions.prompt: Which of these cells is the most important in the release of histamine, which promotes inflammation?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Monocytes become macrophages; they are not the main histamine source.
Incorrect. Macrophages eat germs and release cytokines, not much histamine.
Incorrect. Eosinophils fight parasites.
Correct. Mast cells are the main source of histamine in tissues.
Incorrect. NK cells kill infected cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the mast cell. Mast cells live in tissues and are packed with granules of histamine.

When tissue is injured or an allergen binds their IgE, they release histamine, which widens blood vessels and makes them leaky, promoting inflammation. (Basophils in the blood do this too, but they are not a choice.)

Big idea: mast cells start inflammation and allergic reactions.

questions.prompt: Which of these conditions does not occur during the inflammatory response?

choices.text: histamine and other chemical mediators are released
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Histamine and other chemicals are released during inflammation.
Incorrect. Phagocytes are drawn to the site by chemotaxis.

choices.text: fibrinogen enters tissues from the blood
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Fibrinogen leaks into tissues to form clots.
Correct. Blood vessels dilate, not constrict, during inflammation.
Incorrect. Increased permeability is a key part of inflammation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is vasoconstriction of blood vessels. During inflammation, blood vessels widen (vasodilation), not narrow.

The other events do happen: histamine and other chemicals are released, phagocytes move toward the area (chemotaxis), blood vessels become more permeable, and fibrinogen leaks into the tissue to form clots that wall off the injury.

Big idea: inflammation widens and leaks blood vessels to bring help to the area.

questions.prompt: Plant viruses do not cause disease in people, which is an example of:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Passive immunity comes from receiving antibodies.
Incorrect. Natural acquired immunity comes from surviving an infection.
Incorrect. Herd immunity protects a community when most people are immune.
Correct. Being a species the virus cannot infect is genetic immunity.
Incorrect. Genetic immunity is the right answer.

questions.explanation:
The answer is genetic immunity. Some germs cannot infect humans at all, because our cells lack the receptors or conditions the germ needs.

This built-in, inherited resistance is called genetic (or species) immunity. Plant viruses cannot infect human cells, so we are naturally immune to them.

Big idea: some immunity comes simply from being a different species.

questions.prompt: Recovery from a disease may provide the type of immunity called:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Passive immunity means receiving antibodies from someone else.
Incorrect. Artificial passive immunity comes from antibody injections.
Correct. Recovering from a disease gives naturally acquired active immunity.
Incorrect. Artificial active immunity comes from vaccines.
Incorrect. Naturally acquired active immunity is correct.

questions.explanation:
The answer is naturally acquired active immunity. When you recover from a disease, your own immune system made antibodies and memory cells (active), and you got it from a real infection rather than a medical treatment (natural).

Big idea: natural = from everyday exposure; active = your body made the antibodies.

questions.prompt: The first antibody response to a foreign antigen is usually:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The first response is slow, not fast.
Correct. The first response is slow and makes a small amount of antibody.
Incorrect. The first response makes a small amount of antibody.
Incorrect. Fast and large describes the secondary response.

questions.explanation:
The answer is slow, with a small amount. The first (primary) antibody response takes several days to start, because the few B cells that match the antigen must be found and multiplied.

It also produces fewer antibodies, mostly IgM. The secondary response is faster and much larger.

Big idea: primary responses are slow and small; secondary responses are fast and big.

questions.prompt: A chemical involved in innate immunity is:

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. Lysozyme is innate, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. Histamine is innate, but so are the others.
Incorrect by itself. Leukotrienes are innate, but so are the others.
Correct. All three chemicals are involved in innate immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of these'. Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks down bacterial walls.

Histamine and leukotrienes are chemicals released during inflammation. All three are part of innate immunity.

Big idea: innate immunity uses many chemicals as well as cells.

questions.prompt: What is the function of lymph capillaries?

choices.text: Contracts to keep lymph moving through larger lymph vessels.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the smooth muscle in larger lymph vessels.

choices.text: Empties lymph from the lower body and upper left quadrant into the left subclavian vein.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the thoracic duct.

choices.text: Empties lymph from the upper right quadrant into the right subclavian vein.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the right lymphatic duct.

choices.text: Collect tissue fluid from intercellular spaces.
choices.explanation: Correct. Lymph capillaries collect fluid from the spaces between cells.

choices.text: The vessel formed by the union of lymph vessels from the lower body.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the cisterna chyli.

choices.text: Prevent backflow of lymph in larger lymph vessels.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes valves in lymph vessels.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to collect tissue fluid from the spaces between cells. Lymph capillaries are tiny, dead-end vessels that soak up the extra fluid that leaks out of blood capillaries.

Once inside, this fluid is called lymph. The other choices describe other lymphatic structures: the muscle in larger lymph vessels, the thoracic duct, the right lymphatic duct, the cisterna chyli, and valves.

Big idea: lymph capillaries collect leaked fluid so it can be returned to the blood.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the cisterna chyli?

choices.text: Contracts to keep lymph moving through larger lymph vessels.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes smooth muscle in lymph vessels.

choices.text: Empties lymph from the lower body and upper left quadrant into the left subclavian vein.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the thoracic duct.

choices.text: Empties lymph from the upper right quadrant into the right subclavian vein.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes the right lymphatic duct.

choices.text: Collect tissue fluid from intercellular spaces.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes lymph capillaries.

choices.text: The vessel formed by the union of lymph vessels from the lower body.
choices.explanation: Correct. The cisterna chyli forms where lymph vessels from the lower body join.

choices.text: Prevent backflow of lymph in larger lymph vessels.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. This describes valves.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the vessel formed by the union of lymph vessels from the lower body. The cisterna chyli is a sac-like enlargement at the bottom of the thoracic duct, in the upper abdomen.

It collects lymph from the legs and the intestines (including fat-rich chyle) before it travels up the thoracic duct.

Big idea: the cisterna chyli is the collecting point at the start of the thoracic duct.

questions.prompt: Which type of hypersensitivity involves soluble antigen-antibody complexes?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Type I is IgE-mediated allergy.
Incorrect. Type II is antibodies attacking cells.
Correct. Type III involves soluble antigen-antibody complexes.
Incorrect. Type IV is T-cell-mediated (delayed).
Incorrect. Type V is sometimes used for stimulating antibodies (as in Graves' disease).

questions.explanation:
The answer is type III. In type III hypersensitivity, antibodies bind to soluble antigens floating in the blood, forming clumps called immune complexes.

These complexes settle in blood vessels, joints, and kidneys and cause inflammation. Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction are examples.

Big idea: type III = immune complexes.

questions.prompt: The fixed cells in lymph nodes and nodules that produce antibodies are called:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lymphocytes is too general; plasma cells are the antibody-producing form of B cells.
Incorrect. Stem cells make new blood cells.
Correct. Plasma cells produce antibodies.
Incorrect. Macrophages eat germs.
Incorrect. Axillary nodes are lymph nodes in the armpit, not cells.
Incorrect. 'Lymphatic' is not a type of cell.

questions.explanation:
The answer is plasma cells. When B cells are activated, they turn into plasma cells, which stay in the lymph nodes and nodules and pump out antibodies.

Lymphocytes is too general, macrophages eat germs, and the other choices are not cells that make antibodies.

Big idea: plasma cells are the body's antibody factories.

questions.prompt: Which of the following might explain why most people are sick more often as children than as adults in their 20s through 50s?

choices.text: The immune system does not appear until the preteen years.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The immune system is present from birth.

choices.text: The thymus is so active in children that it fights bacteria so hard that it produces strong symptoms of disease.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus does not cause disease symptoms this way.

choices.text: Because of their small size, children's bodies cannot contain as much lymphoid tissue as those of adults.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Body size is not the reason.

choices.text: We build up many varieties of memory lymphocytes during childhood, providing immunity to more and more antigens during adulthood.
choices.explanation: Correct. Memory lymphocytes built up in childhood protect adults.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that we build up many kinds of memory lymphocytes during childhood. Children meet many germs for the first time, so they get sick more often.

Each infection leaves behind memory cells, so as adults we are protected against many germs we have already met.

Big idea: immune memory builds up over a lifetime.

questions.prompt: Because the appendix is a narrow tube, it traps microorganisms from the digestive tract, and these microorganisms enter its wall and activate memory lymphocytes for long-term immunity. Another immune organ that traps microorganisms is the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus trains T cells; it does not trap germs.
Incorrect. The bone marrow makes blood cells.
Correct. Tonsil crypts trap germs, like the appendix.
Incorrect. The spleen filters blood rather than trapping germs from a tract.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the palatine tonsil. Like the appendix, tonsils have deep pits (crypts) that trap germs.

The trapped germs activate lymphocytes in the tonsil tissue, helping build long-term immunity. The thymus trains T cells, the bone marrow makes cells, and the spleen filters blood.

Big idea: tonsils and the appendix trap germs to help the immune system learn.

questions.prompt: The immune system cell type that is preferentially destroyed by the AIDS virus is the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. B cells are not HIV's main target.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells have CD8, not CD4.
Correct. HIV preferentially destroys helper T cells.
Incorrect. There is no such thing as a 'helper B lymphocyte'.
Incorrect. HIV mainly targets helper T cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the helper T lymphocyte. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, enters cells using the CD4 protein on helper T cells.

As helper T cells are destroyed, the immune system loses its coordinators.

Big idea: HIV destroys helper T cells, causing AIDS.

questions.prompt: Which cell secretes cytokines that will stimulate proliferation of other immune cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells present antigens to T cells.
Correct. Helper T cells release cytokines that stimulate other immune cells.
Incorrect. NK cells kill infected cells directly.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the helper CD4+ T lymphocyte. Helper T cells release cytokines (like interleukin-2) that make other immune cells, including B cells and cytotoxic T cells, multiply and become active.

Big idea: helper T cells coordinate the immune response by releasing cytokines.

questions.prompt: One location where lymphoid tissue is found is "in the frequently infected mucous membranes of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts." Specifically, this refers to

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lymph trunks are vessels, not tissue in mucous membranes.

choices.text: the intestinal and tracheobronchial lymph nodes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. These are lymph nodes, not MALT.
Incorrect. These are lymph vessels that carry chyle.
Correct. MALT is lymphoid tissue in mucous membranes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is MALT, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. MALT is lymphoid tissue in the mucous membranes of the digestive, respiratory, urinary, and reproductive tracts, the places where germs most often try to enter.

It includes the tonsils, Peyer's patches, and the appendix.

Big idea: MALT guards the body's openings.

questions.prompt: The sinuses within lymph nodes

choices.text: are separated from the bloodstream by a blood-node barrier.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lymph nodes do not have a blood-node barrier.

choices.text: consist of star-shaped epithelial cells that secrete immune-boosting hormones.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Star-shaped epithelial cells that secrete hormones are in the thymus.

choices.text: contain macrophages living along a reticular fiber network.
choices.explanation: Correct. Macrophages line the reticular fiber network in the sinuses.

choices.text: surround clumps of lymphoid tissue called white pulp.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. White pulp is in the spleen, not lymph nodes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that lymph node sinuses contain macrophages living along a reticular fiber network. Lymph flows slowly through spaces (sinuses) inside lymph nodes.

A mesh of reticular fibers runs through these spaces, and macrophages sit on it, catching and eating germs and debris as lymph passes by.

Big idea: lymph nodes filter lymph using macrophages.

questions.prompt: In the spleen, lymphoid tissue is confined to the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Red pulp mainly filters red blood cells.
Correct. Lymphoid tissue is in the white pulp.
Incorrect. Trabeculae are connective tissue supports.
Incorrect. The hilus is where blood vessels enter and leave.
Incorrect. Lymph nodes are separate organs, not part of the spleen.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the white pulp. In the spleen, lymphocytes are gathered in the white pulp, around the small arteries.

The red pulp is mostly blood and macrophages. Trabeculae are support walls, and the hilus is where vessels enter.

Big idea: white pulp = immune tissue in the spleen.

questions.prompt: The purpose of this is to counteract the effects of _________ released during the allergic response.
questions.context: Use the following information for questions 34 through 38. Mr. Shasta is allergic to some specific plant pollens. Each summer he develops symptoms which include sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes, and he usually takes medication that contains an antihistamine.
questions.explanation:
The answer is histamine. Mr. Shasta's sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes are caused by histamine released from mast cells when pollen binds their IgE.

Antihistamines block histamine's receptors, reducing these symptoms.

Big idea: antihistamines counter histamine in allergic reactions.

questions.prompt: Substances such as pollens that cause allergies are called ___________.
questions.context: Use the following information for questions 34 through 38. Mr. Shasta is allergic to some specific plant pollens. Each summer he develops symptoms which include sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes, and he usually takes medication that contains an antihistamine.
questions.explanation:
The answer is allergens. An allergen is a normally harmless substance, like pollen, that causes an allergic reaction in some people.

Big idea: allergens trigger type I hypersensitivity.

questions.prompt: True or False: These substances are pathogenic.
questions.context: Use the following information for questions 34 through 38. Mr. Shasta is allergic to some specific plant pollens. Each summer he develops symptoms which include sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes, and he usually takes medication that contains an antihistamine.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Allergens like pollen are not pathogenic; they do not cause disease on their own.

The problem is the immune system's overreaction to them.

Big idea: allergies are an overreaction to harmless substances.

questions.prompt: True or False: The immune (allergic) response to an allergen is protective.
questions.context: Use the following information for questions 34 through 38. Mr. Shasta is allergic to some specific plant pollens. Each summer he develops symptoms which include sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes, and he usually takes medication that contains an antihistamine.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The allergic response to an allergen does not protect the body, because the allergen was never harmful.

The immune reaction itself causes the symptoms, and in severe cases (anaphylaxis) it can be dangerous.

Big idea: hypersensitivity is a harmful overreaction.

questions.prompt: State one possible serious consequence of a severe allergic reaction.
questions.context: Use the following information for questions 34 through 38. Mr. Shasta is allergic to some specific plant pollens. Each summer he develops symptoms which include sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes, and he usually takes medication that contains an antihistamine.
questions.explanation:
A serious consequence is anaphylaxis (anaphylactic shock), a whole-body reaction that drops blood pressure and can close the airway. Severe allergic asthma attacks can also be serious.

Anaphylaxis is an emergency treated with epinephrine.

Big idea: severe allergic reactions can be life-threatening.

questions.prompt: True or False: Hemolytic disease of the newborn typically results from immunization of an RH- mother with Rh+ blood from her first pregnancy, the antibodies reacting against the fetus in a later pregnancy.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. If an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby, some of the baby's blood can enter her blood, usually at birth. Her immune system makes anti-Rh antibodies.

In a later pregnancy with another Rh-positive baby, these IgG antibodies can cross the placenta and attack the baby's red blood cells (hemolytic disease of the newborn). An injection (RhoGAM) given to the mother prevents this.

Big idea: this is an example of a type II hypersensitivity (antibodies attacking cells).

questions.prompt: Which of the following lymphoid organs does not directly fight antigens?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Tonsils trap and fight antigens.
Incorrect. The spleen fights antigens in the blood.
Correct. The thymus trains T cells but does not directly fight antigens.
Incorrect. Peyer's patches fight antigens in the gut.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the thymus. The thymus is where T cells mature; it does not directly fight antigens.

Its environment is kept separate from blood-borne antigens (the blood-thymus barrier). The tonsils, spleen, and Peyer's patches all trap and respond to antigens directly.

Big idea: the thymus trains T cells; other lymphoid organs fight germs.

questions.prompt: B lymphocytes are to ________ as T lymphocytes are to ________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. T cells recognize antigens, but their weapon is causing cell death.
Correct. B cells make antibodies; cytotoxic T cells trigger programmed cell death.
Incorrect. This reverses the roles.
Incorrect. This reverses the roles.

questions.explanation:
The answer is antibodies; programmed cell death. B lymphocytes defend the body by making antibodies (humoral immunity).

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes defend the body by making infected cells undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis), using perforin and granzymes (cell-mediated immunity).

Big idea: B cells make antibodies; T cells kill infected cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not considered an organ of the immune system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The spleen filters blood and is an immune organ.
Incorrect. Lymph nodes filter lymph and are immune organs.
Incorrect. Red bone marrow makes immune cells.
Incorrect. The thymus trains T cells.
Correct. The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine organ, not an immune organ.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pancreas. The organs of the immune (lymphatic) system include the red bone marrow and thymus (where immune cells are made and trained), and the spleen and lymph nodes (where immune cells gather and filter fluids).

The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine organ that makes enzymes and hormones like insulin. It is not part of the immune system.

Big idea: lymphatic organs are bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, and tonsils (plus MALT).

questions.prompt: _____________ Immunity upon activation splits into small and large fragments which triggers an amplification cascade

choices.explanation: Correct. Complement proteins split into fragments that trigger an amplifying cascade.
Incorrect. Innate immunity is the broad category; complement is the specific system described.
Incorrect. Active immunity describes making your own antibodies.
Incorrect. Adaptive immunity uses B and T cells, not a protein-splitting cascade.

questions.explanation:
The answer is complement. The complement system is a group of blood proteins. When activated, a complement protein is split into a small fragment and a large fragment.

The large fragment joins with others to split the next protein, and so on, so each step activates many more molecules. This chain reaction (an amplification cascade) quickly produces lots of germ-fighting proteins. Small fragments like C3a and C5a cause inflammation.

Big idea: complement works as a cascade, a chain reaction that amplifies the response.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a sign of inflammation?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Redness is a cardinal sign of inflammation (the official key marked this by mistake).
Incorrect. Pain is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Incorrect. Heat is a cardinal sign of inflammation.
Correct. Mucus production is not one of the cardinal signs.
Incorrect. Swelling is a cardinal sign of inflammation.

questions.note: The official key marks A (Redness), but redness is a cardinal sign of inflammation; mucus production (D) is the option that is not.
questions.explanation:
The answer is mucus production. The classic signs of inflammation are redness, heat, swelling, and pain (and sometimes loss of function).

These come from widened, leaky blood vessels and chemical signals that sensitize nerves. Mucus production can happen in irritated airways, but it is not one of the cardinal signs of inflammation. (The official key marked redness, which is actually a classic sign.)

Big idea: the four cardinal signs of inflammation are redness, heat, swelling, and pain.

questions.prompt: B Cells and T Cells are created in the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thymus is where T cells mature, not where they are created.
Incorrect. The hypothalamus is part of the brain.
Incorrect. The liver makes blood cells only before birth.
Correct. B and T cells are created in the bone marrow.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the bone marrow. All blood cells, including B cells and T cells, are made from stem cells in the red bone marrow.

B cells also mature in the bone marrow. T cells travel to the thymus to mature, but they are created in the bone marrow.

Big idea: lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow; T cells then mature in the thymus.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of the lymphatic and immune system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Draining excess interstitial fluid is a main lymphatic function (the official key marked this by mistake).

choices.text: Maintaining water homeostasis in the body
choices.explanation: Correct. Water homeostasis is mainly controlled by the kidneys, not the lymphatic system.
Incorrect. Lacteals transport dietary fats.
Incorrect. Carrying out immune responses is a main function.

questions.note: The official key marks A, but draining excess interstitial fluid is a main job of the lymphatic system; "maintaining water homeostasis" (B) is not one of its listed functions.
questions.explanation:
The answer is 'maintaining water homeostasis in the body'. The three main functions of the lymphatic and immune system are: draining excess interstitial fluid (the fluid around cells) and returning it to the blood, transporting dietary fats from the intestine, and carrying out immune responses.

Water balance in the body is mainly the job of the kidneys and hormones. (The official key marked 'draining excess interstitial fluid', but that is actually one of the lymphatic system's main functions.)

Big idea: the lymphatic system returns fluid, carries fats, and defends the body.

questions.prompt: If that pathogen is still not cleared by innate immunity - what is activated? ________ immunity
questions.explanation:
The answer is adaptive immunity. Innate immunity responds first, within minutes to hours. If it cannot clear the germ, the adaptive immune system is activated.

Adaptive immunity uses B cells (antibodies) and T cells that target the specific germ. It takes days to build the first time but creates memory.

Big idea: innate immunity is the first responder; adaptive immunity is the specialized backup.

questions.prompt: The lymph from the right foot empties into the ______ _____ vein
questions.note: The official key says "left axillary"; lymph from the legs travels up the thoracic duct, which empties into the left subclavian vein (where it meets the left internal jugular vein).
questions.explanation:
The answer is the left subclavian vein. Lymph from the right foot travels up the lymph vessels of the leg, through lymph nodes, into the cisterna chyli and up the thoracic duct.

The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, near where it joins the left internal jugular vein. (The official key said 'left axillary', which is not where the thoracic duct empties.)

Big idea: lymph from most of the body, including both legs, returns to the blood through the thoracic duct on the left side.

questions.prompt: ____________cell acts as an intermediary between humoral and cell-mediated immunity
questions.explanation:
The answer is the helper T cell. Helper T cells connect the two arms of adaptive immunity.

They help activate B cells (humoral immunity, antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells (cell-mediated immunity) by releasing cytokines.

Big idea: helper T cells coordinate the adaptive immune response.

questions.prompt: Antivirals work by _______ _______ replication.
questions.explanation:
The answer is inhibiting viral replication. Viruses can only multiply inside our cells by using the cell's machinery.

Antiviral drugs block a step in this process, such as copying the virus's genetic material or assembling new viruses, which slows the infection so the immune system can clear it.

Big idea: antivirals stop viruses from making more copies of themselves.

questions.prompt: Chemical signals prompt neutrophils to flatten out of capillaries is called ______
questions.explanation:
The answer is diapedesis. During inflammation, chemical signals make neutrophils stick to the walls of capillaries and then flatten and squeeze between the cells of the vessel wall into the tissue.

This squeezing out of the blood vessel is called diapedesis.

Big idea: white blood cells leave the blood to reach infected tissue.

questions.prompt: The primary function of _________ immunity is to reject transplanted tissues.
questions.note: The official key says "humoral"; transplant rejection is mainly carried out by T cells (cell-mediated immunity).
questions.explanation:
The answer is cell-mediated immunity. Transplanted organs are rejected mainly by T cells. The recipient's T cells recognize the donor's MHC proteins as foreign and attack the tissue.

That is why transplant patients take drugs that suppress T cells. (The official key said 'humoral'; antibodies can contribute to some rejection, but the main driver is cell-mediated immunity.)

Big idea: T cells reject transplants, so matching donors and suppressing T cells help prevent rejection.

questions.prompt: The function of ________ ________ are to generate memory lymphocytes for long-term immunity
questions.explanation:
The answer is Peyer's patches. Peyer's patches are clusters of lymphoid tissue in the wall of the small intestine (mostly the ileum).

They sample bacteria from the gut and help generate memory lymphocytes, providing long-term immunity against gut germs. (The appendix does this too.)

Big idea: the gut has its own immune tissue (MALT), including Peyer's patches.

questions.prompt: What chemical barrier is found throughout the whole body? _________ ________
questions.explanation:
The answer is antimicrobial peptides. Antimicrobial peptides, such as defensins and cathelicidins, are small proteins made by skin, mucous membranes, and white blood cells throughout the body.

They kill germs by damaging their membranes. They are part of the innate chemical barriers.

Big idea: the body's first line of defense includes chemical barriers like antimicrobial peptides.

questions.prompt: What mechanical barrier is found throughout the whole body? __________ cells joined by tight junctions
questions.explanation:
The answer is epithelial cells. Epithelial cells cover the skin and line the digestive, respiratory, and other tracts.

They are joined by tight junctions, which seal the gaps between cells, forming a wall that germs cannot easily get through.

Big idea: epithelial barriers are the body's first line of defense.

questions.prompt: In the thymus, where is it speculated that T cells die?___________
questions.note: The official key says "trabeculae"; textbooks describe the thymic (Hassall's) corpuscles as the structures once thought to be where T cells are destroyed.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the thymic (Hassall's) corpuscles. These are swirls of flattened cells in the thymus's medulla.

For a long time, scientists thought they were where T cells that failed selection were destroyed. Today they are thought to help regulatory T cells develop. (The official key said 'trabeculae', which are just partitions of connective tissue.)

Big idea: most young T cells die in the thymus because they fail its tests; only useful, safe T cells survive.

questions.prompt: What type of cell acts as an intermediary between humoral and cell-mediated immunity? _______ _____ cell
questions.explanation:
The answer is the helper T cell. Helper T cells are the link between humoral immunity (B cells and antibodies) and cell-mediated immunity (cytotoxic T cells).

They release cytokines that activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells.

Big idea: helper T cells are the coordinators of adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: The cells and signaling molecules that initiate inflammatory responses are mast cells and _________.
questions.explanation:
The answer is histamine. Mast cells release histamine when tissue is injured or when they detect allergens.

Histamine widens blood vessels and makes them leaky, starting the redness, swelling, and heat of inflammation.

Big idea: mast cells and histamine kick off inflammation.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the process by which cells move out of the capillaries and into the tissues?
questions.explanation:
The answer is extravasation. Extravasation is the general term for white blood cells leaving the blood vessels and entering the tissues.

It includes rolling and sticking to the vessel wall (margination) and squeezing through it (diapedesis).

Big idea: white blood cells must leave the blood to fight infections in tissues.

questions.prompt: The function of the _________ is to cleanse interstitial fluid.
questions.note: The official key says "spleen", which cleanses blood; lymph nodes cleanse lymph (interstitial fluid that has entered lymph vessels).
questions.explanation:
The answer is the lymph nodes. Interstitial fluid that leaks out of blood vessels is collected by lymph vessels, where it is called lymph.

Lymph passes through lymph nodes, which filter out germs, debris, and cancer cells before the fluid returns to the blood. (The official key said 'spleen', but the spleen filters blood, not interstitial fluid.)

Big idea: lymph nodes clean lymph; the spleen cleans blood.

questions.prompt: ______________ is the process of capturing and digesting of a foreign particle
questions.explanation:
The answer is phagocytosis. Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is when a cell, like a macrophage or neutrophil, wraps its membrane around a germ or particle, pulls it inside, and digests it with enzymes.

It is a key part of innate immunity.

Big idea: phagocytes capture and destroy germs.

questions.prompt: What is the correct term to describe the migration of white blood cells toward bacteria?
questions.explanation:
The answer is chemotaxis. Chemotaxis is movement toward a chemical signal.

Bacteria and damaged tissue release chemicals, and white blood cells follow the trail to the infection site.

Big idea: chemical signals guide immune cells to where they are needed.

questions.prompt: _____________are mainly used to kill infectious microbes and tumor cells
questions.note: The official key says "platelets", which help blood clot and do not kill microbes or tumor cells. Uncertain: the intended answer is not clear; natural killer cells (and activated macrophages) kill both infected cells and tumor cells.
questions.explanation:
The best answer is natural killer (NK) cells (macrophages are also accepted). NK cells patrol the body and kill virus-infected cells and tumor cells without needing prior training. Activated macrophages also kill microbes and tumor cells.

The official key said 'platelets', but platelets help blood clot; they do not kill microbes or tumor cells. Because the intended answer is not completely clear, this question is marked uncertain.

Big idea: the innate immune system includes cells that kill infected and cancerous cells.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the process where phagocytes migrate to the site of inflammation?
questions.explanation:
The answer is chemotaxis. Phagocytes like neutrophils and macrophages move toward the site of inflammation by following chemical signals released by germs and damaged cells.

This directed movement is called chemotaxis.

Big idea: chemotaxis brings phagocytes to infections.

questions.prompt: Lysozyme: name two cells it is secreted from in the soluble innate immune system. ____________ and ________ cells
questions.explanation:
The answers are phagocytes and Paneth cells. Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls.

It is released by phagocytes (like neutrophils and macrophages) and by Paneth cells at the base of the intestinal crypts. It is also found in tears and saliva.

Big idea: lysozyme is a soluble innate defense found in many places.

questions.prompt: _________ is a disease where the immune system attacks histone proteins
questions.explanation:
The answer is lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus). In lupus, the immune system makes antibodies against the contents of the cell nucleus, including DNA and histone proteins (which DNA wraps around).

These antibodies form clumps that damage many organs, such as the skin, joints, and kidneys. Anti-histone antibodies are especially linked to drug-induced lupus.

Big idea: lupus is an autoimmune disease that targets the cell nucleus.

questions.prompt: Collectins, ficolins and pentraxins: what type of receptors do they have? _________ _________ _________
questions.explanation:
The answer is pattern recognition receptors. Collectins, ficolins, and pentraxins are proteins that recognize common patterns found on germs, such as certain sugars on their surfaces.

Because they recognize general patterns rather than specific antigens, they are pattern recognition molecules of the innate immune system. They can coat germs and activate complement.

Big idea: innate immunity recognizes general 'danger patterns' on germs.

questions.prompt: Name two things phagocytes release. _________ and _________ (ENTER ALPHABETICALLY)
questions.explanation:
The answers are chemokines and cytokines. Phagocytes like macrophages release cytokines, chemical messengers that boost inflammation and activate other immune cells.

They also release chemokines, a type of cytokine that attracts more white blood cells to the area.

Big idea: phagocytes not only eat germs but also call in reinforcements.

questions.prompt: ______is a mechanism by which microorganisms can be contained, killed and processed for antigen presentation and represents a vital facet of the innate immune response to pathogens, and plays an essential role in initiating the adaptive immune response.
questions.explanation:
The answer is phagocytosis. Phagocytes swallow germs, contain them in a bubble inside the cell, and kill them with enzymes and toxic chemicals.

Some phagocytes, like macrophages and dendritic cells, then display pieces of the germ to T cells (antigen presentation), which helps start the adaptive immune response.

Big idea: phagocytosis is both an innate defense and a bridge to adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: Which part of the immune system is germline encoded (can’t be changed)?
questions.note: The official key says "GL encoded", which only restates the question; the innate immune system uses germline-encoded receptors.
questions.explanation:
The answer is innate immunity. 'Germline encoded' means the receptors are built from genes inherited exactly as they are, and they do not change during a person's life.

Innate immunity's receptors, such as Toll-like receptors, are germline encoded and recognize general germ patterns. In contrast, B and T cells rearrange their genes to build a huge variety of unique receptors. (The official key just said 'GL encoded', which repeats the question.)

Big idea: innate receptors are fixed; adaptive receptors are custom-built.

questions.prompt: The main role of _______ _______ cells is to lyse viral infected cells.
questions.explanation:
The answer is natural killer (NK) cells. NK cells are innate lymphocytes that destroy virus-infected cells and some cancer cells.

They release perforin and granzymes, causing the target cell to burst (lyse) or self-destruct.

Big idea: NK cells are fast-acting killers in the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: The process of ________ ________ ensures that B and T cells do not attack the body itself.
questions.explanation:
The answer is negative selection. While B cells mature in the bone marrow and T cells mature in the thymus, any that react strongly against the body's own molecules are destroyed.

This keeps immune cells from attacking the body itself. When it fails, autoimmune disease can result.

Big idea: negative selection creates self-tolerance.

questions.prompt: The ______mainly acts as a filter for purifying the blood, removing microbes and worn out or damaged red blood cells.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the spleen. The spleen filters blood. Its red pulp removes old and damaged red blood cells, and its white pulp contains lymphocytes that respond to germs in the blood.

Big idea: the spleen is the blood's filter.

questions.prompt: Pieces of an antigen that trigger an immune response are known as ____________
questions.explanation:
The answer is epitopes. An epitope is the specific small part of an antigen that an antibody or T cell receptor recognizes.

A single antigen, like a viral protein, can have many epitopes.

Big idea: the immune system recognizes small, specific parts of antigens.

questions.prompt: ______ immunity is activated immediately upon infection.
questions.explanation:
The answer is innate immunity. Innate defenses are always ready and act immediately: barriers, phagocytes, inflammation, complement, and NK cells.

Adaptive immunity takes days to build the first time.

Big idea: innate immunity is the first, immediate response.

questions.prompt: Plasma cells produce _________
questions.explanation:
The answer is antibodies. Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and turned into antibody factories.

Each plasma cell releases thousands of antibodies per second, all targeting the same antigen.

Big idea: plasma cells produce antibodies for humoral immunity.

questions.prompt: Name one role of neutrophils and two things that they produce?
questions.answer: - phagocytosis -(ROS) Reactive oxygen species , antimicrobial peptides
questions.explanation:
One main role of neutrophils is phagocytosis: they eat and destroy bacteria and fungi.

Two things they produce are reactive oxygen species (ROS), toxic chemicals like hydrogen peroxide that kill germs they have swallowed, and antimicrobial peptides, such as defensins. Neutrophils can also release nets of DNA (NETs) that trap germs.

Big idea: neutrophils are front-line killers of the innate immune system.

questions.prompt: How does the innate immune system recognize antigens?
questions.answer: innate recognizes antigens (PAMPs) by PRRs(Pattern Recognition Receptors)
questions.explanation:
The innate immune system recognizes germs using pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), such as Toll-like receptors.

PRRs detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), features common to many germs but not found on human cells, like bacterial cell-wall molecules or viral RNA. This lets innate cells react quickly to many kinds of germs.

Big idea: innate immunity recognizes general 'germ patterns', not specific antigens.

questions.prompt: Complement immune components: how do they circulate in the blood? Why is this?
questions.answer: circulate in the pro-form (inactive) as they are a powerful inducer of inflammation
questions.explanation:
Complement proteins circulate in the blood in an inactive form (a 'pro-form').

They stay inactive because, once switched on, they are very powerful: they punch holes in cells and cause strong inflammation. If they were always active, they would damage the body's own tissues. They are only activated on the surface of germs or by antibodies.

Big idea: powerful defense proteins are kept 'switched off' until needed.

questions.prompt: Where are antimicrobial peptides found? What do they do?
questions.answer: antimicrobial peptides found all over body - disrupt microbial membranes
questions.explanation:
Antimicrobial peptides are found all over the body: on the skin, in mucous membranes of the airways and gut, in saliva and tears, and inside white blood cells.

They kill germs mainly by poking holes in or disrupting the germs' outer membranes.

Big idea: antimicrobial peptides are a widespread chemical barrier of innate immunity.

questions.prompt: Innate immunity: what does it recognize? What does it interact with?
questions.answer: recognizes broad class of pathogens and interacts with molecular structures
questions.explanation:
Innate immunity recognizes broad classes of germs rather than one specific germ.

It interacts with common molecular structures on germs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns, like bacterial cell-wall pieces), using pattern recognition receptors.

Big idea: innate immunity is general; adaptive immunity is specific.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure 1.
questions.explanation:
Label 1 is the adenoids and tonsils, the lymphatic tissue at the back of the nose and throat.

They trap germs entering through the mouth and nose.

Big idea: tonsils guard the entrance to the body.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure 2.
questions.explanation:
Label 2 is Peyer's patches, lymphoid tissue in the wall of the small intestine.

They watch for germs in the gut and start immune responses.

Big idea: Peyer's patches are part of the gut's immune tissue.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure 3.
questions.explanation:
Label 3 is the appendix, the small tube attached to the start of the large intestine.

It contains lymphatic tissue that helps the immune system sample gut bacteria.

Big idea: the appendix is part of the lymphatic system.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure 4.
questions.explanation:
Label 4 is the thymus, in the upper chest behind the breastbone.

The thymus is where T cells mature.

Big idea: T cells are trained in the thymus.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure 5.
questions.explanation:
Label 5 is the lymph nodes, the clusters shown along the body (here in the armpit area).

Lymph nodes filter lymph and are where B and T cells meet germs.

Big idea: lymph nodes are checkpoints of the lymphatic system.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not one of the body’s innate barriers?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mucous membranes are an innate barrier.
Incorrect. Vibrissae (nose hairs) are an innate barrier.
Incorrect. Helpful bacteria act as a barrier by competing with harmful germs.
Correct. Lymphocytes are adaptive immune cells, not a barrier.
Incorrect. Sweat is a chemical barrier.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lymphocytes. Innate barriers are the first line of defense that physically or chemically block germs: mucous membranes, nose hairs (vibrissae), helpful bacteria that crowd out harmful ones, and sweat.

Lymphocytes (B and T cells) are part of the adaptive immune system, not barriers.

Big idea: barriers keep germs out; lymphocytes fight them specifically once inside.

questions.prompt: Correctly identify the locations that each of the following are produced, respectively: B cells, phagocytes, T cells

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Phagocytes are made in the bone marrow, not the thymus.
Correct. B cells and phagocytes: bone marrow; T cells: thymus.
Incorrect. B cells mature in the bone marrow.
Incorrect. The adenoids and lymph nodes do not produce these cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bone marrow, bone marrow, thymus. B cells are made and mature in the bone marrow. Phagocytes (like neutrophils and monocytes) are also made in the bone marrow.

T cells are made in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus, which is the location this key means for T cells.

Big idea: bone marrow makes immune cells; T cells finish in the thymus.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of dendritic cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Presenting antigens is the main job of dendritic cells.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells release signals that help start inflammation.
Incorrect. Dendritic cells can interact with nerves in tissues.
Correct (per the key). Fever is mainly triggered by pyrogens from other white blood cells.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is initiating fever. Dendritic cells catch germs and present antigens to lymphocytes, which starts adaptive immunity. They also release signals that start inflammation and can communicate with nerves in tissues.

Fever is mainly triggered by pyrogens acting on the hypothalamus, which are usually credited to macrophages and other white blood cells, so it is not listed as a dendritic cell function here.

Big idea: dendritic cells are messengers between innate and adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: Which is not secreted during the inflammatory response?

choices.explanation: Correct (per the key). Pyrogens cause fever; the key treats them as not part of the local inflammatory response.
Incorrect. Histamine is released by mast cells during inflammation.
Incorrect. Heparin is released by mast cells.
Incorrect. Cytokines are released during inflammation.

questions.note: Uncertain: pyrogens (such as IL-1 and TNF from macrophages) are released during inflammation and cause fever, so every listed substance can be secreted; the official key marks pyrogens.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is pyrogens, but this question is uncertain. During inflammation, mast cells release histamine and heparin, and many cells release cytokines.

Pyrogens (like interleukin-1) are also released, mainly by macrophages, and they cause fever. So all four are released during an inflammatory response; the key may treat fever as separate from local inflammation.

Big idea: inflammation and fever are driven by chemical signals from immune cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would contain a class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC)?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Helper T cells look at MHC II on other cells; they do not carry it.
Correct. Macrophages are antigen-presenting cells with MHC II.
Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells do not carry MHC II.
Incorrect. NK cells do not carry MHC II.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the macrophage. MHC class II molecules are found only on antigen-presenting cells: macrophages, dendritic cells, and B cells.

They display pieces of germs to helper T cells. Helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells do not normally have MHC class II.

Big idea: MHC II is on antigen-presenting cells; MHC I is on almost all cells.

questions.prompt: Name the class of immunoglobulin that best matches the description: The most common immunoglobulin, this class provides immunity to developing fetuses.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgG. IgG is the most common antibody in the blood.

It is the only antibody that crosses the placenta, giving the developing baby protection.

Big idea: IgG = most common, crosses the placenta.

questions.prompt: Name the class of immunoglobulin that best matches the description: This class of immunoglobulin can be found in secretions such as saliva and tears.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgA. IgA is found in body secretions such as saliva, tears, mucus, and breast milk.

It protects mucous membranes.

Big idea: IgA guards body surfaces.

questions.prompt: Name the class of immunoglobulin that best matches the description: The first immunoglobulin a new bacteria will encounter, this class causes the agglutination of microorganisms
