questions.explanation:
The answer is IgM. IgM is the first antibody made when the body meets a new germ.

Its five-unit shape makes it great at clumping germs together (agglutination) and activating complement.

Big idea: IgM = first responder antibody.

questions.prompt: Name the class of immunoglobulin that best matches the description: This immunoglobulin is most effective against parasites, but is also often the cause of allergic reactions.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgE. IgE helps fight parasites and is also responsible for allergic reactions.

It sits on mast cells and basophils and triggers histamine release.

Big idea: IgE = parasites and allergies.

questions.prompt: Name the class of immunoglobulin that best matches the description: This immunoglobulin class is found on the surface of B cells.
questions.explanation:
The answer is IgD. IgD is found mainly on the surface of B cells.

It acts as an antigen receptor that helps activate B cells.

Big idea: IgD = B cell receptor.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not a function of the spleen?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Filtering blood is the spleen's main job.
Incorrect. The spleen stores a supply of platelets.
Correct (per the key). B cells develop in the bone marrow.
Also not a spleen function (the spleen filters blood, not lymph), but the key does not mark it.

questions.note: Uncertain: the spleen filters blood, not lymph, so D is also "not a function of the spleen"; the official key marks only C.
questions.explanation:
The official answer is 'develops B cells'. B cells develop in the bone marrow. The spleen is where mature B cells gather and respond to germs in the blood, but it is not where they develop.

However, choice D is also not a spleen function: the spleen filters blood, not lymph (lymph nodes filter lymph). So this question really has two correct answers. The spleen does filter blood and store platelets.

Big idea: the spleen filters blood; lymph nodes filter lymph.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be present at birth?

choices.explanation: Correct. NK cells are innate and present at birth.
Incorrect. Memory cells form after exposure to germs.
Incorrect. Babies' own humoral immunity develops after birth.
Incorrect. Plasma cells form after B cells are activated by germs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is natural killer cells. NK cells are part of the innate immune system, which is ready from birth.

Memory cells, plasma cells, and humoral (antibody) immunity come from the adaptive immune system after meeting germs. (Newborns do have some antibodies from their mother, but they did not make them.)

Big idea: innate defenses are present at birth; adaptive defenses develop with exposure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following disorders is not the result of the immune system targeting friendly cells?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. MS is autoimmune (attacks myelin).
Incorrect. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune (attacks insulin-making cells).
Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune (attacks joints).
Correct. Ataxia telangiectasia is a genetic immunodeficiency, not autoimmune.

questions.explanation:
The answer is ataxia telangiectasia. It is a genetic disease that weakens the immune system (an immunodeficiency) and affects coordination; it is not caused by the immune system attacking the body.

Multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and rheumatoid arthritis are autoimmune diseases, where the immune system attacks the body's own (friendly) cells.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases attack self; immunodeficiencies weaken defense.

questions.prompt: A mother’s antibodies being transferred to a child through breast milk is an example of:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Active immunity means making your own antibodies.
Incorrect. Artificial active immunity comes from vaccines.
Correct. Antibodies in breast milk are natural passive immunity.
Incorrect. Artificial passive immunity comes from antibody injections.

questions.explanation:
The answer is naturally acquired passive immunity. The baby receives ready-made antibodies (passive) through normal breastfeeding (natural).

Big idea: passive = antibodies from someone else; natural = not from a medical treatment.

questions.prompt: Which is not true about primary and secondary immune responses?

choices.text: Primary responses take longer to resolve than secondary responses
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). Primary responses take longer.

choices.text: IgM is more abundant in the secondary response than the primary response
choices.explanation: Correct (this is false). IgM is more abundant in the primary response.

choices.text: Memory cells are only active in the secondary response
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is treated as true). Memory cells are what make the secondary response.

choices.text: The primary response is weaker than the secondary response
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this is true). The primary response is weaker.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B. IgM is more abundant in the PRIMARY response, not the secondary. The secondary response makes mostly IgG.

The other statements are true: primary responses are slower, memory cells drive the secondary response, and the primary response is weaker.

Big idea: primary = slow, weaker, mostly IgM; secondary = fast, stronger, mostly IgG.

questions.prompt: The body's reaction after a transfusion of an incompatible blood type is an example of what kind of hypersensitivity?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Type I is IgE-mediated allergy.
Correct. Transfusion reactions are type II.
Incorrect. Type III involves immune complexes.
Incorrect. Type IV is T-cell-mediated.

questions.explanation:
The answer is type II. In a mismatched blood transfusion, the patient's antibodies bind to the donor's red blood cells and destroy them.

Antibodies attacking cells is type II hypersensitivity.

Big idea: type II = antibodies against cells.

questions.prompt: A type I hypersensitivity reaction includes an exaggerated response from which antibody?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA protects mucous membranes.
Incorrect. IgD sits on B cells.
Correct. IgE causes type I reactions.
Incorrect. IgG is involved in types II and III.

questions.explanation:
The answer is IgE. Type I hypersensitivity (allergy) is caused by IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils, which release histamine when they meet the allergen.

Big idea: type I = IgE.

questions.prompt: An adult without a thymus would:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Losing the thymus does have some effect.
Incorrect. Adults still have existing T cells.

choices.text: Be at risk to new antigens
choices.explanation: Correct. Fewer new T cells means more risk from new antigens.

choices.text: Be completely unable to defend against any infection
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Existing immune cells still provide defense.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that they would be at risk to new antigens. In adults, many mature T cells already exist and live a long time, so removing the thymus does not wipe out T cells.

But without a thymus, few new T cells are made, so the person may have trouble responding to brand-new germs.

Big idea: the thymus mainly supplies new T cells.

questions.prompt: As a person ages, their immune system becomes less effective. Which of the following is a cause of age-related immune system decay?

choices.explanation: Correct. The thymus shrinks with age, reducing new T cells.
Incorrect. The spleen does not die with age.
Incorrect. Mental capacity does not control immunity.
Incorrect. Vaccine antigens do not build up and harm immunity.

questions.explanation:
The answer is atrophy of the thymus. As people age, the thymus shrinks and makes fewer new T cells.

This is one reason older people respond less well to new infections and vaccines. The spleen does not die with age, and vaccines do not cause immune decay.

Big idea: thymus shrinkage contributes to immune aging.

questions.prompt: What best describes the purpose of Toll-like receptors?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Specific antigens are recognized by B and T cell receptors.

choices.text: Shuttle proteins in and out of cell membranes
choices.explanation: Incorrect. TLRs are sensors, not transporters.
Correct. TLRs recognize general patterns on pathogens.

choices.text: Block access to a cell’s MHC
choices.explanation: Incorrect. TLRs do not block MHC.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to recognize general patterns of pathogens. Toll-like receptors are innate immune sensors that detect features common to many germs, such as bacterial cell-wall molecules or viral RNA.

They do not recognize specific antigens; that is the job of B and T cell receptors.

Big idea: TLRs spot general 'germ patterns'.

questions.prompt: Humoral or antibody-mediated immune response would be more effective than a cell-mediated response in which situation?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Viruses inside cells are targeted by cytotoxic T cells.
Incorrect. Fungal infections rely heavily on T cells and phagocytes.
Incorrect. Cancer cells are mainly attacked by T cells and NK cells.
Correct. Antibodies can neutralize viruses outside cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is an extracellular viral infection. Antibodies (humoral immunity) work in body fluids, outside cells.

They can neutralize viruses floating between cells before they infect new ones. Viruses hiding inside cells, fungal infections, and cancer are better handled by T cells (cell-mediated immunity).

Big idea: antibodies work outside cells; T cells work on infected cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes B cell sensitization?

choices.text: When a helper T cell sensitive to the same antigen attaches to the B cell’s MHC complex
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Help from a helper T cell comes after sensitization.

choices.text: When an antibody brings an antigen into the B cell to be displayed on the surface
choices.explanation: Correct. The B cell's surface antibody brings the antigen in to be displayed.

choices.text: When the B cell differentiates into plasma cells to produce antibodies
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Becoming plasma cells comes later.

choices.text: When the B cell differentiates into memory cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Becoming memory cells comes later.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is B. A B cell has antibodies (B cell receptors) on its surface. When one binds its antigen, the B cell pulls the antigen inside, breaks it up, and displays pieces on its surface. This first step is called sensitization.

Then a helper T cell that recognizes the same antigen activates the B cell, and later the B cell becomes plasma cells and memory cells.

Big idea: B cell activation starts when its receptor binds its specific antigen.

questions.prompt: The _____ segment of an antibody determines its class, while the _____ segment determines which antigen it is sensitive to.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the regions.
Correct. Constant determines class; variable determines the antigen.
Incorrect. The heavy chain's constant region sets the class, but the variable regions of both chains bind antigen.
Incorrect. The light chain does not determine class.

questions.explanation:
The answer is constant, variable. An antibody's constant region (the stem of the Y) is the same within each class and determines whether it is IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, or IgE.

The variable region (the tips of the Y) differs between antibodies and determines which antigen it binds.

Big idea: constant region = class; variable region = target.

questions.prompt: The spleen and the lymph nodes are two examples of lymphatic organs. Compare and contrast the two, including at least two similarities and two differences.
questions.answer: (2pts for similarities, 1 each) Removes abnormal cells, triggers immune response, contain lymphocytes, activates B and T cells, both connected to lymphatic vessels, etc (2 pts for differences, 1 each) One spleen vs lots of lymph nodes, spleen filters blood instead of lymph, spleen recycles blood cells, spleen split up into red and white pulp, etc
questions.explanation:
Similarities: both the spleen and lymph nodes contain lymphocytes, remove abnormal cells and germs, trigger immune responses by activating B and T cells, and are connected to the lymphatic system.

Differences: there is one spleen but hundreds of lymph nodes; the spleen filters blood while lymph nodes filter lymph; the spleen recycles old red blood cells; and the spleen is divided into red pulp and white pulp.

Big idea: both are secondary lymphatic organs, but they filter different fluids.

questions.prompt: HIV/AIDS is an immunodeficiency disease that targets the helper T cells of the immune system, while leaving regulatory T cells unaffected. What are the functions of helper and regulatory T cells, and how does this imbalance cause the symptoms of AIDS?
questions.answer: (1 pt for function of helper T cells) Coordinate and stimulate cell and antibody-mediated immune response (1 pt for function of regulatory T cells) Suppress/regulate the immune response (1 pt for how this causes symptoms) The death of helper T cells hinders the coordination of the immune response and leads to an overabundance of suppressing factors by the regulatory T cells, resulting in a weak or non present immune response
questions.explanation:
Helper T cells coordinate and stimulate both the antibody (humoral) response and the cell-mediated response. Regulatory T cells suppress and calm the immune response to prevent overreactions.

In HIV/AIDS, helper T cells die but regulatory T cells remain. With few helpers and many suppressors, the immune response becomes weak or almost absent, so the person cannot fight off infections and certain cancers.

Big idea: a healthy immune system balances activation and suppression.

questions.prompt: T-cells mature into several distinct types of T-cells in:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lymph nodes are where mature T cells meet germs.
Incorrect. The spleen holds mature lymphocytes.
Correct. T cells mature in the thymus.
Incorrect. The tonsils trap germs in the throat.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the thymus. T cells are made in the bone marrow, then travel to the thymus to mature, which is where the 'T' comes from.

In the thymus, they become helper T cells or cytotoxic T cells and learn not to attack the body. Lymph nodes, spleen, and tonsils are where mature T cells meet germs.

Big idea: T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a function of Lymphatic system:

choices.text: picks up and returns interstitial fluid to blood
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Returning tissue fluid to the blood is a main function.
Incorrect. Lacteals carry fats from the digestive system.
Incorrect. Lymph nodes defend against germs.

choices.text: promotes the accumulation of tissue fluid
choices.explanation: Correct. The lymphatic system prevents fluid buildup.

questions.edited: Option D changed from "maintains fluid homeostasis in the body" (a real lymphatic function) to "promotes the accumulation of tissue fluid".
questions.explanation:
The answer is D. The lymphatic system prevents fluid from building up in tissues by collecting extra fluid and returning it to the blood.

If it promoted fluid buildup, it would cause swelling (edema). The other choices are real functions: returning fluid, carrying fats from the gut through lacteals, and defending against germs.

Big idea: the lymphatic system drains fluid, carries fats, and fights infection.

questions.prompt: What cell acts as a messenger between innate and adaptive immune system

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine during inflammation.
Incorrect. Neutrophils eat germs but do not present antigens to T cells well.
Incorrect. NK cells kill infected cells directly.
Correct. Dendritic cells present antigens to T cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is dendritic cells. Dendritic cells are part of the innate system: they capture germs in tissues.

They then travel to lymph nodes and show pieces of the germ to T cells, starting the adaptive response. Mast cells, neutrophils, and NK cells mostly act in the innate system.

Big idea: dendritic cells connect innate and adaptive immunity.

questions.prompt: Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. MHC is not a disease.

choices.text: Way to differentiate self and foreign cells.
choices.explanation: Correct. MHC helps the immune system tell self from foreign.
Incorrect. MHC is not a blood disorder.
Incorrect. Antibody classes (IgG, IgA, etc.) are different.

questions.explanation:
The answer is a way to tell self from foreign cells. MHC molecules are proteins on the surface of cells that display small pieces of protein.

T cells check these displays. If they see normal self pieces, they leave the cell alone; if they see foreign pieces, they attack. That is also why organ donors must be matched.

Big idea: MHC is the cell's ID badge.

questions.prompt: Chemokines help immune system by:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chemokines are signals, not searchers.
Correct. Chemokines guide immune cells to where they are needed.
Incorrect. Pyrogens raise body temperature.
Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine.

questions.explanation:
The answer is guiding the movement of cells. Chemokines are chemical signals released at sites of infection.

White blood cells follow chemokine trails to find the infection (this movement is called chemotaxis). Fever comes from pyrogens, and histamine comes from mast cells.

Big idea: chemokines are chemical 'come here' signals.

questions.prompt: Cytotoxic T-cells:

choices.text: Destroy non-self-cells by causing them to lyse
choices.explanation: Correct. Cytotoxic T cells kill target cells.
Incorrect. Helper T cells stimulate B cells.
Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine.
Incorrect. 'Toxic' refers to killing cells, not poisoning the body.

questions.explanation:
The answer is A. Cytotoxic (killer) T cells find infected cells, cancer cells, or foreign cells.

They release proteins like perforin that punch holes in the cell and make it burst (lyse) or self-destruct. Helper T cells stimulate B cells, mast cells release histamine, and 'poisoning' is not a function.

Big idea: cytotoxic T cells kill damaged or foreign cells directly.

questions.prompt: The accumulation and adhesion of leukocytes to the blood vessel walls is called:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vasodilation is widening of blood vessels.
Correct. Pavementing is white blood cells sticking to the vessel walls.
Incorrect. Coagulation is blood clotting.
Incorrect. Fibrinolysis is breaking down clots.

questions.explanation:
The answer is pavementing (also called margination). During inflammation, white blood cells move to the edges of blood vessels and stick to the walls, like paving stones.

This lets them squeeze out into the infected tissue. Vasodilation is widening vessels, coagulation is clotting, and fibrinolysis is breaking down clots.

Big idea: white blood cells stick to vessel walls before leaving the blood.

questions.prompt: The Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgD (and IgM) are found on B cell surfaces.
Correct. IgA is found in mucus and other secretions.
Incorrect. IgM is the first antibody made by the fetus.
Incorrect. IgE is involved in allergic reactions.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that IgA is frequently found in mucus. IgA is the antibody in body secretions, including mucus, saliva, tears, and breast milk.

It guards the surfaces where germs try to enter. IgD is on cell surfaces, IgM is the first antibody the fetus makes, and IgE causes allergic reactions.

Big idea: IgA protects mucous membranes.

questions.prompt: Graves’ disease is due to:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Too much insulin causes low blood sugar.
Correct. Graves' disease causes too much thyroxine.
Incorrect. Too little insulin causes diabetes.
Incorrect. Too little thyroxine is hypothyroidism (for example, Hashimoto's disease).

questions.explanation:
The answer is overproduction of thyroxine. Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease: the body makes antibodies that switch on the thyroid gland.

The thyroid then makes too much thyroid hormone (thyroxine), causing a fast heartbeat, weight loss, and bulging eyes. Insulin problems cause diabetes, and too little thyroxine is hypothyroidism.

Big idea: in Graves' disease, autoimmune antibodies overstimulate the thyroid.

questions.prompt: The complement system consists of a number of proteins that are synthesized in:

choices.explanation: Correct. The liver makes most complement proteins.
Incorrect. The spleen filters blood but is not the main source.
Incorrect. Bone marrow makes blood cells, not complement.
Incorrect. The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and hormones.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the liver. Most complement proteins are made by the liver and released into the blood.

Complement proteins help kill germs by punching holes in them, marking them to be eaten, and calling in white blood cells.

Big idea: the liver makes many blood proteins, including complement.

questions.prompt: Name the 5 classes of immunoglobulin. State the most abundant type.
questions.answer: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE; IgG is the most abundant.
questions.explanation:
The five classes are IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE. IgG is the most abundant antibody in the blood. It gives long-term protection and crosses the placenta.

IgA protects mucous membranes, IgM is made first in an infection, IgD is on B cells, and IgE causes allergies.

Big idea: GAMED, the five antibody classes.

questions.prompt: Name two symptoms of the autoimmune disease lupus.
questions.answer: Any two: butterfly (malar) rash, joint pain/swelling, fatigue, fever, photosensitivity, kidney problems, mouth ulcers.
questions.explanation:
Any two of these: a butterfly-shaped rash on the face, joint pain or swelling, tiredness, fever, sensitivity to sunlight, kidney problems, or mouth sores.

Lupus is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, so it can affect many organs.

Big idea: in autoimmune diseases, the immune system attacks self.

questions.prompt: As part of the immune system, white blood cells fight germs. Another name for white blood cells is:
questions.explanation:
The answer is leukocytes. 'Leuko' means white and 'cyte' means cell.

Leukocytes include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

Big idea: leukocytes are the immune system's cells.

questions.prompt: Leukocytes are found in lots of places, including an organ in your belly that filters blood and helps fight infections known as the:
questions.explanation:
The answer is the spleen. It sits in the upper left part of the belly, filters blood, removes old red blood cells, and holds white blood cells that fight germs in the blood.

Big idea: the spleen is the lymphatic organ that filters blood.

questions.prompt: The four main types of germs are:
questions.explanation:
The four main types are bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa (single-celled parasites).

Bacteria are tiny living cells. Viruses are not alive on their own and need cells to copy themselves. Fungi include yeasts and molds, and protozoa include the parasite that causes malaria.

Big idea: different kinds of germs need different defenses.

questions.prompt: Lymph nodes are found in the:
questions.answer: Lymphatic system: clustered along lymphatic vessels, especially in the neck, armpits (axillae), groin, chest and abdomen.
questions.explanation:
Lymph nodes are part of the lymphatic system. They sit along lymph vessels, clustered in the neck, armpits, groin, chest, and belly.

They filter lymph and trap germs, which is why they swell when you are sick.

Big idea: lymph nodes are checkpoints where immune cells meet germs.

questions.prompt: When someone’s immune system overreacts to something harmless it’s called:
questions.explanation:
The answer is an allergy (a hypersensitivity reaction). The immune system treats something harmless, like pollen or peanuts, as dangerous.

It makes IgE antibodies, which trigger histamine release and cause sneezing, itching, or swelling.

Big idea: allergies are immune overreactions.

questions.prompt: Cells that ingest pathogens are _______
questions.explanation:
The answer is phagocytes. 'Phago' means eat and 'cyte' means cell.

Phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages swallow germs and digest them.

Big idea: phagocytosis is 'cell eating'.

questions.prompt: The ______________ system returns interstitial fluid to the bloodstream.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the lymphatic system. Fluid leaks out of capillaries into the spaces between cells (interstitial fluid).

Lymph vessels collect this extra fluid and return it to the blood near the heart. Otherwise tissues would swell.

Big idea: the lymphatic system is the body's drainage system.

questions.prompt: What do B cells produce?
questions.explanation:
B cells produce antibodies (immunoglobulins). When activated, a B cell becomes a plasma cell that releases lots of antibodies.

Antibodies stick to specific germs and mark them for destruction.

Big idea: B cells make antibodies.

questions.prompt: This is a series of enzymatic proteins found in normal blood that will seek out and destroy many types of bacteria and other foreign cells.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the complement system. It is a group of about 30 proteins in the blood that switch each other on in a chain reaction.

They can punch holes in bacteria, coat germs so phagocytes eat them, and call in white blood cells.

Big idea: complement 'complements' (helps) antibodies and phagocytes.

questions.prompt: A substance made from weakened pathogens that triggers an immune response is a ____.
questions.explanation:
The answer is a vaccine. A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs, or pieces of them, that cannot make you sick.

The immune system still learns to recognize them and makes memory cells, so it can fight the real germ quickly.

Big idea: vaccines train the immune system safely.

questions.prompt: State 3 components of the immune system's first line of defense.
questions.answer: Any three: skin, mucous membranes (mucus), cilia, stomach acid, tears/saliva (lysozyme), nasal hairs, normal flora.
questions.explanation:
Any three of these: skin, mucous membranes and mucus, cilia, stomach acid, tears and saliva (which contain the enzyme lysozyme), nose hairs, or helpful normal bacteria.

The first line of defense blocks germs from entering the body at all.

Big idea: barriers are the first line of defense.

questions.prompt: State 4 parts of the inflammatory response.
questions.answer: Redness, heat, swelling, pain (also loss of function)
questions.explanation:
The four classic signs are redness, heat, swelling, and pain (loss of function is sometimes added as a fifth).

Blood vessels widen, bringing more blood (redness and heat). They also leak fluid (swelling), and the swelling and chemicals press on nerves (pain). This brings white blood cells to the injury.

Big idea: inflammation brings immune help to an injured area.

questions.prompt: ______ T cells stimulate proliferation of B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
questions.explanation:
The answer is helper T cells. Helper T cells release cytokines that tell B cells and cytotoxic T cells to multiply and attack.

Big idea: helper T cells coordinate the adaptive immune response.

questions.prompt: An allergic reaction is which type of hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation:
The answer is type I (immediate) hypersensitivity. An allergen binds IgE antibodies on mast cells.

The mast cells quickly release histamine, causing allergy symptoms within minutes.

Big idea: type I = IgE = allergies.

questions.prompt: Which of the following diseases occurs as a result of overproduction of thyroxine?
questions.note: The original test provides no answer choices for this question. The original test gives no answer choices; this is the expected disease.
questions.explanation:
The answer is Graves' disease. It is an autoimmune disease where antibodies switch on the thyroid gland, making it produce too much thyroxine (hyperthyroidism).

Symptoms include a fast heart rate, weight loss, nervousness, and bulging eyes.

Big idea: some autoimmune diseases overstimulate an organ instead of destroying it.

questions.prompt: Which of the following immune cells secrete chemicals such as histamine?
questions.note: The original test provides no answer choices for this question. The original test gives no answer choices.
questions.explanation:
The answer is mast cells (and basophils, their relatives in the blood). They store histamine in granules and release it during allergies and inflammation.

Histamine widens blood vessels and makes them leaky, causing redness, swelling, and itching.

Big idea: mast cells release histamine.

questions.prompt: The Palatine Tonsil is located behind the nose.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The palatine tonsils are at the back of the throat, on both sides of the oropharynx, where you can see them when you open your mouth wide.

The tonsils behind the nose are the pharyngeal tonsils, also called the adenoids.

Big idea: tonsils form a ring of lymphatic tissue guarding the throat.

questions.prompt: Monoclonal is multiple clones of cells.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. 'Mono' means one, so monoclonal means coming from a single clone: many identical cells copied from one original cell.

Monoclonal antibodies are all identical and target exactly one antigen. 'Polyclonal' means from many different clones.

Big idea: monoclonal = one clone; polyclonal = many clones.

questions.prompt: Scleroderma is a type of autoimmune disorder for the Endocrine System.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Scleroderma is an autoimmune disease of connective tissue: it causes the skin (and sometimes organs like the lungs and digestive tract) to become hard and thick.

It is not an endocrine (hormone) disease.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases are classified by which tissues they attack.

questions.prompt: Myasthenia gravis affects the red blood cells.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies block the receptors where nerves signal muscles (the neuromuscular junction).

This causes muscle weakness, like drooping eyelids and trouble chewing or swallowing. It does not affect red blood cells.

Big idea: autoimmune diseases can target nerve-muscle connections.

questions.prompt: Immnoglobin D is only found on the surface of T cells.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. IgD is found mainly on the surface of B cells, not T cells.

There it acts as a receptor that helps activate the B cell. T cells use T-cell receptors, not antibodies.

Big idea: antibodies are made by B cells and found on B cells.

questions.prompt: Phagocytosis is the process of destroying pathogens by creating antibodies.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Phagocytosis is 'cell eating': a phagocyte, like a macrophage or neutrophil, wraps around a germ, swallows it, and digests it.

Making antibodies is the job of B cells (plasma cells), not phagocytosis.

Big idea: phagocytes eat germs; B cells make antibodies.

questions.prompt: All of the following are symptoms of anaphylaxis except:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Low blood pressure is a dangerous sign of anaphylaxis.
Correct. Fever is not a typical sign of anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Swelling (angioedema) is common in anaphylaxis.
Incorrect. Itching and hives are common.
Incorrect. Blurred vision can happen in anaphylaxis.

questions.explanation:
The answer is fever. Anaphylaxis is a severe, fast allergic reaction. Huge amounts of histamine cause blood vessels to widen and leak.

That leads to low blood pressure (hypotension), swelling of the face and throat (angioedema), itching and hives, and sometimes blurred vision. Fever is a sign of infection, not anaphylaxis.

Big idea: anaphylaxis is a life-threatening allergy treated with epinephrine.

questions.prompt: What are macrophages a longer living version of?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Neutrophils are short-lived phagocytes.
Incorrect. Mast cells release histamine.
Incorrect. Macrophages are phagocytes, but they develop from monocytes.
Correct. Macrophages develop from monocytes.
Incorrect. Interferons are proteins, not cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is monocytes. Monocytes are white blood cells in the blood.

When they leave the blood and enter tissues, they grow bigger and become macrophages, which can live for months. Neutrophils are also phagocytes but live only a few days.

Big idea: monocytes in the blood become macrophages in tissues.

questions.prompt: All nucleic cells in the body except for erythrocytes present with which MHC Class?

choices.explanation: Correct. All cells with a nucleus display MHC class I.
Incorrect. MHC II is only on antigen-presenting cells.
Incorrect. MHC class III genes code for proteins like complement, not surface displays.
Incorrect. Only class I is on all cells with a nucleus.
Incorrect. Class I is correct.

questions.explanation:
The answer is MHC class I. Every cell that has a nucleus displays MHC class I, which shows small pieces of the proteins the cell is making.

If a cell is infected or cancerous, cytotoxic T cells see the abnormal pieces and kill it. Red blood cells have no nucleus, so they do not display MHC I. MHC class II is found only on antigen-presenting cells.

Big idea: MHC I = almost every cell; MHC II = antigen-presenting cells.

questions.prompt: Which lymphatic organ is located at the sternum?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The spleen is in the upper left abdomen.
Correct. The thymus is behind the sternum.
Incorrect. The thyroid is an endocrine gland in the neck.
Incorrect. The skin is a barrier, not a lymphatic organ.
Incorrect. The parathyroids are endocrine glands in the neck.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the thymus. The thymus sits in the upper chest, right behind the sternum (breastbone). It is where T cells mature.

The spleen is in the belly, the thyroid and parathyroid are glands in the neck, and the skin is not a lymphatic organ.

Big idea: the thymus is a lymphatic organ behind the sternum.

questions.prompt: What is the most common immunoglobulin?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. IgA is the main antibody in secretions, not the most common in the blood.
Incorrect. IgD is rare and found on B cells.
Incorrect. IgE is the least common.
Correct. IgG is the most common antibody.
Incorrect. IgM is made first, but there is much less of it.

questions.explanation:
The answer is IgG. It makes up about 75–80% of the antibodies in the blood.

It gives long-lasting protection and is the only antibody that crosses the placenta. IgA is the most common in body secretions, but IgG is the most common overall in the blood.

Big idea: IgG is the main antibody in the blood.

questions.prompt: What do damaged cells release?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Chemokines are released too, but they are a subtype of cytokines.
Correct (per the key). Damaged cells release cytokines.
Incorrect. Interferons are mainly released by virus-infected cells.
Incorrect. Phagocytes are cells, not something released.
Incorrect. Macrophages are cells, not something released.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is cytokines, but this question is uncertain. When cells are damaged, they release chemical signals called cytokines, which start inflammation and call in immune cells.

Chemokines are a type of cytokine, so they are also released. Cytokines is the broader answer. Interferons are mainly released by virus-infected cells, and phagocytes and macrophages are cells, not chemicals.

Big idea: cytokines are the immune system's chemical messages.
questions.note: Uncertain: damaged cells release several mediators; chemokines (A) are a subset of cytokines, so B is the broader answer.

questions.prompt: Label the immune system diagram (labels A-L).
questions.explanation:
This diagram shows the lymphatic organs. In the neck are the cervical lymph nodes and the palatine tonsils. The right lymphatic duct drains the upper right part of the body, and the thoracic duct drains everything else.

The thymus sits in the chest behind the sternum and trains T cells. Lymph nodes cluster in the armpits (axillary) and groin (inguinal). The spleen is in the upper left belly. The appendix and Peyer's patches guard the gut. Bone marrow makes all blood cells. Lymphatic vessels connect everything. Some labels close together, like the two neck labels, are judgment calls.

Big idea: the lymphatic system is a network of vessels and organs that drains fluid and fights infection.
questions.note: Answers are listed in label order A-L. Uncertain: A vs H (both in the neck), E/F (cecum region) and L are judgment calls.

questions.prompt: The process in which cancer is spread to a new site is called _________________.
questions.explanation:
The answer is metastasis. Cancer cells break away from the original tumor, travel through the blood or lymph, and start new tumors somewhere else in the body.

Lymph nodes are often the first place cancer spreads.

Big idea: metastasis is what makes cancer much more dangerous.

questions.prompt: What is the complement system?
questions.answer: A group of about 30 plasma proteins (made mainly by the liver) that activate in a cascade via the classical, lectin or alternative pathways. They opsonize pathogens (C3b), promote inflammation and chemotaxis (C3a, C5a) and lyse cells through the membrane attack complex (C5b-C9).
questions.explanation:
The complement system is a group of about 30 proteins in the blood, mostly made by the liver. When activated by germs or antibodies, they switch each other on in a chain reaction (a cascade).

Complement proteins coat germs so phagocytes can eat them more easily (opsonization), call in white blood cells and increase inflammation, and build a 'membrane attack complex' that punches holes in bacteria to burst them.

Big idea: complement helps antibodies and phagocytes destroy germs.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of memory cells?
questions.answer: Memory B and T cells are long-lived cells that remember a specific antigen, so on re-exposure they produce a faster, stronger secondary response (the basis of long-term immunity and vaccines).
questions.explanation:
Memory cells are long-lived B cells and T cells that 'remember' a specific germ after the first infection or a vaccine.

If the same germ comes back, memory cells respond much faster and stronger (the secondary response), often stopping the infection before you feel sick.

Big idea: memory cells are the reason vaccines and past infections protect you.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of kinin?
questions.answer: Kinins (e.g. bradykinin) are inflammatory mediators that cause vasodilation, increase capillary permeability, stimulate pain receptors and help attract leukocytes.
questions.explanation:
Kinins, like bradykinin, are chemicals made during inflammation. They widen blood vessels and make capillaries leaky, causing redness and swelling.

They also trigger pain receptors (which is why injuries hurt) and help attract white blood cells.

Big idea: kinins help create the signs of inflammation.

questions.prompt: What are the causes of rheumatoid arthritis? Give a general overview of the disease.
questions.answer: RA is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial membrane of joints. Causes/risk factors: genetics (e.g. HLA-DR4), female sex, smoking, possibly infections. The inflamed synovium forms a pannus that erodes cartilage and bone, causing symmetric joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness and deformity, plus systemic effects (fatigue, nodules, lung and heart involvement).
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a long-lasting autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the lining of the joints (the synovial membrane). The inflamed lining thickens and slowly damages cartilage and bone.

Causes and risk factors include genes, being female, smoking, and possibly infections that trigger the immune system. Symptoms include painful, swollen joints on both sides of the body, morning stiffness, joint damage, and tiredness. It can also affect the lungs, heart, and eyes.

Big idea: RA is an autoimmune disease of the joints, unlike 'wear-and-tear' arthritis.

questions.prompt: List 7 parts of the body’s first line of defense and their role in the immune system.
questions.answer: Any seven: skin (physical barrier), mucous membranes (barrier), mucus (traps microbes), cilia (sweep mucus out), nasal hairs (filter), stomach acid (kills microbes), lysozyme in tears and saliva (breaks down bacterial walls), sweat/sebum (antimicrobial, acidic), normal flora (competition), urine flow (flushing).
questions.explanation:
Any seven of these: skin (a physical wall), mucous membranes (line openings), mucus (traps germs), cilia (sweep mucus out), nose hairs (filter air), stomach acid (kills swallowed germs), and lysozyme in tears and saliva (breaks down bacteria).

Also: sweat and skin oils (acidic and germ-killing), helpful normal bacteria (crowd out harmful ones), and urine flow (flushes germs out).

Big idea: the first line of defense keeps germs out before they enter the body.

questions.prompt: What is the humoral immune response in comparison to the cell- mediated immune response?
questions.answer: Humoral immunity: B cells become plasma cells that secrete antibodies, which act on extracellular pathogens and toxins in body fluids. Cell-mediated immunity: T cells (cytotoxic T cells, with helper T cells) directly destroy infected, cancerous or foreign cells; it targets intracellular pathogens and transplants. Helper T cells support both.
questions.explanation:
In the humoral response, B cells become plasma cells that release antibodies into body fluids. Antibodies work against germs and toxins outside of cells, like bacteria in the blood.

In the cell-mediated response, T cells do the work: cytotoxic T cells find and kill infected cells, cancer cells, or foreign transplanted cells. This works against germs hiding inside cells, like viruses. Helper T cells support both responses.

Big idea: humoral = antibodies outside cells; cell-mediated = T cells attacking infected cells.
